findings.title: reportPost skips the post-visibility rule every other post interaction enforces, leaking existence and author name of drafts/hidden/scoped posts
findings.expected: Every interaction that takes a postId runs canViewPost first (the H3 invariant: createComment, toggleLike, toggleBookmark, votePoll, toggleCommentLike, loadComments all do), so a member holding only an id learns nothing about a post they may not see.
findings.actual: reportPost fetches the post with a bare findUnique (select id + author.name) and proceeds. Any verified member can report an id for a DRAFT letter, an admin-hidden post, or a city/batch-scoped post outside their audience; the reply oracle distinguishes 'That post is already gone' from success, and success creates an AdminThread whose subject and opening line hand the reporter the AUTHOR'S NAME ('A post by <name>', visible to them at /messages/<threadId>).
findings.argument: report-action.ts lines 91-95: `prisma.post.findUnique({ where: { id: postId }, select: { id: true, author: { select: { name: true } } } })` with no canViewPost/decidePostVisibility call anywhere in the function; contrast src/lib/post-visibility.ts's header comment listing the six interaction paths that were fixed for exactly this hole (audit H3). openReportThread then writes the author name into the thread subject and the reporter's own notification.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient (grep reportPost for canViewPost: absent). Live: with a test account not in a letter's city scope, call reportPost(letterId, 'x') via the action endpoint and observe success plus a /messages thread naming the author, where opening /letters/<id> 404s.

findings.title: Hidden letters 404 for the admin and the author because letters/[id] checks isHidden before canViewPost, defeating both documented exemptions
findings.expected: decidePostVisibility deliberately admits the author (above the hidden check, 'the only way they can respond to the moderation', pinned by a test and listed in bugs.md Settled) and admits admins ('a moderator following a link from /admin/content lands on the post itself'). Commit 1c220ba's message repeats the admin promise.
findings.actual: Line 67 `if (!letter || letter.kind !== 'letter' || letter.isHidden) notFound();` runs BEFORE the canViewPost call at line 88, so a hidden letter answers 404 to everyone including its author and site admins. /admin/content links a hidden letter to /letters/<id> (src/lib/admin-content-query.ts:79), so the moderation list's own 'Open' action lands on the hoopoe 404; the author of a moderated letter likewise cannot reach it to edit or delete it.
findings.argument: The page pre-empts the shared rule with a local isHidden check; canViewPost (which would return ok for admin via the role exemption and for the author via the authorId exemption) is only consulted afterwards. Since plain posts have no reading page, letters are the ONE surface where the author/admin hidden-post exemptions could ever manifest, and this line makes both unreachable.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: as admin, hide any letter from /admin/content, then click its Open item -> expect 404. Code check: confirm decidePostVisibility returns ok:true for the same inputs (unit-testable without a DB via post-visibility-rule.ts).

findings.title: Comment counts on cards include blocked authors' comments while the thread excludes them
findings.expected: Owner decision (audit Low 78): a blocked member's comments leave the thread; every count shown next to a list agrees with the list's own filters.
findings.actual: The `_count.comments` filter is `{ isHidden: false, deletedAt: null }` with no AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING, while loadComments' VISIBLE_COMMENT (line 1367) adds `author: { isBlocked: false } }`. A post with comments from a since-blocked member shows e.g. '3' on the card and renders 2 in the thread (or a '[deleted]' stub). Same omission at feed/actions.ts:1256 (loadSavedPosts) and letters/[id]/page.tsx:61 (initialCommentCount on the letter page); letters/page.tsx:82 fetches the same wrong count but never renders it (dead weight).
findings.argument: Commit 1c220ba updated the list where-clauses and VISIBLE_COMMENT but not the three `_count: { select: { comments: { where: ... } } }` fragments, so the count and the thread now disagree exactly when a commenter is blocked. Note authorless (purged) comments are always deletedAt-stamped by tombstoneComments, so only the blocked case diverges.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: pick any post with comments, `SELECT count(*) FROM "Comment" WHERE "postId"=... AND "isHidden"=false AND "deletedAt" IS NULL` vs the same joined to User.isBlocked=false; or block a throwaway commenter account and compare the card number to the opened thread.

findings.title: Profile page ignores targetBatches: tab counts disagree with the tab lists, and the Photos grid shows images from posts outside the viewer's batch audience
findings.expected: The page's own comment says 'Same visibility contract as loadPosts()'s authorId path'. loadPosts applies batchScopeWhere plus the author exemption; profile counts and the Photos grid should match.
findings.actual: `visiblePostsWhere` (lines 144-153) filters isHidden/groupId/PUBLISHED_ONLY/cityScope but never batchScopeWhere. (a) postCount/letterCount count batch-targeted posts the Posts/Letters tab (ProfileAuthorFeed -> loadPosts) will not return to an out-of-batch viewer, so the switcher can read 'N posts' over an empty tab. (b) photoPosts (line 165) feeds the Photos grid from the same where, so images attached to a batch-targeted post are shown to viewers decidePostVisibility would refuse. (c) Related: for an admin viewing a blocked member's profile (allowed, Low 98), the counts include everything while loadPosts' unconditional AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING returns an empty list.
findings.argument: grep confirms batchScopeWhere/targetBatches appear nowhere in profile/[id]/page.tsx. targetBatches has no composer UI today but is an accepted, validated field on the public createPost action (postSchema line 229), and pre-existing targeted rows are enforced everywhere else, so the leak and the mismatch are both reachable.
findings.proofPlan: Live: create a post with targetBatches='ISC-1999' via the action from a test account with an image attached; view that profile from an account with a different batch: Photos grid shows the image and the count says 1 while the Posts tab is empty.

findings.title: Feed keyset pagination silently ends when the cursor post is deleted between pages
findings.expected: Load more continues from where the previous page ended even if a post on the boundary has since been deleted (charter edge: cursor at a deleted row).
findings.actual: The keyset uses Prisma's `cursor: { id }` + `skip: 1`. Prisma resolves the cursor by looking up that row's order-by values; when the row has been hard-deleted (author delete, admin deletePost, account purge cascade), the documented behaviour is that findMany returns NO results. rows=[] -> hasMore=false, nextCursor=null, and the member's infinite scroll quietly declares the feed finished with all older posts unreachable until a full reload. Same shape in loadComments (line 1414) where a purge can hard-delete a childless root comment that a reader is holding as a thread cursor.
findings.argument: Post deletion is a hard `post.delete` (deletePostWithImages line 78), so a cursor id can genuinely stop existing between two Load more clicks; the code never distinguishes 'empty because exhausted' from 'empty because the cursor vanished'. A hidden or blocked-author cursor row still exists so those survive; only true deletion breaks it.
findings.proofPlan: Live with throwaway data (or a rolled-back transaction is not possible through the app, so): create >21 posts on a test account, load page 1, delete the 20th post (the returned nextCursor id), call loadPosts with that cursor and observe an empty page with hasMore=false while older posts exist. Alternatively pin Prisma's behaviour with a one-off read-only findMany using a random nonexistent cursor id.

findings.title: @-mentions cannot find teachers: the shared people-search endpoint excludes them on a Catch-ups-only rationale, and its comment mis-states its consumers
findings.expected: Typing @ in the composer or a comment finds any member, teachers included (teachers are first-class authors across the feed, letters and comments).
findings.actual: The route filters `accountType: { notIn: ["teacher", "ex_teacher"] }`, justified by the comment 'This endpoint's only consumers are the Catch-ups people surfaces'. That claim is false: MentionDropdown (src/components/posts/mention-dropdown.tsx:50) fetches this exact endpoint for composer/comment @-mentions, so mentioning any teacher silently returns no results and the mention can never be inserted.
findings.argument: grep shows three consumers: use-user-search.ts (the two Catch-ups pickers) and mention-dropdown.tsx. The exclusion (owner decision 2026-08-18, scoped to Catch-ups invitations) was applied at the shared endpoint rather than at the Catch-ups callers, regressing mentions. Per the brief, a comment that mis-describes its code is itself bug evidence.
findings.proofPlan: Browser: in the feed composer type '@' plus a teacher account's name (a teacher exists in seed/live data); the dropdown stays empty while the same name resolves in the directory. Code: the three-consumer grep above.

findings.title: reportPost's report -> thread -> notify chain has no transaction; a mid-chain failure leaves a pending Report whose retry answers success without ever creating the thread
findings.expected: A report either fully materialises (Report row + AdminThread + reporter notification + admin notification) or the member's retry completes the missing parts.
findings.actual: report.create (line 130), openReportThread (two more writes), notifyAdmins and writeAudit run as four separate awaits with no $transaction. If openReportThread throws (pool timeout, dropped connection), the Report row exists with no thread and no notifications, and the member sees an error. On retry, the openAlready dedupe (line 114) finds the pending Report and returns `{ success: true, alreadyReported: true }` forever, so the thread and the admin page can never be created by the member again; it even selects `thread.id` and ignores that it is null. The report is only discoverable via /admin/reports, with no conversation attached.
findings.argument: Check-then-act dedupe keyed on the Report row treats the FIRST write of a four-write chain as proof the whole chain ran. The same shape exists in reportUser (line 210 onward) where the unique-index catch also returns success without a thread if the racing winner failed mid-chain.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices for the mechanism; to confirm consequence, read-only query for Report rows with status pending and no AdminThread (thread relation null) in the live DB - any hit is this bug already realised.

findings.title: Letters index lacks the author exemption the feed carries: an author who removes a city loses sight of their own scoped letter
findings.expected: Audit M30's rule, spelled out in loadPosts: the author is not part of their own audience, they are its source - a scoped post stays visible to its own author in every list. loadPosts implements this twice (feed/actions.ts:1044 and :1075).
findings.actual: The letters index where-clause applies `batchScopeWhere(userBatch)` and `AND [cityScopeWhere(viewerCities)]` with no `OR authorId: session.user.id` arm. A member who writes a letter scoped to a city and later removes that city from their UserPlace list (people move) sees the letter in the FEED and at its own URL, but it vanishes from /letters for them - three surfaces, two answers.
findings.argument: createPost validates cityScope against the author's UserPlace at write time, so the divergence only opens when the place list changes afterwards; nothing re-validates or exempts the author here. Same for a batch-targeted letter (crafted-call only today).
findings.proofPlan: Live with a test account: write a letter scoped to own city X, remove X in settings, load /feed (letter present) and /letters (letter absent).

findings.title: createPost's 10-second twin check compares only content/kind/status, so a same-caption different-photos (or different-poll/title) post is silently swallowed
findings.expected: The double-submit guard (audit M35) collapses only true duplicates; a second post that differs in any stored field is a new post.
findings.actual: The twin findFirst matches authorId+content+kind+status within DOUBLE_SUBMIT_MS (10s) and returns the FIRST post's id as success. A member sharing photos one at a time with the same short caption ('Beautiful!', '📸 today') inside 10 seconds gets 'Post shared!' while the second post - different images, different poll options, or a different letter title - was never created.
findings.argument: images/title/pollOptions/cityScope/targetBatches are absent from the twin where-clause (lines 232-240), and the success path (241-244) is indistinguishable to the client from a real create, so nothing on screen betrays the drop.
findings.proofPlan: Live: post twice within 10s with identical one-word content but different attached images from a test account; count Post rows (1, not 2) and note both submissions toasted success.

findings.title: Comment hearts have no in-flight guard and every toggle ignores the server's returned state, so double-taps and stale tabs desync the UI from the row
findings.expected: PostCard's likeBusy ref exists precisely so a double-tap cannot fire two racing toggles; a toggle's response carries the authoritative liked/bookmarked boolean for the client to reconcile with.
findings.actual: CommentItem.handleLike has no busy ref: two rapid taps send two toggleCommentLike calls; server delete-first semantics make the pair land as one like, while the optimistic UI ends on 'unliked' - heart and count point the wrong way until reload. Additionally all three toggle handlers (post like at post-card.tsx:167, bookmark at :207, comment like) discard result.liked/result.bookmarked on success, so a stale second tab that toggles inverts silently against the server.
findings.argument: The audit fixed the server half (B-040) and gave the POST heart a client guard; the comment heart never got it, and no success path reads the returned boolean anywhere.
findings.proofPlan: Browser: rapid double-click a comment heart on a slow connection (or throttled network); UI shows unliked, reload shows liked. Code diff of handleLike vs post-card's likeBusy pattern.

findings.title: Long posts are split at a hard 300-char boundary: formatting or a mention spanning it renders as raw markers, an emoji can split into lone surrogates, and the remainder starts on a new line mid-word
findings.expected: 'Read more' reveals the same rendering the full text would get; bold typed via the composer's live formatting always renders as bold.
findings.actual:
leadText/restText are `content.slice(0, 300)` / `content.slice(300)` rendered through renderRichText SEPARATELY (lines 350, 365). A `**bold**` pair, `@[Name](id)` mention, or ZWJ emoji crossing index 300 is cut: the emphasis never matches in either half so literal asterisks show even after expanding; a surrogate pair split yields U+FFFD; and because the remainder is a second

, the continuation begins on a new line at an arbitrary character.
findings.argument: String.slice counts UTF-16 units and the emphasis regexes require both delimiters in the same string; the composer serialises native bold to exactly these markers, so any member bolding a phrase around the 300th character of a long post hits it.
findings.proofPlan: Browser: post 350 chars with a bold span from char 290-310; the card shows literal ** in both collapsed and expanded states, and expanding breaks the line mid-word.

findings.title: Admins can read members' unpublished letter drafts by direct URL, while deleteDraft's comment asserts they cannot
findings.expected: feed/actions.ts:332-335 (deleteDraft): 'a draft is never visible to anyone else, admins included'. Drafts are private writing; publishDraft's rationale ('writing privately harms nobody') presumes nobody else reads them.
findings.actual: decidePostVisibility returns ok for `viewer.role === 'admin'` BEFORE the status !== 'published' check, so canViewPost admits an admin to any draft, and /letters/[id] then renders the full draft (with the 'Draft, only visible to you' banner, to an admin). No admin surface lists draft ids (admin content applies PUBLISHED_ONLY), so exposure needs an id, but the rule and the comment disagree - and the comment is the one stating the privacy promise.
findings.argument: Ordering in decidePostVisibility: admin exemption (line 180) precedes the draft refusal (line 207). Either the rule should refuse drafts to admins or the deleteDraft comment and the drafts privacy story are wrong; one of the two is a defect.
findings.proofPlan: Unit-level: call decidePostVisibility with an admin viewer and a status:'draft' post - returns ok:true. Browser: open another member's draft URL as admin (draft id from Prisma Studio) - page renders.

findings.title: Report dialog lets details reach 500 chars, then prefixes the reason so the combined string exceeds the server's 500 cap and the report is refused opaquely
findings.expected: A form that advertises a 500-char field submits successfully at 500 chars.
findings.actual: `fullReason = details ? `${reason}: ${details}` : reason` prepends the selected reason (~10-20 chars plus ': ') to details capped at maxLength=500 (line 97); report-action.ts:87 refuses `trimmed.length > 500` with 'Please provide a valid reason' - a member who filled the form to its own limit gets a dead-end error that names nothing they can fix.
findings.argument: Client cap and server cap measure different strings; the at-limit boundary (six-value rule) fails by exactly the prefix length.
findings.proofPlan: Browser: pick any reason, paste 495+ chars of details, submit - error toast despite the field accepting the text.

findings.title: Letter crash-net localStorage key is not account-scoped: the next person on a shared browser gets the previous member's unsaved letter restored into their composer
findings.expected: A private draft belt-and-braces copy is only ever offered back to the account that wrote it.
findings.actual: `draftKey = rv:letter-draft:${postId ?? 'new'}` carries no user id. Member A writes at /letters/new without saving (the 2.5s idle writer at line 263 stores content+title), signs out; member B signs in on the same browser, opens /letters/new, and the restore effect (line 270) silently loads A's words with 'Picked up where you left off' - A's private writing disclosed to B, and B may publish it under their own name.
findings.argument: Restore keys only on defaultLetter && !initialContent && the key's presence; sign-out does not clear it (clearLocalDraft only runs on a successful save).
findings.proofPlan: Browser: type in /letters/new as account A, wait 3s, sign out, sign in as B, open /letters/new - A's text appears.

findings.title: No length cap on the feed search term: loadPosts LIKE-scans title, content and author name with an unbounded pattern
findings.expected: Audit M44 capped the people-search q at FULL_NAME_MAX for exactly this reason ('a query string is public input'); the feed search is the same class of input.
findings.actual: `opts?.search` flows through escapeLike into three `contains` clauses with no slice or cap; the header pill's `?q=` and the action argument are both unbounded, so a member (or script inside the rate-unlimited read path) can hand Postgres a multi-hundred-KB pattern to run per post row per request.
findings.argument: escapeLike only escapes wildcards; ILIKE cost grows with pattern length times scanned text (content up to 20k chars per letter). loadPosts has no rate limit (reads are unmetered by design), so this is the one feed query where input size is entirely caller-chosen.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace plus, if desired, a single timed read-only loadPosts call with a 500KB q against the live route to measure the query_timeout margin.

findings.title: Replying to a reply notifies the root comment's author, not the person actually replied to, while the UI promises 'Replying to <them>'
findings.expected: The member the composer names ('Replying to B', comments-section.tsx:454) learns someone answered them.
findings.actual: Depth-1 promotion rewrites parentId to the ROOT before the notification block, so the 'replied to your comment' notification goes to the root author A; B - whose reply was tapped and whose name the composer displayed - is never notified, and A is told of a 'reply to your comment' that actually addresses B.
findings.argument: Line 781-783 reassigns `parentId = parent.parentId`; lines 843-864 then notify `parentComment.authorId` fetched by the promoted id. The original parent's author is never read again.
findings.proofPlan: Live with three test accounts: A roots, B replies, C taps Reply on B's reply and posts - check Notification rows: one for A, none for B.

findings.title: A draft's saved city audience silently widens to Everyone if the city was removed from the profile before a save lands
findings.expected: A save that cannot honour the chosen audience refuses or keeps the stored value; an audience never silently widens (B-048's whole point was the desk and the row agreeing).
findings.actual: editPost's cityScopeUpdate resolves the sent city against the author's current UserPlace list and folds a miss to `cityScope: null` (Everyone). If a member removes city X in settings while a draft scoped to X sits open in another tab, the next autosave (which sends cityScope unconditionally) clears the scope; the desk still shows 'X only', and publishing sends the letter to the whole community.
findings.argument: Line 564 `cityScopeUpdate = { cityScope: ownPlace?.city ?? null }` - validation failure and deliberate 'Everyone' are the same stored value, with no error and no signal back to the desk. Also related: the autosave effect (create-post-form.tsx:367) does not include audienceCity in its deps, so an audience-only change never autosaves at all.
findings.proofPlan: Live: save a draft scoped to own city X, delete X from settings in a second tab, type one character in the desk, wait for autosave, read the row's cityScope (null) while the desk chip still says X.

findings.title: No reference counting on post image bytes: the same owned URL attached to two rows lets deleting one purge the other's images
findings.expected: Deleting a post removes only bytes no live row still displays (the M17 invariant: never a live post with broken pictures).
findings.actual: ownedUploadUrls accepts any URL under uploads/<userId>/ including one already stored on an earlier post, and deletePostWithImages queues every parsed URL into PendingImagePurge unconditionally; the drain then deletes the object. A member who attaches the same own upload to two posts (crafted call today; also legacy pre-C2 URLs grandfathered onto drafts via the editPost path at line 508) and deletes one leaves the other permanently 404ing its photos.
findings.argument: No path checks whether another Post/Photo row references a URL before purging; the purge queue dedupe (if any) is by URL within one delete, not by cross-row reference.
findings.proofPlan: Live with a test account: createPost twice via the action with the same images JSON, delete post 1, fetch post 2's image URL - 404 from the image host.

findings.title: Home page's inline published Round reveals anonymous askers to Keepers (M10 fix incomplete)
findings.expected: Anonymity of question submission has no Keeper exception: the shared askerVisible() helper in src/lib/catchups.ts (created for audit M10) is the one place the rule lives, and the round reader (round/[editionId]/page.tsx:302-309) uses it with a comment saying 'Not p.showAsker || keeper, which is what this said until 2026-08-21'.
findings.actual: loadPublishedIssue() — the query that renders the published Round INLINE on the Catch-up home when the latest edition is published — computes `const askerVisible = p.showAsker || isKeeper;` (shadowing the imported helper, which the same file imports at line 22 and uses correctly at line 340 for the collecting/answering console). A Keeper viewing the home page of a just-published Round sees the name and bird avatar of every anonymous asker, in the payload and on screen. Secondary: a non-Keeper author of an anonymous question is denied their own byline here, which the shared helper grants.
findings.argument: The M10 fix was applied to round/[editionId]/page.tsx but the home page carries its own mirrored heavy query ('Mirrors the heavy query in round/[editionId]/page.tsx', line 83) with the pre-fix expression. The home is the surface every member lands on from the catchup_published notification path via the index card, so the two surfaces of the same Round disagree: /catchups/round/<id> hides the anonymous asker, /catchups/<id> names them to Keepers. The doc comment on askerVisible() in catchups.ts claims the home 'has always hidden them there too' — true only of the console prompt list, not of loadPublishedIssue. The stale pre-M10 rule is also still documented on CatchupPromptView.asker in src/lib/catchups-types.ts:132.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace only, no DB needed: diff [catchupId]/page.tsx:154-166 against round/[editionId]/page.tsx:301-321. Or in a browser: as a Keeper of a test Catch-up where a second test account submitted a question with 'Ask anonymously', publish the Round, open /catchups/<id> (asker shown) vs /catchups/round/<editionId> (asker hidden).

findings.title: Rejoining via the invite link never clears the personal bin, so the 30-day sweep still removes the member
findings.expected: A member who binned their copy (CatchupPref.deletedAt set) and then deliberately follows the invite link again has rejoined: the pending removal should be disarmed and notifications resume — exactly what addCatchupMembers does for people it adds (it clears archivedAt/deletedAt for newlyAdded, actions.ts:1724-1734).
findings.actual: joinCatchupByToken upserts the GroupMember row with `update: {}` and never touches CatchupPref. For a binned member (still a GroupMember until the sweep) the action returns success and the join page (src/app/catchups/join/[token]/page.tsx:99-105) silently redirects them into the Catch-up home, which renders normally. But deletedAt stays set: the index keeps the Catch-up in 'Recently deleted' instead of the active list, groupMemberIds() in catchups-notify.ts:56-64 keeps excluding them from every notification, and the nightly retention sweep (src/lib/retention.ts:187-208) deletes their GroupMember row when the 30 days run out — silently un-joining someone who explicitly rejoined.
findings.argument: The bin's semantics are 'delete = gentle leave in 30 days' (setCatchupDeleted docblock). Following the invite link is the natural 'I changed my mind' path — the same link lives in the group's chat — and both the action and the page treat an existing binned member as already-joined without disarming the countdown. addCatchupMembers explicitly handles this state for the Keeper-add path (with a comment saying re-listing an existing member must NOT un-bin them — but a member following the link themselves is their own consent, the case that comment's carve-out does not cover). leaveCatchup deletes the pref row, so a full leaver rejoining is clean; only the binned-not-yet-swept member hits this.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only query: SELECT from CatchupReminderPref where deletedAt is not null joined against GroupMember to show the state persists. Browser proof with a test account: bin a Catch-up (Recently deleted shows a countdown), follow its invite link, land on the home via redirect, return to /catchups — the card is still in Recently deleted with the countdown running.

findings.title: openAnswering has no accepted-prompt guard: a zero-question Round can be opened for answering, resurrecting the B-062 spam loop
findings.expected: The lazy advance refuses collecting -> answering when the Round has zero accepted prompts (planNextAction, catchups.ts:630-640: extend once, then dormant), because opening an empty Round 'would invite the whole group to answer nothing, then nudge every one of them daily for a week ... then publish an empty keepsake' (audit B-062). The Keeper's early trigger should evaluate the same guard — this file's own header says permissions and limits are 'enforced in the action', never trusted from the client.
findings.actual: openAnswering builds answeringPatch and CASes only on status='collecting' — it never counts prompts. The UI hides the button when no accepted prompt exists (catchup-home-shell.tsx:123-127), but a stale tab (Keeper B's page rendered before Keeper A removed the last question via curatePrompt — two-Keeper Catch-ups are a supported feature via setCatchupKeeper) or a direct action call opens answering on an empty Round: 7-day window, daily catchup_reminder to every member about zero questions, /answer shows 'No questions in this Round yet', 0 entries at close triggers the too-few extension (+3 days, re-notify everyone), then an empty Round publishes and notifies the whole group, and nextOpensAt schedules the next cycle.
findings.argument: answeringPatch (catchups.ts:469-476) carries no prompt-count knowledge; the count guard lives only in planNextAction, which openAnswering bypasses by design (it is the early trigger). There is no reverse transition, so once opened empty there is no recovery besides riding the loop out or pausing forever. closeAndPrepare took the mirror-image care (it re-evaluates shouldExtendForTooFew exactly like the natural close, actions.ts:1106-1109); openAnswering did not get the mirror of the no-questions rule.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: confirm no prompt count between actions.ts:1076 (status check) and 1083 (transaction). Browser proof on a test Catch-up: as Keeper with the question list open in two tabs, remove the only question in tab 1, click 'Open answering' in tab 2 — it succeeds and the Round is answering with zero prompts.

findings.title: MAX_CATCHUP_PEOPLE caps each call's argument, not the roster: a Catch-up can grow without bound
findings.expected: catchup-caps.ts describes MAX_CATCHUP_PEOPLE (100) as 'The one number for how many people a Catch-up may hold' and 'the reach limit as much as the roster limit' — i.e. a ceiling on the group's size and on notification fanout.
findings.actual: createCatchupWithPeople enforces 100 at creation, but addCatchupMembers only validates `userIds` (the array passed to THIS call) against the max — it never reads the current member count. A Keeper adding 100 at a time repeatedly grows the roster past any bound (100 -> 200 -> ...). joinCatchupByToken is also uncapped, so a widely-forwarded link grows it too. Every notification trigger then fans out createMany over the full membership inside advanceEdition's transaction, and the daily reminder deletes+recreates rows for the whole set.
findings.argument: The M29 fix ('Same ceiling as creation: adding is the same reach', actions.ts:1659) capped per-call reach, which does not implement the invariant the constant's own module documents. At the 2,000-user ceiling the absolute worst case (one Catch-up holding everyone) is ~2,000 notification rows per trigger — survivable but exactly the forced-enrolment broadcast the 100 cap was argued to prevent, and the comment/code disagreement means the next reader believes a guarantee that does not exist.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: actions.ts:1660-1667 has no groupMember.count. Read-only query: SELECT groupId, count(*) FROM "GroupMember" GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC against catchup groups to see whether any roster already exceeds 100. Test-account proof: two successive addCatchupMembers calls of 100 distinct ids both succeed.

findings.title: A Catch-up can be left permanently Keeperless once createdById is null; the spec's re-adopt rule is implemented nowhere
findings.expected: Spec section 7: 'If the Keeper leaves and createdById goes null, any remaining member may act as Keeper / re-adopt it.' Every path that removes the last role-holder should either refuse or promote a successor (chooseGroupSuccessor exists for exactly this rule).
findings.actual: chooseGroupSuccessor is called ONLY from account-purge (src/lib/account-purge.ts:61). Two paths strand a Catch-up with no effective Keeper: (1) leaveCatchup's founder refusal is `if (ctx.catchup.createdById && createdById === viewerId)` — once the creator's account was purged (createdById SetNull) that guard is inert, so the promoted successor (or last 'keeper'/'admin' role-holder) can leave, and nothing promotes anyone; (2) the retention sweep (src/lib/retention.ts:201-203) deletes the GroupMember rows of binned copies with no succession check, so sweeping the last role-holder does the same. isEffectiveKeeper then returns false for every member, loadKeeperScope refuses everyone, and setCatchupKeeper — the only way to mint a new Keeper — itself requires an existing Keeper. Rounds keep auto-cycling forever with no one able to curate, extend, pause or end.
findings.argument: createdById null is a reachable state (purge SetNull is in the schema at Catchup.createdBy). After purge, succession promotes one member — but that person can then leaveCatchup freely (the refusal checks createdById, not 'am I the last effective Keeper'), and removeCatchupMember protects only the creator. There is no admin repair surface either: /admin/catchups is read-only oversight ('No keeper' is rendered as a meta line, admin/catchups/page.tsx:138, with no control next to it).
findings.proofPlan: Read-only query: catchups where createdById IS NULL and no GroupMember of that group has role in ('admin','keeper') — any row is already stranded. Code trace for the reachable path: purge creator (succession promotes X with role 'admin'/'keeper') -> X calls leaveCatchup -> guard at actions.ts:1818 passes because createdById is null.

findings.title: advanceEdition failures are console-only while the sibling swallow points report to Sentry (M09 fix incomplete)
findings.expected: Audit M09's principle, written into this same file: the engine's swallowed failures must be 'Reported, not just logged: this is the engine, and nobody notices it stop -- the symptom is Rounds that never open.' advanceDueCatchups' outer catch and openNextRoundIfDue both call report() (Sentry).
findings.actual: advanceEdition — the function that performs every transition, extension and reminder — swallows all its own errors with `console.error("[catchups] advanceEdition failed", err)` and returns. Because it never throws, the reporting catch in advanceDueCatchups can never see these failures. A systematic failure inside applyEditionAction (e.g. the notification createMany hitting a constraint, or a transaction timeout on every attempt) would leave Rounds stuck at their deadlines with nothing in Sentry; the only trace is Vercel function logs nobody watches.
findings.argument: The M09 remediation added report() to two of the three swallow points in this file and left the widest one on console.error. The nightly cron and every page view route through advanceEdition, so this is precisely the 'engine failing on every page view with no outward sign' scenario M09 describes. The admin 'Past its date' page would eventually surface the symptom, but only if an admin looks.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: catchups.ts:1087-1090 vs :1186-1191 and :1194-1200. Confirm report-error.ts routes to Sentry and that console.error inside a Vercel function does not.

findings.title: Revoking the Keeper hat overwrites a legacy group-admin role with 'member', silently stripping group moderation
findings.expected: setCatchupKeeper's own docblock: the Catch-up Keeper hat and the group 'admin' role must stay decoupled, because 'admin' is read outside this feature (deletePost lets a group admin delete anyone's post in that group). Granting writes 'keeper' precisely to preserve that separation; revoking should be equally careful.
findings.actual: setCatchupKeeper(catchupId, userId, false) runs updateMany({ where: { groupId, userId }, data: { role: "member" } }) unconditionally. On a Catch-up attached to a legacy real group (batch groups still exist and createCatchup(groupId) still creates on them), toggling the hat off for a member whose row is role 'admin' demotes them from group admin to member — removing their deletePost moderation over that group's posts as a side effect of a Catch-ups control. The decoupling the comment defends holds in the grant direction only.
findings.argument: The where clause matches any membership row regardless of current role; there is no `role: 'keeper'` predicate, which is the one-word fix shape (`where: { groupId, userId, role: "keeper" }`). The UI likely renders the toggle 'on' for admins (isEffectiveKeeper honours 'admin'), making the off-click natural for a Keeper tidying the list.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only query: any GroupMember with role='admin' in a group that has a Catchup and is not the catchup creator (the creator is guarded at actions.ts:1943). Code trace of the where clause is sufficient to confirm the mechanism.

findings.title: nudgeGroup is unmetered despite whole-group fanout that bypasses 'off' preferences
findings.expected: Actions that fan out to a whole group are metered — createCatchup and createCatchupWithPeople both call rateLimit("catchups", ...) citing audit M2, and the bucket exists (rate-limit.ts:75, 5/hour).
findings.actual: nudgeGroup notifies every non-answerer, bypassing reminderMode 'off' by design, with no rate limit and no cooldown. A Keeper (or a script holding a Keeper session) can call it in a loop; each call deletes and recreates the reminder rows (notifyReminder's replace semantics prevent build-up in the bell but each recreation re-marks them unread), re-pinging up to the whole roster arbitrarily often — the one notification the member explicitly turned off.
findings.argument: notifyReminder with bypassOff:true has no coalescing window (the delete+create pair runs fresh every call, catchups-notify.ts:157-198). The blast radius is one group, which is why this is Low rather than Medium, but it is the same reach the creation meter exists for.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: actions.ts:1989-2026 contains no rateLimit call; compare :348 and :452. Test-account proof: two immediate nudges both succeed and both re-unread the reminder.

findings.title: submitEntry's status check is separated from its write by the 3s Spotify fetch, so answers can land after close
findings.expected: Spec 3.4: 'entries lock at close.' The answering-status check should hold when the row is written, or the write should carry its own guard (the transitions all CAS on status for exactly this reason).
findings.actual: The `edition.status !== "answering"` check (line 1352) is followed by resolveSpotify — a network call with a 3-second timeout (line 1389) — before the unguarded upsert (line 1398). A Keeper's closeAndPrepare, or the clock-driven advance from any concurrent page view, can move the Round to preparing in that window; the entry is then created or updated after close and appears in the published Round. The empty-row delete at line 1433 is similarly unguarded.
findings.argument: Every state transition in this feature is compare-and-swapped, but the entry write trusts a snapshot that is up to ~3s old whenever a song is attached (and a few ms old otherwise). Consequence is bounded — the answer appears in the Round it was written for, seconds late — hence Low, but it is the one write into a live Round with no status predicate. A conditional shape (guard the upsert on the edition still being 'answering', e.g. by re-checking inside a transaction) closes it.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of the ordering (1352 -> 1389 -> 1398). Deterministic repro without load: stub resolveSpotify latency locally, submit an entry with a songUrl, and run closeAndPrepare from a second session during the fetch; the entry row exists with the edition in 'preparing'.

findings.title: Extending the deadline of a dormant Round extends from the long-dead deadline: success reported, nothing changes
findings.expected: A Keeper pressing 'extend by N days' on a Round in collecting expects the question window to reopen for N days — the control exists to buy time.
findings.actual: A dormant Round (collecting, questionsCloseAt long past, extension bit spent) still renders the ExtendDeadlineCard (catchup-home-shell.tsx:111-121 gates only on status collecting/answering) and extendDeadline accepts it. extendPhasePatch computes the new deadline from the OLD deadline (`from = ms(ed.questionsCloseAt) ?? now`), so on a Round dormant for longer than the chosen extension (max 7 days) the new questionsCloseAt is still in the past: the CAS applies, the action returns success ('deadline extended'), and the Round remains dormant. The Keeper gets a success toast for a no-op.
findings.argument: Extend-from-deadline is the right semantics for a LIVE window (the docblock argues it well), but it silently degenerates once the deadline is stale by more than the extension. The answering phase cannot hit this (loadFreshEdition auto-advances a stale answering Round to preparing first, and extendDeadline then refuses); only the dormant-collecting state, which advanceEdition deliberately leaves in place, exposes it. The intended dormant revival path is submitPrompt's first-question reset, but the extend control sits on screen implying it works.
findings.proofPlan: Pure-function check, no DB: extendPhasePatch({status:'collecting', questionsCloseAt: now-30d, ...}, 7, now) returns questionsCloseAt = now-23d, and computeStatus on the patched row with prompts=0 still yields the dormant 'none' plan. UI proof on a test dormant Round: press extend, get the success toast, watch nothing change.

findings.title: submitPrompt's cap-check comment overstates the transaction: two concurrent submissions can both pass the 40 cap and mint duplicate positions
findings.expected: The comment claims 'inside the same transaction as the cap check so two questions arriving together cannot both see room for the last slot.'
findings.actual: Under Postgres READ COMMITTED (the default; nothing requests Serializable here), two concurrent transactions each run the aggregate, each read _count=39 and _max=38, and each insert: the Round ends at 41 accepted prompts and two prompts share position 39. A plain transaction does not serialize a count-then-insert. The 40 cap is a runaway ceiling so the overshoot is harmless; the duplicate position is tolerated by the createdAt tiebreak on the answer page and reader — but NOT on the home console, whose query has no orderBy (loadHome's `prompts: { include: ... }`, [catchupId]/page.tsx:265-269) and whose sort compares position only, so tied rows can shuffle between renders (the exact symptom audits Lows 27/34/57 fixed on the other two surfaces).
findings.argument: Per the audit charter, a comment that mis-describes its own guard is itself the finding: the next session will trust the claimed serialization. The `wasFirst` flag (dormant revival) read from the same count has the same race, though its conditional updateMany already caps the damage to one deadline reset.
findings.proofPlan: Mechanism is provable from Postgres semantics (no SERIALIZABLE/FOR UPDATE in the transaction). A rolled-back two-connection test through run-sql.mjs (orchestrator only) reproduces the double-insert; for the render shuffle, a Round with two same-position prompts re-rendered twice can show them swapped on the home console.

findings.title: Hearting an ex-member's answer notifies them with a link their own membership loss 404s
findings.expected: A leaver's or removed member's published answers stay (owner decision), and leaving 'stops your notifications' (leaveCatchup docblock) — including future ones about this Catch-up.
findings.actual: notifyLove checks only self-love; toggleEntryLove (actions.ts:1496-1506) checks the LIKER's membership but not the AUTHOR's. Hearting an answer whose author has since left (or been removed) creates a catchup_love notification for them linking to /catchups/round/<editionId>, and the round page notFound()s non-members (round/[editionId]/page.tsx:178-179). clearCatchupNotifications at leave time only clears rows that already exist; this one arrives after. The ex-member gets a bell item that dead-ends in the hoopoe 404.
findings.argument: The audience-derivation helper (groupMemberIds) that every broadcast trigger routes through is bypassed by notifyLove, which addresses one user directly. A one-line membership (or binned-pref) check on the author before creating the row closes it.
findings.proofPlan: Test accounts: A answers, Round publishes, A leaves via leaveCatchup, B hearts A's answer; A's bell shows the love notification and clicking it 404s. Or read-only: confirm no groupMember check in notifyLove/toggleEntryLove.

findings.title: Reminder copy and answer-page copy disagree about 'last day' near the close boundary (24h windows vs IST calendar days)
findings.expected: The bell and the page it links to describe the same deadline the same way. Audit Low 28 moved the answer page's label to IST calendar days (valleyDaysBetween) precisely because ceil-on-milliseconds called things a day early.
findings.actual: dueReminder/daysLeftUntil still count 24-hour windows: daysLeft=1 ('Last day to answer {group}'s Catch-up') begins exactly 24h before answersCloseAt. closesLabel on the answer page (answer/page.tsx:56-69) counts IST calendar days: until midnight IST of the close day it says 'Answers close tomorrow.' For a Round whose close time-of-day is in the IST morning (the cron-advanced case closes at 07:30 IST, so most quiet-group Rounds), the member receives 'Last day to answer' and taps through to a page saying 'close tomorrow' — a contradiction that persists from close-minus-24h until midnight IST, ~16 hours.
findings.argument: The two computations were deliberately split (Low 28 touched only the label), but the reminder message text is calendar language ('Last day') driven by window arithmetic. Either the reminder should bucket on valley days, or its copy should avoid calendar words. The 'reminderMode: last' filter (isLastDay = days <= 1, catchups-notify.ts:175) inherits the same skew: 'last only' members are pinged on what the site itself calls the day before.
findings.proofPlan: Pure-function check: daysLeftUntil(close=tomorrow 07:30 IST, now=today 09:00 IST) = 1 while valleyDaysBetween(close, now) = 1 -> 'close tomorrow'; compare the two rendered strings. No DB needed.

findings.title: JWT session cookie never refreshes: every member is hard signed out 30 days after sign-in, regardless of activity
findings.expected: NextAuth's default 30-day session is documented (in @auth/core init.js) as '30 days of being idle' — the idle clock is meant to reset because the /api/auth/session endpoint re-signs the JWT and re-sets the cookie with a fresh expiry on every read. An active member should stay signed in indefinitely.
findings.actual: Nothing in this app ever hits the session endpoint: there is no SessionProvider and no useSession anywhere in src (grep confirmed), and next-auth/react's signIn only calls __NEXTAUTH._getSession which is a no-op (() => {}) without a provider. Server-side auth() goes through the RSC branch of node_modules/next-auth/lib/index.js (getSession(...).then(parseSessionResponse)) which DROPS the Set-Cookie refresh — RSC renders and server actions never apply it. So the cookie's Expires and the JWT's exp both stay fixed at sign-in time + 30 days. A member who signs in on launch day and uses the site daily is silently signed out on day 30 (a synchronized wave for everyone who joined the same week), potentially mid-composition; the next server action returns 'Not authenticated' and the next navigation bounces to /login.
findings.argument: src/lib/auth.ts:256-258 sets session: { strategy: 'jwt' } with no maxAge (default 30d, @auth/core/lib/init.js:38). The only code path that refreshes a JWT cookie is @auth/core/lib/actions/session.js:45-51 (re-encode + sessionStore.chunk with newExpires), reachable only via GET /api/auth/session; no app code fetches it. next-auth/lib/index.js RSC branch returns parseSessionResponse(authResponse) and discards authResponse's Set-Cookie headers. Related nit: src/app/api/dev-login/route.ts:42's comment 'Matches the session.maxAge in src/lib/auth.ts' — auth.ts sets no maxAge; it matches the library default.
findings.proofPlan: Sign in with a test account in a browser; record the __Secure-authjs.session-token cookie's Expires and the decoded JWT exp. Browse several pages and run a server action; re-read the cookie: Expires is unchanged. Optionally set session.maxAge to 2 minutes locally and confirm active browsing does not extend it (redirect to /login at minute 2).

findings.title: Blocked member can complete the password-reset flow and is told 'we are signing you in now', then every sign-in refuses with 'Invalid email or password' — an endless misleading loop
findings.expected: A blocked member's recovery flows either say something coherent or refuse consistently; a flow should not claim success it cannot deliver, and the one action a blocked member takes to 'fix' their login should not appear to work while sign-in stays impossible.
findings.actual: requestPasswordReset (line 258 findUnique selects id/name/email/password — never isBlocked) mails a blocked member a real reset link. resetPassword (line 373 transaction) also never checks isBlocked: it changes the password, stamps emailVerified, bumps credentialVersion, queues the 'password moved' mail, and returns ok — the reset page shows 'That's done. Your new password is saved and we are signing you in now.' The auto sign-in then hits src/lib/auth.ts:185-191 (isBlocked after a CORRECT bcrypt compare) and returns null → generic 'Invalid email or password'; reset-client.tsx:143 falls back to /login, where the brand-new password is again 'invalid'. The member cycles reset → success → invalid forever with no signal anywhere that the account is blocked. Possibly deliberate secrecy about blocks (H4 records 'blocked' only for admin analytics), but the reset flow's explicit success promise contradicts it.
findings.argument: No isBlocked reference exists anywhere in email-actions.ts (grep). authorize's blocked branch (auth.ts:185) is the only refusal, mapped by login-client.tsx:409 to the generic sentence because a blocked refusal returns null (no CredentialsSignin code). The 2026-08-20 H4 work wired blocking at the door and in the session callback but never into the reset flow.
findings.proofPlan: Create a throwaway account via signup, block it from the admin panel, then run forgot-password → reset-password end to end: confirm the reset mail arrives, the reset reports success, and the immediate auto sign-in plus a manual login with the new password both show 'Invalid email or password'. Also confirm User.emailVerified was stamped by the reset on the blocked row.
findings.taxonomy: deleted/blocked-user references / state-machine gap across flows

findings.title: Three auth clients await server actions with no try/catch — a rejected action strands the form on a disabled busy button forever (the exact B-042 class already fixed elsewhere with callAction)
findings.expected: Audit B-042 established the pattern: every client await of a server action goes through callAction (or try/catch) so a rejected fetch (dropped network, deploy skew, server 500) surfaces an error and re-enables the form. verify-email-banner.tsx:97, verify-email-dialog.tsx:104, trivia-gate.tsx and both sign-in/signup forms all follow it.
findings.actual: Three auth surfaces bypass it: reset-client.tsx:117 (`const result = await resetPassword({ token, password })` after setBusy(true), no try/catch — rejection leaves 'Saving...' disabled forever, and since resetPassword can also throw AFTER the password committed (see companion finding), the member may not learn their password actually changed); forgot-client.tsx:90 (`await requestPasswordReset(formData)` after setSending(true) — stuck 'Sending...'); verify-client.tsx:110 (`await resendVerification()` inside handleResend with setBusy(true) and no try/finally — stuck 'Sending...'). These are exactly the pages used by people on flaky connections in a stressed moment; the only recovery is a full page reload.
findings.argument: A server action invoked from an event handler that rejects (network failure, deploy skew, uncaught server error) produces an unhandled promise rejection — no error boundary catches event-handler rejections — so the code after the await, including every setBusy(false)/setError call, never runs. login-client.tsx:365-428 and signup-form.tsx:395-476 wrap the same shape in try/catch; these three do not.
findings.proofPlan: In dev tools, load /reset-password with a valid token, switch the network to offline, submit: the button sits on 'Saving...' permanently with no message and a console unhandled-rejection. Repeat on /forgot-password and the /verify-email resend button.
findings.taxonomy: unhandled promise rejection / missing catch on client await

findings.title: resetPassword awaits two post-commit writes with no catch, so a transient DB error after the password has changed turns success into a thrown action — and the adjacent comment claims the opposite ('never awaited for success')
findings.expected: Once the burn-token-plus-set-password transaction commits (line 373-409), nothing best-effort should be able to convert the success into an error: the comment at line 429-430 states the password-changed mail is 'Queued rather than sent, and never awaited for success: a mail failure must not undo a password change that has already been written.'
findings.actual: Both `await burnTokens(peek.userId, 'reset')` (line 424) and `await enqueueMail({ kind: 'password-changed', ... })` (line 431) are plainly awaited with no try/catch, and enqueueMail performs up to three DB statements (fold findFirst, count, create) that throw on a pool/network error. A throw here also skips mintHumanPass (line 442), so even if the client handled the rejection, the auto sign-in would fail the bot check (no widget renders on /reset-password). The member's link is burned, their sessions are ended, the password IS changed — but they are shown nothing (companion finding: reset-client has no catch) and a retry says 'That link has already been used.' The comment mis-describes the code, which is itself evidence per this audit's brief: the intent (fire-and-forget) was written down and not implemented.
findings.argument: prisma.$transaction at 373 commits before line 424 runs; tryRosterAutoVerifyQuietly (421) and the later writeAudit-style helpers swallow their own errors, but burnTokens (auth-tokens.ts:266-271) and enqueueMail (email-queue.ts:438-494) do not. Any Prisma error between commit and return propagates out of the 'use server' function.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices (mechanism is unconditional); to demonstrate live, wrap enqueueMail with a dev-only forced throw after the transaction in a scratch branch and run the reset flow: password changes, client sticks on 'Saving...'. Fix shape: try/catch (log) around lines 424-436, or move both behind after().
findings.taxonomy: errors thrown after commit / comment mis-describes code

findings.title: A mail scanner's GET auto-confirms an email address: /verify-email redeems the token during render, so a hostile signup with someone else's address is 'confirmed' by the victim's link-scanning gateway without any human click
findings.expected: Email confirmation proves the mailbox OWNER acted. Corporate/consumer mail gateways (Outlook SafeLinks, some AV appliances) issue GETs against every link in inbound mail; a confirmation that flips state on bare GET is granted by the scanner, not the person.
findings.actual: VerifyEmailPage calls confirmEmailToken(token) unconditionally during server render of a GET (line 31), and confirmEmailToken (email-actions.ts:180-203) claims the token and sets User.emailVerified in one transaction. So: attacker signs up with victim@corp.example (passes trivia + Turnstile), the confirmation mail lands in the victim's inbox, the gateway prefetches the link, and the attacker's account clears the Stage-1 email gate (posting, uploads, admin-thread messages) with the victim never having clicked. The B-021/Low-22 work handled prefetch GRACEFULLY (used → already/superseded) but kept confirm-on-GET as a deliberate one-click design ('a confirm button asks somebody to click twice'), so this may be settled — flagging because the hostile-signup consequence, as opposed to the double-click one, is not argued anywhere in the comments.
findings.argument: confirmEmailToken's claim (tx.authToken.updateMany where usedAt null + tx.user.update emailVerified) runs for any bearer of the URL; there is no POST step, no session requirement (deliberately public), and no interaction gate. Stage-2 verification and admin review still stand between such an account and contact details, which bounds the damage.
findings.proofPlan: Against dev: sign up a throwaway with a second address you control, take the printed dev link (email:dev console output), and fetch it with curl -s (a bare GET, no JS); read the row: emailVerified is set. Decision for the owner: keep one-click (accept scanner-confirms) or add a confirm button POST.

findings.title: sendTimeLabel's docstring says 'Formatted in the BROWSER's timezone' while the code pins VALLEY_TIME_ZONE; the rendered 'tomorrow at 5:30 am' carries no IST marker for members abroad
findings.expected: The comment and code agree, and a clock time shown to a member in another timezone is either in their local time (as the docstring claims) or labelled with its zone.
findings.actual: Lines 38-43 document 'Formatted in the BROWSER's timezone: the server cannot know where the reader is', but line 49 passes timeZone: VALLEY_TIME_ZONE, so the label is always the IST clock face. The inner comment at 54-56 acknowledges the pin ('that is the day the time above is now printed in'), so the code is internally consistent (IST time + valleyDayKey day) — only the docstring lies, which is exactly the comment-drift class this audit is told to treat as evidence. User-visible edge: a member in New York whose confirmation queued reads 'Your link goes out tomorrow at 5:30 am' and reasonably expects 5:30 am local (the real send is ~8 pm their today). Matches the project-wide valley-day policy, so the copy may be deliberate; the docstring is not.
findings.argument: The function is shared by the banner and the dialog; useSyncExternalStore hydration wiring is correct. The defect is the stale first paragraph plus the unlabelled zone in the rendered string.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: compare lines 38-43 against 49. For the copy question, render the queued state with a browser timezone set to America/New_York and read the sentence.

findings.title: An account with password NULL is permanently stranded: login refuses ('no-password-set') and the reset flow silently refuses to mail it, so there is no self-service path to set a first password
findings.expected: Either no such rows can exist, or the one flow whose job is 'I cannot sign in' (forgot-password) offers the path to set a first password — auth.ts:159-161 explicitly calls this person 'an invited member who never finished signing up. Different problem, different help', but no different help exists.
findings.actual: requestPasswordReset line 265: `if (!user?.password) return { ok: true }` — a passwordless row gets the same 'link is on its way' screen and no mail, ever. authorize (auth.ts:158-171) refuses with the generic sentence. The LoginAttempt reason 'no-password-set' exists purely to let the owner notice from analytics. Nothing in the app mints such rows today (settings/actions.ts comment: 'nothing mints these today'), so this is latent — it bites the day an import script, invite feature, or hand-inserted row creates one, and the member's only path is messaging the admin, which they cannot do signed out.
findings.argument: The refusal is deliberate for the membership-oracle property (same { ok: true } either way), but the branch conflates 'no account' with 'account that needs a first password'; mailing a reset link to the latter would leak nothing (the address demonstrably has an account-holder reading it) and resetPassword already works against a NULL password column (it only writes).
findings.proofPlan: Read-only query: SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE password IS NULL — if zero, file as latent with the invite/import warning; if nonzero, those members are live dead-ends. Then trace: requestPasswordReset with such an address enqueues nothing.

findings.title: Profile tab counts and Photos grid ignore batch targeting (and two more visibility-contract gaps)
findings.expected: The page comment says visiblePostsWhere applies 'the same visibility contract as loadPosts()'s authorId path' for the tab counts AND the Photos grid, so a batch-targeted post should be invisible (photos included) to viewers outside its target batch, and counts should equal what the list shows.
findings.actual: visiblePostsWhere (lines 144-153) contains NO batchScopeWhere fragment at all, no author-exemption in its city filter, and no AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING. Three concrete divergences from loadPosts (feed/actions.ts:1042-1077): (1) a batch-targeted post's PHOTOS render in the profile Photos grid (lines 165-173) and are counted, for any confirmed viewer outside the target batch, while decidePostVisibility would refuse the same post as 'other-batch'; (2) on your OWN profile, your own city-scoped post for a city you no longer list is counted OUT (cityScopeWhere without the {authorId} exemption loadPosts carries per audit M30) but listed IN, so the segment badge disagrees with the list; (3) an admin viewing a blocked member's profile sees nonzero counts over an empty list (loadPosts applies AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING unconditionally, the counts never do).
findings.argument: Compare page.tsx visiblePostsWhere {authorId, isHidden:false, groupId:null, PUBLISHED_ONLY, AND:[cityScopeWhere(viewerCities)]} against loadPosts' baseWhere+top-level OR: loadPosts adds OR:[batchScopeWhere(userBatch).OR..., {authorId: session.user.id}] (feed/actions.ts:1063-1077) and AND:[{OR:[cityScopeWhere, {authorId: session.user.id}]}] (1042-1046) and AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING (1056). The counts (158-162) and photoPosts query (165-170) use only visiblePostsWhere, so batch-targeted image posts flow into photos/photoCount for everyone, and the profile's own posts count applies a stricter city filter than the list. The images render directly (raw at line 340), so this is content shown outside its declared audience, not just a wrong number.
findings.proofPlan: Test account A posts a photo post with targetBatches='ISC-2004'. Sign in as test account B (batch 2010, email-confirmed): open A's profile — the Photos tab shows the image and the counts include the post while the All/Posts list omits it. For the city case: as A, add city X, post with cityScope X, remove city X; A's own profile list shows the post but the count is one lower.

findings.title: Pasting a full Instagram URL stores it verbatim and renders a double-prefixed dead link
findings.expected: A member pasting their full profile URL ('https://instagram.com/ananya') into the Instagram contact row gets a working link, the way the linkedin/facebook/website kinds do (those check for an http(s) prefix before prepending).
findings.actual: socialHref returns early for kind 'instagram' with `https://instagram.com/${v.replace(/^@/, "")}` BEFORE the startsWith('http') check that every other kind gets, so a pasted URL becomes 'https://instagram.com/https://instagram.com/ananya' (a 404 on instagram.com) and socialDisplay shows '@https://instagram.com/ananya'. Nothing normalizes on write either: updateContactMethods (profile-actions.ts:326) stores instagram as typed, the contacts editor (contacts-editor.tsx) has no per-kind normalization, and validators.ts only caps it at 100 chars — a full URL fits.
findings.argument: social.ts lines 11-17: `if (kind === "instagram") return ...` precedes `if (v.startsWith("http://") || v.startsWith("https://")) return v;`. The profile page builds the Get in touch method from it at profile/[id]/page.tsx:260-261. The editor placeholder says '@handle' but there is no validation rejecting or normalizing a URL, so the broken state saves silently and ships on the public profile. The inverse hole exists for linkedin/facebook: a bare handle ('john-doe') becomes 'https://john-doe', a dead hostname.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient, or: on a test account, save 'https://instagram.com/anything' in the Instagram row, open the profile's Get in touch sheet, inspect the anchor href — it reads instagram.com/https://instagram.com/anything.

findings.title: adminUpdatePerson writes batchYear without re-deriving batchType, so the credential drifts and batch-targeted visibility breaks
findings.expected: batchType is 'derived, never typed' and must be re-derived whenever batchYear or yearLeft moves — updateProfileField (profile-actions.ts:185-198) does exactly this so 'the credential can never drift out of step with the years', and registerUser derives it at signup.
findings.actual: adminUpdatePerson updates {name, accountType, batchYear, birdOverride} (lines 127-138) and never touches batchType. An admin correcting a member's batch year (the exact hand-fix workflow this action was built for, per its own header comment about the week of 2026-08-18) leaves batchType derived from the OLD pair — or leaves it set while clearing batchYear, or leaves a null batchType after fixing a swapped-years signup. The member's batchTargetKey (post-visibility-rule.ts:227, built from batchType+batchYear) then either goes null (excluded from ALL batch-targeted posts aimed at their batch) or names the wrong credential ('ISC-2011' vs a stored 'ICSE-2011' target). Also: flipping accountType alumnus<->teacher here clears neither the tenure pair nor batch fields, leaving stray data the profile's own editor gates against; and unlike updateProfileField, a batchYear fix here never triggers tryRosterAutoVerifyQuietly.
findings.argument: Diff the two writers: profile-actions.ts:188-198 reads current {batchYear, yearLeft} and sets data.batchType = batchTypeFromLeaving(...) whenever either of the pair moves; admin/people/actions.ts:127-138 writes batchYear raw. batchLine/formatBatch read only batchYear so the byline looks right, which is what makes the drift invisible until a batch-targeted post is missed.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only DB query after reproducing on a test row: set a test user's batchYear via the admin person page to a different year; SELECT batchType, batchYear, yearLeft — batchType still reflects the old pair. Then confirm a post with targetBatches for the corrected batch does not reach that user's feed.

findings.title: Onboarding register step bypasses the shared place validation all other UserPlace writers use
findings.expected: place-input.ts's header says the schema exists so 'all three writers share one definition' — sign-up (onboarding), settings, and admin — after audit B-111 added coordinate bounds, placeId verification, and caps precisely because 'lat/lng feed the map's cluster maths' and 'an unknown id aborts the whole transaction on a foreign key'.
findings.actual: saveOnboardingRegister uses its own local placeSchema (lines 22-28): lat/lng are bare z.number().nullable() with NO -90..90/-180..180 bounds (zod v4 rejects NaN/Infinity but lat 9999 passes straight into UserPlace and the map math); placeId lacks .positive() and is NEVER checked against the Place table (no resolvePlaces call), so a crafted or stale placeId hits the FK and aborts the whole transaction (P2003 thrown unhandled out of the action) losing the member's admission number, occupation, organisation and cities in one go — the exact failure mode B-111's fix degrades gracefully in the other two writers; and the cap is 20 places vs MAX_PLACES 30 elsewhere, so 21-30 cities saved via the profile would be refused if resubmitted through the wizard.
findings.argument: Compare onboarding/actions.ts:22-28 + 78-106 (local schema, tx.userPlace.createMany with p.placeId as given) against settings/actions.ts:153-159 and admin/people/actions.ts:164-169, which both call parsePlaces + resolvePlaces (place-input.ts:24-38, 73-88). The place-input.ts doc comment claiming all three share it mis-describes the code, which the audit brief treats as bug evidence in itself.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices for the drift; to confirm the abort: from a signed-in test account, call saveOnboardingRegister with places=[{placeId: 999999999, label:'X', city:'X', lat:null, lng:null}] and observe the thrown P2003/generic failure with nothing saved; then the same payload through updateUserPlaces saves it degraded to a free-typed place. For coordinates, save lat 9999 through onboarding and read the UserPlace row back.

findings.title: Signup accepts batchYear earlier than yearLeft — the impossible pair the profile editor refuses
findings.expected: The charter question: impossible year combinations are refused everywhere. The profile editor's yearClash (profile-actions.ts:239-241) refuses batchYear < yearLeft outright ('the two fields swapped at signup', per batchTypeFromLeaving's own comment about audit Low 110), so signup should refuse the same pair instead of storing it.
findings.actual: registerUser cross-checks only yearLeft < yearJoined (lines 77-83). batchYear=2005 with yearLeft=2010 passes the schema (both calendar-valid), batchTypeFromLeaving returns null (utils.ts, the Low-110 guard), and the row stores the swapped pair: the profile then prints 'Batch 2005' beside 'In the valley ...–2010', batchType is silently null (excluded from every batch-targeted post), and the batch group auto-join puts them in 'Batch of 2005'. Nothing tells the member; fixing it later requires field-by-field edits that happen to pass yearClash in the right order. Related asymmetry in the same clash rule: batchYear < yearJoined with yearLeft null is also accepted by every writer.
findings.argument: auth/actions.ts:77-93 has no batchYear-vs-yearLeft comparison before create; utils.ts batchTypeFromLeaving explicitly documents that batchYear < yearLeft 'is the two fields swapped at signup' and answers null rather than refusing — the refusal exists only in profile-actions.ts's yearClash, which never runs at signup.
findings.proofPlan: Sign up a throwaway alumnus with yearJoined 2005, yearLeft 2010, batchYear 2005 (fields swapped): signup succeeds; SELECT batchType, batchYear, yearLeft shows the stored impossible pair with batchType NULL, and the profile prints both facts. Delete the throwaway after.

findings.title: Demo: contact editing, admission number, and photo removal fail with a misleading 'check your connection' error
findings.expected: The demo's policy: 'Editing your profile is a highlight of the product, so this is generous', and 'the actions worth naming individually return { error } at their own front door so the UI can show a sentence written for that specific button.' A demo visitor editing their contact rows should either succeed or be told it is a demo.
findings.actual: EDITABLE_PROFILE_FIELDS omits 'phone', 'phones', 'showEmail', 'admissionNumber', and 'photoUrl'. updateContactMethods writes displayEmail+showEmail+phone+phones+... in one update (profile-actions.ts:307-331), so isOwnProfileEdit refuses the WHOLE write (any non-allowlisted key fails the loop) and every contact save on the demo persona's own editable profile dies as a DemoWriteError, surfaced by useAutoSave's catch as 'That did not save. Check your connection.' The same happens for updateProfileField('admissionNumber') and for removeAvatar (photoUrl: null). None of these three actions carries an IS_DEMO front-door message (updateAvatar and chooseBird do), and docs/spec/demo.md never records contacts as intentionally closed.
findings.argument: demo.ts isOwnProfileEdit: `for (const [key] of Object.entries(a.data)) { if (!EDITABLE_PROFILE_FIELDS.has(key)) return false; }` — one missing column vetoes the whole update. The contact editor is reachable: the demo visitor is DEMO_USER_ID, /profile/demo-visitor is isOwnProfile, the pen renders, ContactsEditor commits through updateContactMethods. displayEmail/instagram/linkedin/facebook/links ARE allowlisted, which shows the list intended to permit contact editing and simply predates the phones/showEmail columns.
findings.proofPlan: On the demo deployment (or locally with DEMO_MODE=1 against the demo DB): open your own profile, press Edit, change any contact row, blur — the save banner reads the connection error; the server log shows DemoWriteError. Alternatively unit-level: demoWriteAllowed('User','update',{where:{id:'demo-visitor'},data:{displayEmail:'a@b.c',showEmail:true,phone:null,phones:null,...}}) returns false.

findings.title: Places autosave fires an unserialized wipe-and-recreate per edit: overlapping saves lose data or show a false connection error
findings.expected: Rapid city edits (each LocationPicker change calls commitPlaces immediately) and two-tab editing should converge on the member's final list, with any refusal explained truthfully.
findings.actual: useAutoSave.run (pen.tsx:348-371) only counts in-flight saves, it never queues them, and commitPlaces fires updateUserPlaces on every picker change. Two overlapping wipe-and-recreate transactions: the @@unique([userId,position]) makes the loser abort (the settled, documented outcome in schema.prisma:767-775) — but the abort surfaces to the member as 'That did not save. Check your connection.' while the screen keeps the newer list and the DB holds the older one (router.refresh only runs on success), a divergence that survives until a retry the message never asks for. Worse, if the two requests land in the wrong order WITHOUT overlapping (network reordering, or tab A slower than tab B), both succeed and the EARLIER list wins silently — a lost update the unique cannot catch. The same fire-per-interaction pattern applies to commitHouses (every house-pill answer) where the single-column update means out-of-order arrival silently reverts newer picks.
findings.argument: letterhead-profile.tsx:429-438 (commitPlaces called from CitiesPen's onChange at 579) and 440-447 (commitHouses from HouseChainEditor toggle). No client serialization exists in run(); the server action has no ordering token (no updatedAt precondition like editPost's at feed/actions.ts:598). The abort-on-unique decision in the schema comment covers only the double-insert corruption, not the client-facing consequences.
findings.proofPlan: Two browser tabs on your own profile in edit mode: add city X in tab A and city Y in tab B within a second; observe one tab's error banner and, after reload, a list matching neither tab's screen. Same with rapid single-tab pill answers in the Houses chain while throttling the network in devtools.

findings.title: Roster import's --match-existing backfill verifies members without stamping verifyStateAt
findings.expected: schema.prisma:53: 'STAMP THIS WHENEVER YOU WRITE verifyState: it is the only honest ordering the admin worklist has.' Every src/ writer complies (verification-actions.ts:55, admin-actions.ts:160/206, roster.ts:81).
findings.actual: The script's backfill UPDATE sets verifyState='verified', verifyMethod, verifiedAt=now() but omits verifyStateAt (lines 200-203), so a script-verified member keeps their signup-era timestamp: the admin worklist's verifyStateAt-ordered lists (admin-worklist-query.ts:83-94) place them wrongly, and the 'recently verified' ordering never shows the batch the import just admitted.
findings.argument: Direct read of the UPDATE statement versus the four Prisma writers; admin-worklist-query.ts orders by verifyStateAt in both directions and serializes u.verifyStateAt.toISOString() at 157/165.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: after any --apply --match-existing run, SELECT id, "verifyState", "verifiedAt", "verifyStateAt" FROM "User" WHERE "verifyMethod"='office_list' AND "verifiedAt" > "verifyStateAt" — rows returned are the evidence.

findings.title: Three different admission-number ceilings: 10000 in onboarding/settings schemas, 100000 in the profile editor
findings.expected: One cap per column (the audit Low 84 rule: 'a number accepted at sign-up could fail to save afterwards' is the drift class already fixed twice for phones and names).
findings.actual: updateProfileField accepts admission numbers up to 100000 (line 111, and the letterhead field allows 5 digits via digits(v,5) at letterhead-profile.tsx:851), while registerStepSchema (onboarding/actions.ts:31) and profileSchema (validators.ts:164) cap the same column at 10000. A member whose admission number is 12345 saves it on the profile; the onboarding register step would refuse the very number the profile already holds, and whichever bound is actually right, two live writers disagree about the same column.
findings.argument: Direct comparison of the three validators over User.admissionNumber; the onboarding step's HTML max=10000 (register-step.tsx:166) matches its schema, so the disagreement is between the letterhead path and everything else.
findings.proofPlan: Code comparison suffices; the owner should say whether real admission numbers exceed 10000, which decides which side is wrong.

findings.title: Profile pen accepts years up to 2100 that every other writer refuses
findings.expected: Year fields are bounded by the valley's calendar everywhere: signup and profileSchema use yearField (max valleyYear()+0/1/7), the admin person page uses valleyYear()+10.
findings.actual: updateProfileField's YEAR_MAX is a flat 2100 (lines 28-29, message 'A year between 1926 and 2100, please'), and yearClash checks only relative ordering, so the letterhead can store yearJoined 2099 / yearLeft 2100 / batchYear 2100 — 74 years in the future — and the profile prints 'In the valley 2099–2100'. The same member could never have entered those values at signup; the impossible-values gate exists in one form and not the other (the charter's exact question). batchYear<yearJoined (with yearLeft empty) also passes here, another ordering yearClash does not cover.
findings.argument: profile-actions.ts:28-29 vs validators.ts yearField's per-parse valleyYear() refine (the refine exists precisely so the ceiling tracks the calendar; the pen path ignores it) and admin/people/actions.ts:108's valleyYear()+10.
findings.proofPlan: On a test account's own profile, type 2099 into 'In the valley' start year and blur: it saves and renders. The same value in the signup form is refused.

findings.title: chooseBird's header comment describes the abolished re-pick model the code below refuses
findings.expected: Comments record why the shape is deliberate; a comment that mis-describes its code is itself bug evidence (audit brief).
findings.actual: The doc comment ends 'Re-picking is allowed indefinitely.
