The perk is standing, and the write is idempotent, so there is nothing to meter and no state to corrupt by clicking twice' — but the code (lines 243-256, owner decision 2026-08-18) implements one pick per contribution: birdPickedAt spends the pick and a re-pick without a newer paid contribution is refused. A future session trusting the header would 'fix' the gate away; a supporter double-clicking the same bird also gets 'You have already picked your bird. A new contribution opens another pick.' immediately after their pick succeeded, because the first click spent the grant the second one needs.
findings.argument: The header (206-209) and the inner block (238-256) assert opposite policies in the same function; the inner block's comment carries the owner date, so the header is the stale one.
findings.proofPlan: Code reading settles the contradiction; the double-click toast can be confirmed by an admin-role account? No — admins bypass the ledger; use a test supporter account or trace the two sequential calls.

findings.title: Concurrent avatar upload/remove races orphan R2 objects that nothing can ever find again
findings.expected: Every stored avatar object is either referenced by photoUrl or deleted — TRAPS.md names unreferenced R2 objects ('bytes survive its own deletion, silently and for ever, and nothing anywhere reports it') as the H9 failure mode.
findings.actual: updateAvatar's read-prev/update/delete sequence (lines 250-258) is not atomic: two overlapping uploads both read the same prev; both delete it; the update that commits FIRST has its freshly-uploaded object overwritten by the second update, and that first object's URL is then referenced nowhere and deleted never. Same shape between removeAvatar (reads prev, sets null, deletes prev) racing an upload: the upload's new object is orphaned when removeAvatar's update lands second. Storage does grow, quietly, contrary to the rate-limit comment's claim that 'storage never grows (the prior avatar is deleted on replace)'.
findings.argument: No transaction or updatedAt precondition around the read-modify-delete; the loser's `url` value is only ever held in the losing request's memory. Bounded by the uploads rate limit, so cost not correctness, but permanent and unreported per TRAPS.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace, or fire two updateAvatar calls concurrently for a test account and list the avatars/<id>/ prefix in R2 afterwards: two objects, one referenced.

findings.title: Onboarding photo step still ships the uncropped photo into the server's blind centre crop
findings.expected: The profile path's own comment (letterhead-profile.tsx:376-379) records why blind uploads were a defect: 'the old path shipped the ORIGINAL bytes to a hard-coded centre crop, so an off-centre face was silently beheaded' — which is why the profile opens AvatarCropDialog before uploading.
findings.actual: The onboarding photo step calls shrinkForUpload then updateAvatar directly (lines 57-64) with no crop dialog, so the server's fixed resize(512,512,{fit:'cover',position:'centre'}) (settings/actions.ts:238) still beheads off-centre faces for every new member's very first upload — the size half of B-030 was fixed, the framing half was not. The member's recourse is discovering the re-crop on the profile afterwards.
findings.argument: photo-step.tsx has no AvatarCropDialog import or mount; the letterhead path (letterhead-profile.tsx:380-385, 1301-1315) does. Both feed the same action, so the difference is purely which client prepares the frame.
findings.proofPlan: Visual: run the wizard's photo step with a portrait photo whose face sits in the top third; the resulting avatar crops the face. Compare the same file uploaded from the profile's crop dialog.

findings.title: Feed post notifications deep-link to /feed#<postId> but nothing implements the scroll; the module comment claims PostFeed does
findings.expected: Tapping 'X liked your post' / 'X commented on your post' / 'X replied to your comment' lands the member on the post in question (scrolled to it, ideally highlighted), per the comment at notification-links.ts:14-15: 'PostFeed handles the scrolling half of the feed case, once its first page has loaded.'
findings.actual: The click lands at the top of /feed with no scroll and no highlight. If the post is older than the first page (20 posts), it is not rendered on the page at all. This is the majority class of all notifications in the app (every non-letter like/comment/reply).
findings.argument: postNotificationLink returns `/feed#${post.id}` for every non-letter post. The bell navigates via router.push (notification-bell.tsx:235). PostCard does render `<article id={post.id}>` (post-card.tsx:234), but posts are fetched client-side after mount (post-feed.tsx: loadPosts in a useEffect with a skeleton state), so the anchor element does not exist when the router commits the navigation and attempts its one hash scroll. A repo-wide grep for `location.hash` / `scrollIntoView` / `getElementById` finds no reader of the fragment anywhere in src/app or src/components except house-picker.tsx and tour-provider.tsx (unrelated). The app's own lab audit file (src/app/lab/everything/_findings.ts:482) independently states 'The feed fetches its posts after mount and nothing reads the URL hash... it silently gives up' — so the comment in notification-links.ts mis-describes the code beside it, which per the brief is itself bug evidence. Audit B-046 fixed the letter half (routes to /letters/<id>) but the feed half's promised mechanism was never built.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step with a test account: create two accounts, have B like A's 21st-newest post (so it is off the first feed page), open A's bell, click the like notification, observe the feed loads at the top with the post absent. Code trace alternative: confirm no consumer of window.location.hash exists in PostFeed/feed page.

findings.title: Closing a thread ('Sorted') unconditionally clears adminUnread, burying a member reply that arrived after the admin loaded the page
findings.expected: A member message the admin has never seen keeps its unread marker; closing a thread should only clear the marker for messages the closing admin could have seen.
findings.actual: setThreadStatus runs `update({ where: { id: threadId }, data: { status, adminUnread: false } })` with no precondition. Any member reply that commits between the admin loading /admin/messages/[id] and clicking 'Mark sorted' (a human-scale window of minutes, not milliseconds) is silently marked seen and the thread is archived to the collapsed 'Sorted' section with no 'New' chip. The member believes the admins read it; nothing ever resurfaces it unless the member writes again (which reopens via replyToThread's status:'open').
findings.argument: The B-201 fix carefully made replies write only the other side's flag and made mark-seen a conditional updateMany (`where: { adminUnread: true }`), but setThreadStatus (actions.ts:235-238) is a plain update that pairs the status write with `adminUnread: false` regardless of whether lastMessageAt has moved since the admin's page render. replyToThread's transaction (actions.ts:138-157) sets adminUnread: true and status 'open'; a later-committing setThreadStatus overwrites both. Compare: settleReport in admin-actions.ts guards its transition with `where: { status: 'pending' }` — the equivalent guard (e.g. only clear adminUnread when lastMessageAt <= the value the admin's page rendered) is absent here.
findings.proofPlan: Two-session browser test: admin opens a thread; member sends a reply; admin (without refreshing) clicks 'Mark sorted'; verify AdminThread now has status='closed', adminUnread=false while the last AdminMessage is member-authored and was never rendered to the admin. Read-only SQL confirms the row state.

findings.title: Deleting or hiding a letter (and legacy group notifications) leaves bell rows whose links 404; only Catch-ups clean up notifications
findings.expected: A notification never points at a page that answers 404; the codebase already holds this bar elsewhere (audit B-046 treated wrong notification links as a bug, and catchups/actions.ts:1572 clearCatchupNotifications deletes bell rows when their target goes away).
findings.actual: deletePost (hard delete, feed/actions.ts:402-428) and adminRemovePost (isHidden, :435+) delete/hide a letter without touching Notification rows. Existing 'liked your letter' / 'commented on your letter' rows in the author's bell, and 'X replied to your comment' rows in other commenters' bells, all link `/letters/<id>`, and letters/[id]/page.tsx:67 answers notFound() for a missing or hidden letter — the member taps a bell item and gets the 404 hoopoe. Legacy `group_invite` rows linking /groups/<id> (route removed) 404 the same way. Plain feed posts degrade more gently (/feed#id just lands on the feed, see the High finding).
findings.argument: Notification.link is a plain string with no FK, so nothing cascades. The only writers that reconcile bell rows with content lifecycle are the Catch-up actions (deleteMany at catchups/actions.ts:1237 and 1572). No equivalent exists in deletePost/adminRemovePost/adminRemoveComment or in the user-block path. Notifications survive up to 100-per-user (unread indefinitely until the 365-day sweep), so the dangling window is long.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: B comments on A's letter; A deletes the letter; A opens the bell and taps the comment notification; observe the 404 page. Read-only SQL: SELECT count(*) FROM "Notification" WHERE link LIKE '/letters/%' AND link NOT IN (SELECT '/letters/'||id FROM "Post" WHERE kind='letter' AND "isHidden"=false).

findings.title: A legacy unresolved admin_note can be permanently destroyed by mark-all-read plus the 100-row prune, losing the moderation note's only copy
findings.expected: A moderation note reaches its member or at least survives until read in context. The prune's own comment says moderation notices 'must survive being outranked by a hundred likes' (Low 85) — which it implements only for UNREAD rows.
findings.actual: For admin_note rows written before the messaging feature (link '/notice/<id>', full note text stored ONLY in Notification.message — verified via git show 4ab894a:src/lib/admin-note.ts), the AdminThread is created lazily on first visit to /notice/[id]. If the member instead taps 'Mark all read' (markAllNotificationsRead sets read=true without resolving), the row becomes prunable: once 100 newer rows exist, getNotifications' first-page prune (deleteMany where createdAt < cutoff AND read=true) deletes it. The thread was never created, the note text existed nowhere else, and the member never read it. The 365-day retention sweep (retention.ts:127) deletes even unread ones eventually.
findings.argument: Chain: (1) legacy writer stored the full note only in Notification.message with link /notice/<id>; (2) notice/[id]/page.tsx:54-69 is the only code that materialises that note into an AdminThread, and it runs only on a page visit; (3) markAllNotificationsRead (notifications/actions.ts:124-127) flips read=true with no type exemption and no resolution; (4) the prune at notifications/actions.ts:58-60 deletes read rows past the 100th-newest with no type exemption. Population is bounded to notes written between commits 4ab894a and c6d7d71; if that count is zero in production the finding is moot, which is checkable read-only.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only SQL first: SELECT count(*) FROM "Notification" WHERE type='admin_note' AND link LIKE '/notice/%'. If >0, the mechanism is live; a rolled-back transaction can then demonstrate the delete path (BEGIN; UPDATE read=true; run the prune's two queries; ROLLBACK).

findings.title: Bell infinite scroll silently truncates when the cursor row is pruned by a concurrent first-page open (second tab/device)
findings.expected: Scrolling the bell walks every retained notification.
findings.actual: getNotifications paginates with `cursor: { id }`. The prune is skipped on cursor pages so a session cannot delete rows under its OWN cursor (the comment says exactly this), but a second tab or device opening the bell runs the first-page prune concurrently and can delete the first session's cursor row (any read row older than the new cutoff). Prisma's cursor on a nonexistent row returns an empty result set, so the next handleLoadMore gets rows=[], hasMore=false — the sentinel unmounts and the list quietly ends with older rows still in the table.
findings.argument: notification-bell.tsx:196-217 (handleLoadMore) passes the last row's id as cursor; notifications/actions.ts:44-62 prunes read rows on any cursor-less call from any session of the same user; the cursor row is the previous page's oldest row, exactly the kind the prune targets. No fallback (e.g. re-fetch without cursor, or keyset on (createdAt,id) values instead of a row id) exists.
findings.proofPlan: Unit-style check against a throwaway account: insert ~120 read rows, open page 1 in session A, scroll one page; in session B call getNotifications() (triggers prune); in session A call getNotifications({cursor}) with the now-deleted id and observe empty result while rows remain. Also confirms the Prisma missing-cursor behaviour, the one step of this argument taken from documentation rather than this repo's code.

findings.title: Admin-opened notice threads count against the member's own new-thread budget, which also gates reporting
findings.expected: The 5-threads-per-hour budget meters what the MEMBER creates (their messages and their reports — the latter deliberately, per audit H5).
findings.actual: isThreadRateLimited counts `adminThread.count({ where: { memberId, createdAt: gte } })` with no kind filter and no notion of who created the row. openAdminNoticeThread (kind 'notice') writes rows with memberId = the member being moderated. An admin attaching notes while removing several of one member's posts in an hour (notifyAdminNote per removal) consumes the member's entire budget: startThread and both report actions (report-action.ts:82, :180) then refuse with 'That's a lot of messages at once' — the member cannot open a thread to appeal, and cannot report anything, for an hour, having sent nothing.
findings.argument: Every AdminThread row carries memberId regardless of origin; the three creators are startThread (member), openReportThread (member-initiated), and openAdminNoticeThread (admin-initiated). Only the first two are the member's own doing. The count should exclude kind 'notice' (or filter on the first message's authorId).
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient (the count's where-clause has no kind filter). Live check: on a throwaway account, have an admin send 5 notes within an hour, then attempt startThread as the member and observe the refusal.

findings.title: Member /messages list silently caps at 60 threads with no affordance — the same shape as fixed audit B-200 on the admin side
findings.expected: Every conversation a member has remains reachable (the admin queue's identical `take` bug was fixed as B-200 with an 'Show N older' link; see admin/messages/page.tsx's comment).
findings.actual: `take: 60` with orderBy lastMessageAt desc and no count, no pagination, no 'show older' link. A member past 60 threads (each report files one, each moderation note files one, plus their own messages — 5/hour allowed) permanently loses access to older conversations: the bell's notification rows that pointed at them get pruned at 100, and no other route lists them.
findings.argument: The B-200 fix commentary in admin/messages/page.tsx:23-30 explains precisely why a bare take over this table is wrong ('every thread past position sixty became permanently unreachable... with nothing on the page to say so'); the member-side page kept exactly that shape.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices; optionally seed a throwaway account with 61 threads (rate limit makes this slow live — a rolled-back SQL insert count check is enough to show the query returns 60 of 61).

findings.title: deriveSubject/previewOf cut at UTF-16 code-unit offsets, splitting surrogate pairs into U+FFFD mojibake in stored subjects and notification copy
findings.expected: A subject or preview derived from member text never ends in a replacement character. TRAPS.md records that Intl.Segmenter (constructed once) is this codebase's instrument for cutting text (getInitials learned this).
findings.actual: deriveSubject uses `flat.slice(0, 64)` / `cut.slice(0, lastSpace)` and previewOf uses `flat.slice(0, max - 1)`. On emoji-heavy or non-BMP text with no spaces (lastIndexOf(' ') = -1 → `lastSpace > 32` false → raw 64-unit cut), the slice can land mid-surrogate-pair; the lone surrogate is not valid UTF-8, so the pg driver serialises it as U+FFFD. The mojibake persists in AdminThread.subject (shown as the thread title everywhere) and in Notification.message previews (startThread's notifyAdmins, noteOnReportThread, report threads).
findings.argument: String.prototype.slice operates on UTF-16 code units; every astral character (emoji, many Indic-adjacent symbols members will use) occupies two units. deriveSubject's word-boundary fallback only helps when a space exists past index 32; previewOf has no boundary logic at all. Buffer.from(loneSurrogateString, 'utf8') yields EF BF BD — checkable in one node -e line.
findings.proofPlan: Pure-function check, no DB: node -e evaluating deriveSubject/previewOf logic (inline copy) on a 70-emoji string and inspecting the final code unit for an unpaired high surrogate.

findings.title: reportPost double-file TOCTOU: the pending-report dedup is check-then-insert with no unique backstop, unlike reportUser
findings.expected: One pending report per (reporter, post) even under concurrency — reportUser achieves this by catching P2002 on its @@unique (report-action.ts:219-227), whose comment explicitly calls the findFirst 'a fast path, not the guarantee'.
findings.actual: For POST reports there is no unique index (deliberately, because of pre-rule duplicate rows — that decision is documented and not disputed) and also no other backstop: two concurrent submissions (two tabs; the dialog's `submitting` flag cannot cover them) both pass the findFirst at :114, both create Report rows, both open AdminThreads, and both page every admin via notifyAdmins — exactly the 'same complaint looks like a pattern' effect audit M29 set out to stop, surviving in the concurrent case only.
findings.argument: The M29 comment (:97-113) explains why no index was added, but records no decision about the race itself; the sibling function's own comment concedes findFirst alone is not a guarantee. The blast radius is bounded (rate limits cap it) but the sequential-only fix is presented as complete.
findings.proofPlan: Two-tab browser test on a throwaway account submitting the same report simultaneously, then read-only SQL counting pending Report rows and AdminThreads for that (reporter, post).

findings.title: Mark-read-on-open clears an unread flag for a message that arrived after the page's message query (both member and admin thread pages)
findings.expected: The unread flag is only cleared for messages the reader was actually shown.
findings.actual: Member page: findUnique loads messages, then updateMany clears memberUnread (page.tsx:83-86); admin page: findUnique then markThreadSeenByAdmin (admin/messages/[id]/page.tsx:93-95). A reply committing in the gap between the two statements sets the flag and is immediately cleared, and the message was not in the rendered page — the list's unread dot / 'New' chip never appears for it. Honest framing: this window is milliseconds wide and self-heals on the next message; it is reported because the charter asks for the flag-race analysis, and it is the one residue B-201's write-discipline (replies touch only the other side's flag; clears are conditional updateMany) does not cover. The minutes-wide variant of the same loss is the setThreadStatus finding above.
findings.argument: No transaction or lastMessageAt condition ties the clear to the read snapshot; the clear's `where: memberUnread: true` guard prevents lost-update on the flag WRITE but not this read-clear inversion.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices; a live proof needs artificially interleaved requests and is not worth the setup unless the fix for the setThreadStatus finding wants a shared lastMessageAt-conditioned clear anyway.

findings.title: The 730-day AdminMessage retention leaves AdminThread shells forever: subject text (member-written) outlives the transcript, and emptied threads render oddly
findings.expected: The stated retention intent ('Conversations with the admin: 2 years... not a permanent transcript') removes the conversation's content after 730 days.
findings.actual: The sweep deletes AdminMessage rows only; AdminThread rows are never deleted. AdminThread.subject is derived verbatim from the member's first message (up to ~90 chars of their own words — deriveSubject), so a slice of every conversation persists indefinitely, contradicting the retention rationale. Mechanically, a fully-emptied thread still lists on /messages with messageCount 0, lastFromAdmin false → a 'You: ' prefix over an empty preview (thread-list.tsx:76-78), and opens to an empty conversation with a live composer; a member reply to that shell then works (a stranded fragment of a context nobody can see).
findings.argument: retention.ts:111-115 targets prisma.adminMessage only; grep confirms no adminThread.deleteMany anywhere. AdminMessage.thread has onDelete Cascade (child → parent direction only), so message deletion leaves the parent untouched by design.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices for the gap; a rolled-back transaction (BEGIN; DELETE FROM "AdminMessage" WHERE ...; SELECT thread rows; ROLLBACK) demonstrates the shell state, and rendering it needs only a throwaway thread whose messages are deleted the same way.

findings.title: Staged direct-upload objects are never reclaimed: no sweeper, no lifecycle rule, and several refusal paths skip cleanup
findings.expected: An object PUT into `staging/<uid>/...` or `collection/<uid>/...-o.*` via a presigned URL is eventually deleted whether or not finalize/contribute ever runs (a sweeper, an R2 lifecycle rule, or cleanup on every refusal path).
findings.actual: Nothing anywhere lists or expires bucket objects. A browser closed after the PUT, a network drop before finalize, contributePhotoDirect refused by the rate limiter (actions.ts:290-291 returns before any delImageByKey) or by photoSchema validation (actions.ts:308-316, same), and /api/upload/finalize refused at its own rate-limit/gate lines all strand the staged original (up to 20MB) in R2 forever.
findings.argument: presignImagePut (src/lib/storage.ts:152) records nothing server-side, so only the follow-up call knows the key. contributePhotoDirect deletes the staged key on quota refusal (line 304) and on processing failure (411) but NOT on its rate-limit refusal (290-291) or parse failure (308-316). The rate-limit case is systematically reachable: presign and finalize/contribute each consume one `uploads` token (rate-limit.ts:152-166, 40/h), so at the window boundary a presign+PUT succeeds and the very next call is refused. Grep confirms no ListObjects/lifecycle usage anywhere in src/ or scripts/, and runRetentionSweep (src/lib/retention.ts) has no storage step. account-purge's collectImageUrls only reads row-referenced URLs, so even deleting the account never finds staged keys. Adversarially: 40 presigned PUTs/h x 20MB ≈ 19GB/day per verified account, invisible to photoQuotaError (counts Photo rows only) and never reclaimed.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient for the missing-cleanup returns (compare actions.ts:290/308 against 304/411). For the no-sweeper claim: confirm with the owner that no R2 lifecycle rule exists in the Cloudflare dashboard for the staging/ and collection/ prefixes; optionally list bucket objects under staging/ in prod and diff against zero expected.

findings.title: Processed uploads orphan whenever the referencing row is never written; no DB-to-R2 reconciliation exists
findings.expected: A WebP written to `uploads/<uid>/` or `collection/<uid>/` is deleted if the flow that produced it fails before a row references it.
findings.actual: Multiple real paths store an object and then fail without deleting it: (1) /api/upload multi-file loop — file 1 is putImage'd (line 149), file 2 fails, the request 400/422s, file 1's object is orphaned; reachable from the UI because Catch-up answer attachments POST several files in one request (src/components/catchups/answer/photo-attachments.tsx:70). (2) finalize's loop has the same shape (finalize/route.ts:116-125). (3) contributePhoto/contributePhotoDirect run `prisma.photo.create` OUTSIDE the try (actions.ts:218, 418) — a DB failure there throws with both display and thumb objects already stored; if only one of the two parallel putImage calls succeeds (actions.ts:402-405) the other is likewise stranded. (4) A member uploads in the composer then abandons without posting. (5) editPost lets a letter draft drop images (feed/actions.ts:528) and Catch-up re-answers replace `images` (catchups/actions.ts:1412) with no delete/queue of the removed URLs — and because account-purge's collectImageUrls only reads CURRENT rows, even the eventual account purge never finds them.
findings.argument: delImageByKey/PendingImagePurge exist and are used by deletePost/declinePhoto/purge, but every path above either throws past the cleanup or simply overwrites the pointer. There is no reverse index (no listing of a user's prefix) so once the URL leaves every row the bytes are unfindable — the exact 'silent orphan' failure docs/TRAPS.md says the delete path was rebuilt to prevent, here on the write/edit side. Each object is a paid, publicly-fetchable image (privacy: a photo removed from a draft stays live at its URL forever).
findings.proofPlan: Trace-level: confirm photo.create sits outside the try in both contribute paths and that editPost/upsertEntry write the new images value without collecting removed URLs. Live: in a throwaway account, attach two files to a Catch-up answer where the second is a corrupt image; confirm the 4xx response and that the first file's object exists in R2 with no row referencing it.

findings.title: Retention sweep deletes AdminMessage rows without purging their screenshot bytes
findings.expected: When the 2-year retention window deletes admin-thread messages, the screenshot each row's `imageUrl` points at is queued into PendingImagePurge in the same transaction (the mechanism declinePhoto/deletePost/purge already use), so the bytes honour the same retention promise as the words.
findings.actual: `prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(730) } } })` deletes the rows outright. AdminMessage.imageUrl (schema.prisma, `imageUrl String? // one optional screenshot`) is never read, so every screenshot older than two years stays publicly fetchable at its R2 URL forever — and becomes permanently unfindable, because account-purge's collectImageUrls (account-purge.ts:109-112) enumerates admin-thread images from the rows this sweep has already destroyed.
findings.argument: Compare with declinePhoto (collection/actions.ts:620-627), which queues urls inside the same transaction as the row delete precisely because 'afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects'. The sweep is the one deleter of image-bearing rows that skips the queue entirely. Member screenshots sent to admins are among the most personal images in the system (the docs frame 180-730d retention as a GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) obligation), so bytes outliving their rows contradicts the stated retention posture, not just storage cost.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only query: SELECT count(*) FROM "AdminMessage" WHERE "imageUrl" IS NOT NULL — any such row will, at its 730-day mark, orphan its object. Code fix validation: the sweep step needs a findMany-collect + pendingImagePurge.createMany + deleteMany transaction like declinePhoto's.

findings.title: Blank-MIME images (explicitly supported per audit Low 41) are hard-refused by the direct upload path instead of falling back
findings.expected: A JPEG picked on a mobile browser that reports an empty MIME string — the exact case isImageFile (upload-shared.ts:40-43) and isDownscalable (image-downscale.ts:32) were both taught to accept — uploads successfully: either presign answers `direct:false` so the client falls back to the classic route (which sniffs the real bytes), or the client falls back on its own.
findings.actual: presign maps contentType through EXT_BY_TYPE; an empty string yields undefined and a 400 'That photo format isn't supported. Export it as JPG or PNG…'. directUploadPut (upload-client.ts:45) treats any 400-with-error as a definitive verdict and THROWS instead of returning null, so both the Collection contribute dialog (contribute-dialog.tsx:168-179) and the post composer (create-post-form.tsx, via uploadViaPresign -> handleImageFiles catch) surface that message and stop. The member holds a perfectly good JPEG, passed the client's own is-an-image check by filename, and is told its format is unsupported — while the fallback path that would accept it is never tried.
findings.argument: The contradiction is internal: upload-shared.ts's isImageFile comment says refusing blank-MIME files 'left the member holding a photograph the site would not take' (audit Low 41) and was fixed client-side, but the presign contract re-introduces the same refusal one step later with a wrong explanation. Since R2 is configured in production, the direct path runs first for every upload, so the fallback machinery for this file class is unreachable.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: with devtools, POST {kind:'collection', contentType:'', bytes:12345} to /api/upload/presign as a verified member — observe the 400; or construct a File with type:'' in the console and run the contribute dialog flow. Fix validation: presign should answer {direct:false} (or the client should fall back) for a contentType outside EXT_BY_TYPE when the filename says image.

findings.title: contributePhotoDirect reads unrotated metadata (its comment lies): EXIF-portrait photos over 40MP are over-shrunk to roughly half the pixel budget
findings.expected: The comment claims 'Read from the rotated metadata, so a portrait shot's EXIF swap is already applied and the numbers are the upright ones'; storedPixelFit should therefore compute a fit box matching the upright image, resizing a >40MP photo to just-under 40MP.
findings.actual: `sharpImage(original).rotate().metadata()` does NOT apply the rotation: sharp's metadata() reads the header — verified in the installed sharp 0.35.3 (lib/index.d.ts: width/height 'EXIF orientation is not taken into consideration'; src/metadata.cc:300-307 puts the swapped values only in `autoOrient`). For orientations 5-8 the fit box is transposed, and the pipeline's real (rotated) output is fitted 'inside' that transposed box, shrinking by (h/w)^2 of intent. A 50MP portrait phone shot (8160x6144 stored, orientation 6) is stored at ~4136x5493 ≈ 22.7MP instead of ~40MP, silently — in the archive whose stated point is full resolution.
findings.argument: storedPixelFit(upright.width, upright.height) at line 376 receives stored-orientation dims; area is swap-invariant so the >40MP trigger fires correctly, but the returned {width,height} box is landscape while the rotated image is portrait, and `.resize(w, h, {fit:'inside'})` (lines 378-386) scales to the smaller constraint. Only triggers for EXIF-rotated inputs above MAX_STORED_PIXELS (48-50MP phone modes, portrait scans). The fix is `metadata().autoOrient.width/height`.
findings.proofPlan: Local script (no network): sharp a generated 8160x6144 image, .withExif orientation 6, run the exact code block, compare output info.width*height against 40MP — expect ~22.7MP. Also assert sharpImage(x).rotate().metadata().width equals the unswapped value.

findings.title: keyForUrl refuses this bucket's own URLs whenever full R2 credentials are absent, so deletes run from local dev (shared production DB) silently strand production bytes
findings.expected: keyForUrl 'matched against every base this bucket has been served from' (its own docstring, and TRAPS.md's 'keep the old host working in code'): a https://images.rishivalley.space/... URL always resolves to its key so a delete can find the object.
findings.actual: `const base = useR2 ? publicBaseFor(url) : null;` gates ALL host recognition on `useR2`, which requires all five R2 env vars. Local dev is documented as filesystem-only ('R2 in prod, local filesystem in dev', AGENTS.md), yet shares the ONE production database. Any delete tested from dev — deletePost, declinePhoto, updateAvatar replace, a purge — hands production URLs to delImage, which returns TRUE ('was never ours') without deleting; worse, declinePhoto/deletePost then drainPendingImagePurges, which deletes the queue rows on that lying TRUE (account-purge.ts:329-331), so the nightly production sweep never gets a second chance. Row gone from the shared DB, bytes public forever, everything reports success.
findings.argument: publicBases() (upload-shared.ts:84-87) deliberately hardcodes the legacy host so recognition survives env drift — but the useR2 gate in keyForUrl makes even that hardcoded knowledge dead in dev. TRAPS.md explicitly directs sessions to test destructive writes through the app against the shared DB under throwaway accounts, which is exactly the flow that hits this.
findings.proofPlan: Local, no network: with R2 credential vars unset, `node -e` require the compiled storage module (or replicate the 3 lines) and assert keyForUrl('https://images.rishivalley.space/uploads/x/2026/08/a.webp') === null while the same URL resolves once the five vars are stubbed. Then confirm the dev .env genuinely lacks the credential vars (owner check; env files were off-limits to this agent).

findings.title: adminRemovePhoto (and avatar replace/remove, admin merge) delete bytes best-effort with no PendingImagePurge fallback — a transient R2 failure recreates the exact M11 hole
findings.expected: Removing an approved Collection photo deletes its bytes with the same durability declinePhoto has: queue the three URLs, drain, let the nightly sweep retry anything R2 refused.
findings.actual: adminRemovePhoto fires three bare delImage calls and ignores the booleans (lines 669-673). If R2 has a bad minute, the 'removed' photograph stays publicly fetchable at its permanent URL forever — the precise failure audit M11 existed to close — with only a server log line, and nothing retries. Same shape at updateAvatar (settings/actions.ts:258), removeAvatar (:276), and adminMergeUsers (admin/people/actions.ts:389); updateAvatar additionally races itself (two concurrent calls both read the same prev, one new object becomes nobody's prev).
findings.argument: The comments say 'best-effort... cannot turn a moderation click into an error page', which argues against THROWING, not against queueing: PendingImagePurge + nightly drain is the codebase's own answer to exactly this (declinePhoto, deletePost, purge all use it) and would cost two lines. The photo row keeps its URLs so the data isn't lost, but no code path ever re-reads them.
findings.proofPlan: Code diff check only: confirm delImage return values are discarded at the four sites and no purge rows are written. A validator can also grep PendingImagePurge writers to confirm the four absences.

findings.title: A >40MP panorama with aspect ratio above ~6.7:1 fails WebP encode: the areaFit branch bypasses the 16383px dimension ceiling
findings.expected: The resize applies BOTH ceilings — the 40MP area budget and WebP's hard 16383px per-side limit — so any decodable photo (≤100MP) is stored, merely smaller.
findings.actual: `.resize(areaFit ? areaFit.width : WEBP_MAX_DIM, areaFit ? areaFit.height : WEBP_MAX_DIM, ...)` uses areaFit's box INSTEAD of the dimension cap, not in addition. storedPixelFit preserves aspect, so e.g. 25000x2000 (50MP, ratio 12.5) scales to 22360x1788 — width past WebP's 16383 hard limit — and `.webp()` throws. describeProcessingError has no branch for it, so the contributor of a legitimate stitched panorama gets the generic 'Could not process the photo. Please try a different one', and the staged original is deleted.
findings.argument: Trigger condition derived exactly: w*h > 40e6 AND max(w,h)/min(w,h) > 16383^2/40e6 ≈ 6.71. Rare (most phone panoramas are ratio ≤5) but a legal input inside every stated ceiling. Fix: clamp areaFit's dims to WEBP_MAX_DIM (fit:'inside' keeps aspect anyway).
findings.proofPlan: Local sharp script: generate a 25000x2000 white JPEG, run the exact resize+webp block, observe the throw ('Processed image is too large for the WebP format' or similar libvips error).

findings.title: Collection Load-more duplicates tiles (React key collision) when a photo is inserted between page fetches
findings.expected: Appending page N+1 dedupes by id, so a contribution or approval landing between two fetches never renders the same photo twice.
findings.actual: `setPhotos((prev) => [...prev, ...data.photos])` appends raw. Offset pagination (`skip: page*24`, actions.ts:530-537) re-runs the sort per page, so any insert sorting before the current window (every new approval, under the default newest-first) shifts rows down by one: the last tile of page 1 returns as the first row of page 2. Duplicate `key={p.id}` in the masonry map (line 421) logs a React error and renders the tile twice, and the viewer's index-based navigation shows the duplicate.
findings.argument: Audit B-122 fixed the tie-ordering half of this (the orderBy now ends in id — the comment at actions.ts:507-518 records it) but the insert-drift half survives, and its precondition is the product working (people contributing while someone browses). The feed's post-feed.tsx:187 has the identical shape (recorded as a lead, outside this territory).
findings.proofPlan: Browser step with two sessions: load /collection page 1, approve/contribute an auto-approved photo from an admin session, press Load more in the first; observe the duplicated tile and the React duplicate-key console error.

findings.title: MAX_INPUT_PIXELS comment claims 'a full 108MP shot is under this' — 108,000,000 > 100,000,000, so 108MP phone-mode photos are refused with a misleading generic error
findings.expected: Per the constant's own justification, a full-resolution 108MP phone photo (Samsung/Xiaomi 108MP mode, 12000x9000) decodes and is stored (downscaled to 40MP by storedPixelFit on the Collection direct path).
findings.actual: limitInputPixels is 100,000,000; 12000x9000 = 108,000,000 exceeds it, so sharp throws 'Input image exceeds pixel limit'. describeProcessingError matches none of its specific branches for that string, so the member gets 'Could not process the photo. Please try a different one, or a JPG or PNG export of it.' — a JPG export at the same resolution fails identically. Reachable when such a JPEG is ≤20MB (heavily-compressed 108MP files are).
findings.argument: The comment's arithmetic is simply wrong ('even a full 108MP shot is under this'), and the brief treats a comment that mis-describes its code as bug evidence. Either the ceiling should be ~110-120MP (still far under sharp's 268MP default, keeping the bomb argument intact) or the comment and the error copy should tell the truth.
findings.proofPlan: Local: sharp a 12000x9000 JPEG through sharpImage().metadata() — expect the pixel-limit throw; feed the message through describeProcessingError and observe the generic branch.

findings.title: Animated GIFs contributed to the Collection are flattened to a still with nothing said — the M15 fix was applied only to /api/upload
findings.expected: Consistent with audit M15's decided fix ('it is still a still, and the response now SAYS so'), any path that accepts a GIF and stores only its first frame tells the member.
findings.actual: contributePhoto and contributePhotoDirect both accept GIFs (sniffImageType includes 'gif'; presign's EXT_BY_TYPE includes image/gif) and re-encode via sharpImage without `animated: true`, keeping only frame one — with no notice. Only /api/upload/route.ts:128-133 counts frames and warns. A member contributing an animated heritage GIF (or any reaction GIF) to the Collection silently loses the motion.
findings.argument: countImageFrames exists in src/lib/image.ts precisely for this and is imported by the classic route alone. The success toasts ('Added to the Collection') say nothing. Same gap in finalize/route.ts for post images taking the DIRECT path — the M15 notice only fires on the classic proxied route, so the fixed bug re-appears for every direct-path GIF post as well.
findings.proofPlan: Code check: grep countImageFrames call sites (exactly one). Runtime: contribute a 2-frame GIF via the dialog on a dev server, observe the stored .webp is a still and no notice fires.

findings.title: approvePhoto throws raw P2025 when the photo was concurrently declined — the admin is told to check their connection
findings.expected: Two admins working the queue: A declines (row deleted) while B clicks Approve; B is told the photo is no longer there, matching declinePhoto's own 'Photo not found' and togglePhotoLove's mapped P2003 branch.
findings.actual: `prisma.photo.update({ where: { id: photoId } })` throws P2025 on the deleted row; the action has no catch, so the rejection reaches callAction, which shows the generic 'That did not go through. Check your connection and try again.' — a wrong diagnosis that invites retrying a moderation act on a photo that no longer exists.
findings.argument: Every neighbouring path in the same file maps its known Prisma errors (declinePhoto pre-reads and answers 'Photo not found'; togglePhotoLove maps P2003/P2002 explicitly, lines 574-583). approvePhoto is the one queue action without it, and the queue is exactly where concurrent admin actions collide.
findings.proofPlan: Trace-level (P2025 semantics are standard), or live: two admin sessions, decline in one, approve in the other, read the toast.

findings.title: Grace-period purge races sign-in cancellation: account erased after the member cancelled
findings.expected: Signing in at any point before the purge actually runs cancels the deletion request (the product's stated promise, auth.ts:202-206 clears deletionRequestedAt and audits account.delete_cancel). The purge should refuse an account whose request has been cleared.
findings.actual: The sweep reads the due list once (retention.ts:225-238), then loops purgeUserAccount(row.id) sequentially. purgeUserAccount's tx.user.delete (account-purge.ts:281) is unconditional on deletionRequestedAt. A member who signs in between the sweep's findMany and their turn in the loop has the cancellation committed (auth.ts clears the column, writes the cancel audit, shows 'your deletion is cancelled') and is then permanently purged anyway, rows and R2 bytes both.
findings.argument: Check-then-act with no recheck: the WHERE deletionRequestedAt < cutoff exists only in the initial findMany. The purge transaction runs READ COMMITTED with no condition on the column, so the interleaving sign-in's committed UPDATE does not conflict with anything. The loop is sequential (each purge up to a 30s tx plus per-object R2 deletes), so with a full batch of 10 the window is minutes long, once a night at 02:30 IST, only for accounts at exactly day 60+. Fix shape: inside the purge tx, gate the delete on deletionRequestedAt still being < cutoff when invoked from the sweep (adminDeleteUser must stay unconditional), e.g. a conditional deleteMany whose count decides success.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices: confirm account-purge.ts:281 tx.user.delete has no deletionRequestedAt condition and retention.ts only filters in the list read. Optionally prove destructively-safely per TRAPS.md: BEGIN; UPDATE a throwaway user SET deletionRequestedAt = NULL; then run the purge's DELETE by id and observe it succeeds regardless; ROLLBACK.

findings.title: collectImageUrls' in-transaction claim is false under READ COMMITTED: a concurrent upload's bytes leak forever
findings.expected: The comment states: URLs are 'read INSIDE the purge transaction so nothing uploaded between the reading and the delete can slip past.' Every image whose row the cascade removes should be collected into PendingImagePurge.
findings.actual: The purge transaction (account-purge.ts:261-290) sets no isolationLevel, so it runs READ COMMITTED, where each statement takes a fresh snapshot. A post/photo/catchup-entry upload committed after collectImageUrls' SELECTs but before tx.user.delete IS cascaded away by the delete (which sees the newer snapshot) while its URLs were never collected. The bytes stay publicly fetchable at their URL with no row anywhere naming them, which is exactly the H9 failure this module exists to close, and nothing reports it.
findings.argument: Being inside one READ COMMITTED transaction provides no repeatable snapshot across statements; only REPEATABLE READ/Serializable, or collecting after acquiring a lock on the user row (e.g. deleting/locking the User row first, which FK KEY SHARE locks would then make concurrent inserts fail), would make the comment true. The window spans promoteOrphanedGroups + collect + createMany + report clear + tombstone + covers-clear before the delete, i.e. multiple round trips. Realistic scenario: an admin deletes an account whose owner is actively posting (admin delete does not require the target to be blocked or signed out). A comment that mis-describes its code is itself the flagged defect class in this audit's brief.
findings.proofPlan: Prisma docs/code: interactive $transaction without isolationLevel uses the DB default (READ COMMITTED on Postgres). Safe live proof per TRAPS.md: in session A run BEGIN; SELECT images FROM "Post" WHERE "authorId"=X; in session B insert+commit a post for X; back in A, DELETE FROM "User" WHERE id=X and observe the new post cascades; ROLLBACK A. The fix is either isolationLevel REPEATABLE READ (delete then fails serialization on conflict and retries) or re-collecting after the delete is ordered.

findings.title: Sweep's catch-up bin step strips a creator-less group's last admin with no succession
findings.expected: The codebase's own invariant (account-purge.ts promoteOrphanedGroups, group-succession.ts): no group whose creator is gone may be left with zero admin/keeper members, because isEffectiveKeeper (src/lib/catchups.ts:356-364) requires createdById match OR groupRole keeper/admin — with neither, nobody can curate questions, pause, publish or manage members ever again.
findings.actual: The catchup-bin step deletes due members' GroupMember rows (retention.ts:201-204) with no successor promotion. setCatchupDeleted refuses only the CREATOR (catchups/actions.ts:1901), so after a creator is purged (Catchup.createdById -> null, promoteOrphanedGroups hands admin to member M), M may bin their copy; 30 days later the sweep removes M's membership and the group has null creator and zero admin/keeper rows — a Catch-up nobody can tend, silently.
findings.argument: chooseGroupSuccessor is imported ONLY by account-purge.ts (verified by grep), so the purge path is the only membership-removal that rehomes. The sweep's own step comment discusses the restore race and batching but never the admin-orphaning case. The stuck-Round eventually surfaces on the admin worklist (overdueEditionWhere), but the site admin has no in-app verb to appoint a group admin, so the recovery is manual SQL. leaveCatchup (actions.ts:1828) has the identical gap immediately rather than after 30 days — recorded as a lead since catchups actions are another finder's territory.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: grep chooseGroupSuccessor call sites; read isEffectiveKeeper; read setCatchupDeleted's guard (creator-only). Optional read-only query: count groups with creatorId IS NULL and no GroupMember role IN ('admin','keeper') to see whether the state already exists.
findings.taxonomy: missing-invariant on second write path / orphaned state

findings.title: Data export omits categories of data the person provided, against its own completeness claim
findings.expected: The route's own doc: 'an export that silently omits half a person's data is worse than a slow one, and this is the request the law says must be complete' (Art. 20 covers data the person provided; the site's disclosed presence telemetry is personal data under Art. 15).
findings.actual: The sections list carries places, posts, comments, likes, collectionPhotos, catchupAnswers, messagesToAdmin, reportsFiled, contributions — and omits: CatchupPrompt rows the member authored (their own written questions, including anonymous ones), SearchLog rows (their typed queries, stored 'as typed' by design), Visit rows (identifiable presence: paths, device, coarse geo), ContentView (what they looked at), Bookmark, PollVote, PhotoLove, CommentLike, CatchupEntryLove, and Notification.
findings.argument: The header comment enumerates what the file 'carries' and none of the omitted models appear in it, so this may be deliberate scope — but authored prompt TEXT is unambiguously 'what the person wrote on it' (the comment's own criterion) and its absence contradicts the stated rule the way likes' presence supports it (likes are included while photoLoves are not, so the engagement cut-line is also inconsistent). The telemetry tables are explicitly disclosed as identifiable in the schema comments, strengthening the Art. 15 angle.
findings.proofPlan: Read the sections array at route.ts:139-254 against schema.prisma's User relations; confirm no second export surface exists (grep 'account/export'). Owner decision then settles which omissions are scope and which are gaps.

findings.title: Retention sweep's worst case exceeds serverless duration ceilings; no maxDuration declared anywhere
findings.expected: One nightly invocation reliably completes: 10 account purges (each a transaction with a 30s ceiling plus a sequential per-object R2 delete loop), the 200-copy catchup bin, nine deleteMany steps, and a 500-row PendingImagePurge drain (each row a sequential R2 round trip).
findings.actual: Worst case is 10x30s of transactions alone (300s), plus up to 500 sequential R2 DeleteObject calls (~50-150ms each, 25-75s), in a route that exports no maxDuration and a repo whose vercel.json sets none (verified by grep: zero maxDuration in src/app or vercel.json). Vercel's default ceiling (300s with Fluid, far less on legacy Hobby functions) kills the invocation mid-loop; the GitHub job also curls with a 5-minute workflow timeout.
findings.argument: Data integrity survives a kill (each purge tx is atomic, worklist durable, steps idempotent — the comments say so and the code agrees), so the real costs are: purges that committed after the kill point lose their account.purge audit entry forever (writeAudit runs after purgeUserAccount returns, and next night the user row is gone so nothing re-audits), the final retention.sweep audit entry is not written, and the job fails red on a night that mostly worked. A mass-deletion backlog (e.g. a post-launch wave of deletion requests all dated the same week) is the 2k-user scenario that makes the worst case real.
findings.proofPlan: Check the Vercel dashboard's function max duration for the project (owner). Arithmetic from the code: PURGE_BATCH=10 x transaction timeout 30_000 (account-purge.ts:289) + drainPendingImagePurges limit 500 sequential delImage calls. A declared export const maxDuration plus moving writeAudit inside/immediately after each purge would close it.

findings.title: Analytics leaderboards group by user NAME, merging same-named members
findings.expected: Per-member leaderboards (hearts given/got, loyalty, longest visit, most viewed, watchers, top commenters, bookmarkers, photo lovers) aggregate per account.
findings.actual: Eight raw queries GROUP BY u."name" (loadFaces heartsGiven :624-627, heartsGot :629-632, loyal :643-647, longest :649-653, deepest :655-658, mostViewed :662-666, watchers :670-674; loadInteractions topCommenters :848-851, bookmarkers :856-859, photoLovers :861-864). Two members named 'Ananya Rao' become one bar with summed counts; User.name has no uniqueness and an alumni directory at 2k members will collide.
findings.argument: GROUP BY name instead of GROUP BY u.id with name carried via any_value/min or a follow-up lookup (the pattern loadContent's topAuthors already uses correctly two hundred lines up). Admin-only surface, numbers silently wrong rather than crashing — cosmetic with teeth.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: SELECT name FROM "User" GROUP BY name HAVING count(*)>1 to show collisions exist or will; the query shape itself is the proof of mechanism.

findings.title: Admin Messages page fetches every open thread unbounded
findings.expected: Lists on admin pages are windowed (the closed list next to it takes SORTED_PAGE with an explicit show-all escape; audit page takes 100; mail takes 50).
findings.actual: The open-threads findMany (status not 'closed') has no take: every open thread with an 8-field member join and last-message subquery is fetched and rendered on every page view. Threads are auto-created per moderation note ('notice') and per report follow-up as well as by members, and nothing auto-closes them, so at 2k users this list grows without bound and the page slows with it.
findings.argument: Same query shape as the capped closed list one statement below, minus the take — an omission rather than a decision (no comment defends it, unlike every deliberate unbounded read elsewhere in the admin tree).
findings.proofPlan: Read-only count: SELECT count(*) FROM "AdminThread" WHERE status <> 'closed' now and after simulated load; or simply confirm no take in the first findMany versus SORTED_PAGE in the second.

findings.title: Admin edits to member data and all content moderation leave no audit-log entry
findings.expected: The audit log exists for 'every admin action against a member' (schema.prisma AuditLog comment; charter: audit coverage of every admin action).
findings.actual: No writeAudit call in: adminUpdatePerson (rewrites a member's name/accountType/batchYear/bird, people/actions.ts:127), adminUpdatePlaces (:171), adminSetPhotoTrusted (:215), adminUpdateNote (admin-actions.ts:121), adminHidePost (:225), adminRemovePost/adminRemoveComment (feed/actions.ts:439/925), adminRemovePhoto (collection/actions.ts:656 — this one also permanently deletes R2 bytes), retryMail/dismissMail (mail/actions.ts), settleReport (admin-actions.ts:254). An admin can silently rewrite who somebody is (name, batch, cities) or destroy photo bytes with zero attribution anywhere.
findings.argument: The AuditAction union (audit.ts:20-43) has no codes for these, so the gap is structural, and the schema comment's narrower enumeration ('block, delete, role change, verification change') suggests declared scope — but adminRemovePhoto's byte deletion is destruction of data (the log's stated second criterion, 'things that change standing or destroy data', audit/page.tsx:16), so at minimum that one sits inside the log's own declared scope and is missing.
findings.proofPlan: Grep writeAudit call sites versus the admin action inventory; the absence is the proof. Owner then decides which of these deserve codes.

findings.title: dismissMail read-then-delete race can delete a message another admin just requeued
findings.expected: The transition is the decision, conditional on the state it was read with — the pattern retryMail enforces four lines up (updateMany with status in the WHERE, mail/actions.ts:45-48) and settleReport documents as the fix for exactly this class (M01).
findings.actual: dismissMail reads status ('failed' check at :74) then deletes unconditionally at :78. Interleaving: admin A clicks Retry (row becomes queued, attempts reset) while admin B's Dismiss is between read and delete — B's delete removes the just-requeued row and a real email (commonly a password reset whose address was just corrected) is silently never sent.
findings.argument: prisma.outboundEmail.delete({ where: { id } }) has no status condition; deleteMany({ where: { id, status: 'failed' } }) with a count check is the one-line fix already idiomatic in the same file.
findings.proofPlan: Code inspection is sufficient; the two-admin interleaving is the standard M01 scenario the adjacent code comments describe.

findings.title: Duplicate/out-of-order payment.captured resurrects a refunded contribution to "paid" (and re-grants a bird pick)
findings.expected: "refunded" and "disputed" are terminal for money-counting (schema comment: the last two are written only by the webhook, from "paid"; route header: everything here is idempotent). A re-delivered payment.captured event must never move a row out of them, and a refund arriving before its capture must not be silently lost.
findings.actual: The captured branch runs `updateMany({ where: { id, status: { not: "paid" } }, data: { status: "paid", paidAt: new Date(), ... } })`. Any status except "paid" — including "refunded" and "disputed" — transitions back to "paid" with a FRESH paidAt. Razorpay delivery is at-least-once (retries on timeout/non-2xx for up to ~24h, plus the dashboard's manual resend), so a captured event re-delivered after a refund flips the row back to "paid": the public recovery bar on /support, "Given, all time", and the month tile all re-count returned money; the fresh paidAt is newer than birdPickedAt so chooseBird grants a brand-new pick; and the `moved.count === 1` branch sends the supporter a "Your contribution came through" notification after their refund. The mirror half of the same state-machine hole: refund.processed arriving BEFORE a delayed captured (retry reordering) matches nothing (guard is `status: "paid"`), is acknowledged with 200 so Razorpay never resends it, and the late captured then lands the row on "paid" forever with the refund unrecorded.
findings.argument: route.ts:163-175: the only guard on the captured transition is `status: { not: "paid" }`, chosen for the browser-callback race, but it doubles as "any non-paid state is eligible to become paid". The refunded/disputed states were added later in commit 220ebec (audit M58) without narrowing this WHERE to `status: { in: ["created", "failed"] }`. route.ts:229-233 shows the refund branch only transitions from "paid" and route.ts:111/142-144 shows every unmatched event is answered 200 (never retried), so the ordering hole cannot self-heal.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only + rolled-back transaction via run-sql.mjs: BEGIN; UPDATE "Contribution" SET status='refunded' WHERE id=<test row>; then run the captured branch's exact UPDATE ... WHERE id=<row> AND status <> 'paid'; SELECT status, "paidAt"; ROLLBACK — shows refunded→paid with a new paidAt. Live confirmation: in Razorpay test mode, pay, refund, then use the dashboard's 'resend webhook' on the payment.captured event and watch the row and /support bar.
findings.taxonomy: webhook replay / out-of-order delivery / terminal-state violation

findings.title: confirmContribution can be replayed after a refund to restore "paid" and mint a fresh bird pick
findings.expected: The browser-callback writer should only ever move a row from "created"/"failed" to "paid". A row Razorpay has refunded or disputed must stay that way regardless of how many times the (still-valid, never-expiring) checkout signature is presented.
findings.actual: `if (contribution.status !== "paid") { update({ status: "paid", paidAt: new Date() }) }` transitions from ANY non-paid status, including "refunded" and "disputed". The HMAC triple (order_id, payment_id, signature) is handed to the payer's own browser at checkout, is visible in their network tab, and stays valid forever. A member who contributes ₹500, spends the pick, then obtains a refund can replay the server action with the saved triple: the row returns to "paid" with paidAt = now, the refunded money re-enters every public and admin total, and paidAt > birdPickedAt re-opens the pick — a repeatable refund-and-replay loop, since the ownership check passes (it is their own row).
findings.argument: actions.ts:159 verifies the signature (valid forever — it is HMAC(orderId|paymentId), no timestamp), 176 checks ownership, 181-185 does the unguarded transition. Same root flaw as the webhook finding but attacker-triggerable at will rather than dependent on Razorpay redelivery. Fix for both is the same narrowed transition set.
findings.proofPlan: Test mode: pay with a test card, capture the confirmContribution payload from the network tab, refund in the Razorpay dashboard, wait for the row to read "refunded", replay the action (same payload, same session), then read the row: status "paid", fresh paidAt, and /pick-bird admits the member again.

findings.title: Dispute-won and dispute-closed events are ignored, so a chargeback the owner WINS stays un-counted forever
findings.expected: A dispute that is resolved in the merchant's favour (payment.dispute.won / payment.dispute.closed) means the money stayed; the row should return to "paid" so the recovery bar and totals count it again.
findings.actual: `acted` only lists payment.captured, payment.failed, refund.processed and payment.dispute.created. dispute.created moves paid→disputed (un-counting the gift everywhere), but the resolution events fall into the acknowledged-and-dropped branch, so "disputed" is a dead-end state with no exit path anywhere in the app — no webhook transition, no admin action to correct a status. A won chargeback permanently shrinks "Given, all time" and the public bar; the only remedy is hand-written SQL against the shared production database. (payment.dispute.lost also goes unhandled — that case happens to be correct by accident only because "disputed" and "refunded" are both un-counted.)
findings.argument: route.ts:124-144: the acted allowlist plus the `return NextResponse.json({ received: true })` for everything else; route.ts:229-233 is the only writer of "disputed" and there is no reader/writer that ever moves a row out of it (grep for status: "disputed" — only the admin ledger label and the notIn filter).
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient (grep confirms no exit path). Live: raise and cancel a test-mode dispute, or send a signed payment.dispute.won event to a dev server and observe the 200 with no row change.

findings.title: A partial refund un-counts the entire contribution: refund.processed never reads the refund amount
findings.expected: Razorpay supports refunding any portion of a payment from the dashboard, and refund.processed fires with payload.refund.entity.amount. A ₹100 refund on a ₹5,000 gift should reduce the counted total by ₹100 (or at minimum be surfaced as partial), not erase the whole gift.
findings.actual: The refund branch flips the whole row to "refunded" on any refund.processed event without ever reading payload.refund.entity — the WebhookPayment type (route.ts:64-70) only models the payment entity. Every sum filters on status: "paid", so the full contribution.amount vanishes from /support's public bar, "Given, all time", the month tile, and the member's perk ledger (their pick eligibility can drop below ₹500 over a token partial refund). The audit line even asserts the full amount: `${contribution.amount} paise no longer counted as given`.
findings.argument: route.ts:229-245: transition and audit use contribution.amount unconditionally; nothing parses event.payload.refund. Since the owner drives refunds from the Razorpay dashboard where partial amounts are one text field away, this is reachable by an ordinary dashboard action, not only by exotic API use.
findings.proofPlan: Test mode: pay ₹500, refund ₹100 from the dashboard, watch refund.processed arrive and the row flip to "refunded"; /support's bar drops by 500 rather than 100.

findings.title: First-audit Low 116 is only half-fixed: the browser confirm path still leaves failureReason (and never sets method) on a retried-then-successful payment
findings.expected: The first audit's Low 116 (filed at support/actions.ts:170) asked that the transition to "paid" clear failureReason and carry method on BOTH writers, so a failed-then-successful retry never shows a red error line under a successful gift.
findings.actual: The fix landed only in the webhook (route.ts:172 clears failureReason, sets method). confirmContribution's update writes only { status, razorpayPaymentId, paidAt }. Sequence: first attempt fails (webhook writes status "failed" + failureReason), payer retries inside the same Razorpay modal and succeeds, the browser handler wins the race (it usually does — it fires the instant the modal closes) and moves failed→paid; the webhook's captured event then matches nothing (`status: { not: "paid" }`). Result: a "paid" row in /admin/support's "Given" section with the earlier attempt's red destructive-styled failureReason under it (page.tsx:303-307), and method NULL, so the "Most used" tile and funnel count it as "unknown".
findings.argument: actions.ts:181-185 vs route.ts:163-175: the two writers converge on status but not on the row's other fields; whichever wins decides whether the hygiene fix applies. The webhook comment cites "audit Low 116" as fixed, but the file the audit actually named was actions.ts.
findings.proofPlan: Test mode: fail a card attempt, retry successfully in the same modal on a normal (fast) connection so the browser callback wins, then open /admin/support: the paid row shows the stale red reason and method missing. Or read-only: the code diff of 220ebec shows the clearing landed only in route.ts.

findings.title: Admin "Did not go through" tile counts disputed contributions, whose payments did go through
findings.expected: The tile counts attempts that never completed (created + failed). "refunded" is excluded on exactly that reasoning — the payment completed and was returned — and "disputed" is the same case (money moved, then was contested).
findings.actual: `status: { notIn: ["paid", "refunded"] }` leaves "disputed" inside the count, so a chargeback inflates the warn-toned "Did not go through" tile while the same row also renders in the "Given back" section below — the row is double-classified and the tile's number disagrees with the lists under it.
findings.argument: page.tsx:91-93 (the tile's count) vs page.tsx:117-120 where the page's own row-classification treats refunded and disputed identically as `reversed`, separate from `notPaid`. The two classifications of the same status disagree.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: with one disputed livemode row present (or via a rolled-back transaction that sets one), render logic gives tile = created+failed+disputed while the lists put that row under "Given back", not "Attempts that stopped".

findings.title: A refund does not revoke the bird already picked with that money
findings.expected: Refund transitions un-count the gift "everywhere at once" (the branch's own comment). If the perk is part of what the money bought, a fully refunded supporter arguably should not keep wearing the paid-only bird; at minimum the asymmetry should be a recorded decision.
findings.actual: The refund/dispute branch changes only status. User.birdOverride and birdPickedAt are untouched, so a member who pays ₹500, picks a bird, and is refunded keeps the bird indefinitely (future re-picks are correctly blocked because the paid sum drops below the floor). No code comment anywhere (schema, chooseBird, webhook) claims this retention is deliberate, unlike every other money decision in these files, which is argued in place.
findings.argument: route.ts:222-245 writes { status } only; chooseBird (actions.ts:210-267) is the sole writer of birdOverride for members and only runs on a new pick attempt. Flagged as a possible deliberate-by-omission policy rather than a certain defect — the fix session should get an owner ruling rather than assume.
findings.proofPlan: Owner decision plus a code trace (already complete); nothing to measure. If revocation is wanted, the refund branch is the place.
findings.taxonomy: entitlement not revoked on reversal / policy gap

findings.title: City facet filter and map 'See all' return zero results for any stored city whose string differs from its normalized form by more than case (accents, comma-qualified free-typed entries)
findings.expected: Picking a city option the server itself offered (facet dropdown options come from userPlace.groupBy at directory/page.tsx:328; the map drilldown's 'See all N in the directory' link uses the pin's stored city string, alumni-map.tsx:442) filters to at least the person(s) that option came from.
findings.actual: The filter matches zero people whenever the stored UserPlace.city string carries an accent (e.g. GeoNames names like 'Zürich', 'Montréal' — LocationPicker writes city = result.name verbatim, location-picker.tsx:90), a comma-qualified tail (free-typed 'Northfield, Minnesota' — the exact legacy-row shape geocode.ts's qualifier parser exists to serve), or doubled interior whitespace. The member shows on the map and in the dropdown but the filter for their own city shows 'No one matches these filters.'
findings.argument: buildDirectoryWhere folds the INPUT through cityNameVariants -> normalizeCity (city-coords.ts:106-120: NFKD accent-strip, lowercase, whitespace collapse, comma-tail strip) producing e.g. 'zurich' or 'northfield', then compares with `{ city: { equals: v, mode: 'insensitive' } }` (where.ts:79-81), which folds only CASE on the stored side (ILIKE). 'zurich' never equals 'Zürich' and 'northfield' never equals 'Northfield, Minnesota'. Nothing on the write path bare-ASCII-normalizes UserPlace.city (place-input.ts resolvePlaces only titleCases; the round6 backfill copied raw legacy currentCity strings including qualifiers). So the filter's fold and the stored data's form disagree, and equals+insensitive cannot bridge it. The map plots these rows fine (its resolvers all use normalizePlaceString), so map and filter disagree about who exists in a city.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: `SELECT DISTINCT city FROM "UserPlace" WHERE city LIKE '%,%' OR city <> regexp_replace(city, '[^ -~]', '', 'g');` — any row returned is a facet option that yields zero results. Then in a browser as a test account: open the directory City facet, pick that option, observe 0 results while the same person renders on the map/in browse.
findings.taxonomy: unicode-hostile input / inconsistent normalization between write path and query path

findings.title: Map pin people lists (and pin naming) lead with NULL-batchYear members: the pins query lacks the M38 nulls-last fix
findings.expected: The 12-person cap per pin (PIN_PEOPLE_CAP) is filled newest-batch-first — city-coords.ts:161 states 'the map draws newest batch first', and audit M38 established that batchYear desc must carry nulls:'last' because Postgres orders NULLs FIRST on DESC.
findings.actual: The mapped/pins query orders `[{ batchYear: "desc" }, { name: "asc" }]` with no nulls option, so every no-batch member (teachers, half-finished profiles) sorts AHEAD of every real batch. In a city with more than 12 people the drilldown sheet's visible list is monopolised by null-batch profiles while actual recent alumni hide behind 'See all N'; the same rows also decide which city string NAMES a shared grid pin (buildPins takes the first person drawn into a cell).
findings.argument: directoryOrderBy in where.ts got the M38 fix (`nulls: 'last'` on both batch sorts, where.ts:122-133) but the sibling pin query at page.tsx:321 did not; Postgres default for DESC is NULLS FIRST, and buildPins (page.tsx:181) pushes people into pin.people in row order, capping at 12.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: run the exact findMany (or `SELECT id, "batchYear" FROM "User" WHERE ... ORDER BY "batchYear" DESC, name ASC LIMIT 15`) and observe NULL batchYear rows first. Or in-browser: tap a pin containing a teacher and a recent alumnus; the teacher lists first.
findings.taxonomy: missing null handling in sort / regression of a named prior fix (M38) in a sibling query

findings.title: year=faculty is silently clobbered by type=alumni: accountType is assigned twice in buildDirectoryWhere while the UI shows both filter tokens as active
findings.expected: Contradictory filters intersect and honestly return nothing, with both tokens on screen to explain it — the exact rule the Low 73 fix wrote down for the batchYear clauses in this same function (where.ts:53-64).
findings.actual: Tap the Batches 'Faculty' tile (?year=faculty sets accountType IN (teacher, ex_teacher) at where.ts:50-51), then open Filters > Type > Alumni: where.ts:95-96 overwrites `where.accountType = "alumnus"`. The result grid shows ALL alumni under a 'Faculty' heading (directory-client.tsx:520-522 renders yearLabel) with both a 'Faculty' and an 'Alumni' sentence token active (directory-client.tsx:284-298). The member sees two filters and is getting one.
findings.argument: Plain property overwrite: `where.accountType` is assigned at line 51 and unconditionally reassigned at line 96 when filters.type === 'alumni'. Both URL params survive (updateFilters only sets its own key), so the sentence line and the yearLabel render both as active. The same function already carries the fix for this class on batchYear ('One batchYear clause built from all three inputs, so they INTERSECT rather than overwrite').
findings.proofPlan: Browser as test account: /directory?year=faculty&type=alumni — observe result count equals the all-alumni count, 'Faculty' heading and token present. Code trace alone is sufficient.
findings.taxonomy: filter clobber / check-overwrite inconsistency with sibling fix (Low 73 class)

findings.title: loadDirectoryPage server action has no rate limit and no length cap on filter strings, unlike every sibling lookup endpoint
findings.expected: The stated design (users/search route.ts:28-29: 'The read-heavy lookup endpoints share one throttle so a script cannot hammer them') and the M44 pattern (q capped at FULL_NAME_MAX) cover every caller-driven membership read. /api/users/search, /api/users-by-batch and /api/places/search all call rateLimit("search") (120/min).
findings.actual: loadDirectoryPage — a POST endpoint returning 60 membership rows per call with caller-controlled filters — checks only requireVerifiedEmail. A verified account can hammer it without throttle, and filters.q / filters.city arrive uncapped through the server-action body (megabytes allowed), each expanding into four ILIKE '%...%' clauses over User plus a places EXISTS (where.ts:41-48), so one request can carry an arbitrarily large pattern to Postgres. Directory-page GET requests are similarly uncapped but bounded by URL length; the action is not.
findings.argument: actions.ts imports no rate-limit module and performs no length slicing; buildDirectoryWhere applies escapeLike but never truncates. Contrast users/search route.ts:29 (rateLimit) and :38 (slice(0, FULL_NAME_MAX), audit M44). Stability/DoS is explicitly in scope for this audit; pool max is 5/instance with a 5s checkout, so a scripted loop of slow ILIKE scans degrades the whole instance.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient for the absence. For impact, a read-only EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the compiled query with a 100KB pattern against the dev DB shows per-call cost; no live hammering needed.
findings.taxonomy: resource exhaustion / missing rate limit / unbounded input (six-value rule: at-limit and limit+1 unhandled)

findings.title: Teacher/ex_teacher accounts can hold a batchYear, making the batch tile count disagree with the tile's result list and leaking teachers into the Catch-ups batch-invite roster
findings.expected: A batch tile showing 'N people' (page.tsx:290-295 groupBy EXCLUDES accountType teacher/ex_teacher) lists exactly N people when clicked; and /api/users-by-batch, whose consumer is the Catch-ups 'everyone from my batch' picker, agrees with /api/users/search's explicit product rule that teachers are never offered as Catch-up invitees (users/search route.ts:62-66).
findings.actual: buildDirectoryWhere's batchYear clause (where.ts:60-64) and users-by-batch's `batchYear: { in: batches }` (route.ts:50-56) add no accountType exclusion, so a teacher/ex_teacher row with batchYear set is counted by neither tile nor faculty tile's complement but appears in the tile-click list (count N, list N+k) and in the batch-invite roster for a section teachers cannot open.
findings.argument: Such rows are creatable through supported paths: adminUpdatePerson (admin/people/actions.ts:98-138) writes accountType and batchYear independently — flipping an alumnus to ex_teacher with the prefilled year kept stores both; updateUserProfile (settings/actions.ts:86-92) writes batchUpdate with no accountType check. Signup alone prevents it (auth/actions.ts:64 gates batchYear on isAlum), but the edit paths do not, and 'ex_teacher' naturally describes alumni who returned to teach.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: `SELECT id, "accountType", "batchYear" FROM "User" WHERE "accountType" IN ('teacher','ex_teacher') AND "batchYear" IS NOT NULL;` — any row proves live disagreement; otherwise it is a latent edit-path hole demonstrable by tracing adminUpdatePerson.
findings.taxonomy: facet-count vs list disagreement / cross-surface exclusion-set inconsistency

findings.title: Keyset 'Load more' under the batch sorts likely dead-ends at the NULL-batchYear region, and the M39 recovery cannot catch it
findings.expected: Paging with cursor under sort=batch-desc/batch-asc (orderBy batchYear with nulls:'last', id tiebreak) walks the entire result set including the trailing no-batch members.
findings.actual: Prisma compiles cursor pagination into value comparisons against the cursor row's orderBy columns; comparisons against NULL are unknown, so when the page boundary reaches the transition into the nulls-last region the next page comes back empty. actions.ts:91-105's recovery only fires when the cursor row has LEFT the filtered set — here it still counts (findFirst succeeds), so no offset fallback runs, nextCursor returns null, and the button silently disappears with all null-batch members unreached. Exposure is limited: the sort UI was removed (directory-client.tsx:245-249), so only ?sort=batch-* bookmarks/hand URLs reach it; the default sort leads on non-null createdAt and is exposed only on exact createdAt ties.
findings.argument: directoryOrderBy('batch-desc') = [{batchYear desc nulls last},{name asc},{id asc}] (where.ts:123-133); the cursor row at the boundary has batchYear = <last real year> and the following rows have batchYear NULL, which fail both the strict and the equality arm of the compiled comparison. Whether Prisma 7's query compiler adds IS NULL arms for nulls:'last' is the one open question — hence medium confidence.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only against the dev DB: run prisma.user.findMany with the batch-desc orderBy, take just below the count of non-null-batch rows, then a second call with cursor = last non-null row's id; if it returns [] while null-batch rows exist in the filtered set, confirmed. Alternatively enable query logging and read the compiled SQL for the cursor comparison.
findings.taxonomy: pagination edge / NULL comparison in keyset cursor

findings.title: Directory searches are never logged: SearchScope 'directory' has no writer, on a false premise the recording commit wrote down
