findings.expected: The owner asked for 'the most common searches' and the zero-result list; SearchLog's schema and SearchScope union both name a 'directory' scope (search-log.ts:16, schema SearchLog comment), and the directory q= is handled server-side where query + result count are both known.
findings.actual: No code path calls logSearch with scope 'directory' (grep: only feed/people/places call sites). Every query typed into the main people-search surface — and every zero-result miss there — is discarded, so admin analytics' by-scope breakdown silently lacks the site's primary search surface.
findings.argument: Commit 825e449's rationale, repeated in search-log.ts:7-9, is 'the directory filters in the browser' — false when written and false now: DirectoryClient debounces into router.push('/directory?q=') and the server page runs the filtered count and rows (page.tsx:304-317), so the exact after(logSearch) shape used by users/search would drop in. A comment that mis-describes its code is itself the bug evidence per this audit's brief.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: `SELECT scope, count(*) FROM "SearchLog" GROUP BY scope;` — 'directory' absent despite directory usage. Code trace confirms no writer.
findings.taxonomy: dead scope / telemetry blind spot / comment-code mismatch

findings.title: A shared 0.1-degree grid pin is named and 'See all'-linked by only its first member's city string, so the drilldown escape link can show a fraction of the pin's count
findings.expected: The pin drilldown's 'See all N in the directory' lands on a list of (about) N people.
findings.actual: buildPins keys pins by grid cell and stores the FIRST resolved member's city string as pin.city (page.tsx:183); alumni-map.tsx:442 links /directory?city=<that one string>. Two unaliased city names in one ~11km cell (e.g. Hyderabad 17.38/78.47 and Secunderabad 17.44/78.50 both land in cell 17.4/78.5; cityNameVariants aliases neither) produce a pin titled and counted for both, whose link filters to only one — 'See all 40' opening a 2-result page. The unmapped bucket's link is a variant of the same: it falls back to href '/directory' (alumni-map.tsx:701), so 'See all N' from 'Not yet on the map' lands on the default browse map, a dead end.
findings.argument: The count aggregates every string in the cell; the link filters by one string with equals+variants (where.ts:65-82). Combined with PIN_PEOPLE_CAP=12, the sheet cannot show the rest and the escape hatch cannot find them.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: group UserPlace rows by the same toFixed(1) grid key in a script-free SQL (round(lng::numeric,1), round(lat::numeric,1)) and list cells containing >1 distinct normalized city string; any such cell with combined count > 12 demonstrates it. Browser check on the Hyderabad pin if that data exists.
findings.taxonomy: aggregation key vs filter key mismatch / pagination-of-truncated-list edge

findings.title: hasFilter uses raw Number() while the where uses parseBatchYear: an out-of-range year renders the entire membership as 'filtered results' under a wrong heading
findings.expected: A year the filter rejects (parseBatchYear bounds 1926-2100) behaves as no filter — the browse view — or honestly returns nothing.
findings.actual: /directory?year=1800 (or yearFrom=1800): page.tsx:222-224 computes showingYear/yearFrom with bare Number(), so 1800 is truthy and hasFilter is true (page.tsx:242-251), while buildDirectoryWhere's parseBatchYear returns null and adds no batchYear clause. The page therefore renders the People view containing every member (the flat all-members dump the product explicitly avoids) headed by yearLabel "Batch of '00" (directory-client.tsx:241 slices the last two chars of '1800').
findings.argument: Two different parsers over the same param: Number() for view/label state, parseBatchYear for the query. Any value in the gap (digits outside 1926-2100, floats like 2005.5) makes view state and query disagree.
findings.proofPlan: Browser: /directory?year=1800 as a verified test account; observe full membership grid labeled Batch of '00 with resultCount = total members.

findings.title: /api/places/search has no length cap on q, unlike the M44 cap on its sibling
findings.expected: Query strings from the URL are capped before becoming LIKE patterns, per audit M44 (users/search route.ts:38 slices at FULL_NAME_MAX).
findings.actual: raw = q trimmed only; a URL-length-bounded (~8-16KB) pattern is interpolated into three LIKE/ILIKE arms over the 234,934-row Place table per request. Bounded by the 120/min shared throttle and URL limits, so impact is per-request CPU on the site's one expensive query, not a hard outage.
findings.argument: route.ts:89-101 builds prefixPattern/containsPattern from unbounded input; the same audit class was fixed one directory over and this route was named 'the expensive one' in its own comment (route.ts:81-83). GeoNames names cap around 200 chars, so anything longer can be truncated with zero behavior change.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient; optionally a read-only EXPLAIN ANALYZE with a 8KB pattern to price one call.

findings.title: Clearing every place resurrects a stale legacy secondaryCity on the profile
findings.expected: A member who deletes all their cities shows no city anywhere.
findings.actual: updateUserPlaces (and adminUpdatePlaces, admin/people/actions.ts:186-189) syncs only currentCity (null when cleaned is empty) and never touches secondaryCity, which no writer has updated since the round6 migration. profile/[id]/page.tsx:177-184 falls back to [currentCity, secondaryCity] when places is empty, so a pre-migration secondary city the member long since removed reappears on their profile the moment their places list is empty.
findings.argument: Write path covers one of the two legacy mirror columns; the read fallback covers both. The directory itself is unaffected (it reads places/currentCity), but the writer at fault is the directory/settings shared places path.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: `SELECT id FROM "User" u WHERE "secondaryCity" IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "UserPlace" p WHERE p."userId" = u.id);` — any row already shows the ghost; else reproduce with a throwaway account: set two cities pre-style, clear all, view profile.
findings.taxonomy: stale denormalized column / incomplete write-path mirror

findings.title: Admin 'Retry' on a deferral-exhausted row creates an unkillable queued zombie that blackholes all future resets for that member
findings.expected: Retrying a failed mail row makes it eligible for the drain again, whatever counter retired it; the docstring says exactly this ('Leaving the count would put the row back in a queue that will never look at it again').
findings.actual: retryMail resets only attempts (and clears lastError/claimedAt): `data: { status: "queued", attempts: 0, lastError: null, claimedAt: null }`. It never resets `deferrals` or `nextAttemptAt`. A row that failed via the deferral ceiling (MAX_DEFERRALS=10, i.e. ~4.5h of provider trouble — email-queue.ts bookFailure writes `deferrals: 10, status: "failed"`) comes back as status 'queued' with deferrals=10, and the drain's selection (email-queue.ts:727-728 `attempts: { lt: MAX_ATTEMPTS }, deferrals: { lt: MAX_DEFERRALS }`) excludes it forever. Worse, for kind 'reset': every later forgot-password request folds into this zombie (email-queue.ts:449-458 folds any queued/sending row of the same userId+kind and returns without creating a new row), so the member can never receive another reset email; and the admin cannot undo it because dismissMail refuses non-'failed' rows (actions.ts:74-76 'Only a message that gave up can be cleared'). The row also inflates mailHealth 'waiting' forever, until the 180-day retention delete. (Verify rows have a partial escape: verificationMailState's inline claimAndSend skips the deferrals filter, so the member's own banner can still send it; reset/password-changed/deletion-scheduled have no such path.)
findings.argument: Drain filter requires deferrals < 10 (email-queue.ts:728); the giveUp branch of bookFailure leaves deferrals at 10 when it sets status 'failed' (email-queue.ts:256-274); retryMail's updateMany data object omits deferrals and nextAttemptAt; enqueueMail's fold matches status in ['queued','sending'] for (userId, kind) and early-returns; dismissMail's guard is `row.status !== "failed"`.
findings.proofPlan: Rolled-back transaction on the shared DB: BEGIN; INSERT an OutboundEmail row with kind='reset', status='queued', attempts=0, deferrals=10; run the drain's exact SELECT (status='queued' AND attempts<4 AND deferrals<10 AND (nextAttemptAt IS NULL OR <= now())) and observe zero rows; run the fold's SELECT (userId+kind, status IN ('queued','sending')) and observe it matches; ROLLBACK. Plus a read of retryMail's data object confirming the two missing fields.

findings.title: enqueueMail's fold path returns before scheduleDrain, so pressing 'resend' never nudges a stuck queued row
findings.expected: Every enqueue nudges the drain — the comment at lines 483-491 says nudging from inside enqueueMail 'is what stops the next new send path from quietly reintroducing the same wait' (the 2026-08-12 Nirad/Sanjula incident).
findings.actual: The fold branch (`if (waiting) return { queued: true, id: waiting.id };` at line 458) returns before scheduleDrain() at line 491 is reached. If the original enqueue's drain pass was lost (Vercel froze/killed the instance before its after() ran), the row sits queued and the member's own retry — the exact user action for 'my email never came' — does nothing to send it. Sharpest for a password reset: the member is signed OUT, so no authenticated-layout backstop fires from their own browsing, and requestPasswordReset's repeated submissions all fold (email-actions.ts:278-291). The mail then waits for some other member's page view; at low-traffic IST night hours that can be hours for someone locked out of their account. Verify rows self-heal via verificationMailState; reset rows do not.
findings.argument: Control flow: fold check at 449-459 precedes both the rate-limit check and the create+scheduleDrain at 470-491; nothing else drains from the unauthenticated auth pages; the only other trigger is the (main) layout's after() which requires some authenticated page view.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is deterministic (structural early return). Live confirmation: in dev, enqueue a reset for a user, prevent the first drain (EMAIL_DEV_SEND unset), then call requestPasswordReset again and log that scheduleDrain is never invoked on the fold path (add a temporary log or observe no drain queries in Prisma query logging).

findings.title: The layout's after() drain costs ~9 OutboundEmail/QueueLease queries including 3 writes on every authenticated page view even when the queue is empty
findings.expected: The per-page-view mail tick is near-free when nothing is queued, which at 2,000 users is the state 99% of the time.
findings.actual: drainMailQueue has no cheap emptiness precheck. In production with an empty queue, every authenticated page view's after() executes: takeDrainLease updateMany (a WRITE — it succeeds on almost every view, because releaseDrainLease sets expiresAt to epoch, leaving the lease permanently 'expired'), the stale-claim sweep updateMany (write-shaped scan), dailyBudget twice (4 count queries: once at 693, once inside loop iteration at 705), one findFirst, one final count(status='queued'), and releaseDrainLease updateMany (another write) — all serialized on the single QueueLease row 'mail-drain'. Concurrent views that lose the lease each pay a failed updateMany plus a guaranteed-failing INSERT (unique violation, aborted transaction — takeDrainLease lines 622-628, since the row always exists after first creation) plus a count. At 2k users' peak traffic this is a steady stream of single-row write contention and ~6-9 extra pooled queries per view against a pool capped at 5 connections/instance with a 5s checkout timeout, plus extended Vercel function duration for every page render.
findings.argument: email-queue.ts:652-673 (drainMailQueue: sendable check is env-only, then straight to takeDrainLease), 612-629 (take: updateMany-then-create-on-miss; create can only fail once the row exists), 631-638 (release: expiresAt=epoch so the next view re-takes it), 682-747 (drainWithLease: sweep + budget + loop-1 budget + findFirst + final count all run before discovering the queue is empty). layout.tsx:81-87 registers this on every authenticated render.
findings.proofPlan: Enable Prisma query logging locally with NODE_ENV=production semantics (or count statements via pg_stat_statements on the shared DB before/after N page views): load one authenticated page with an empty queue and count the OutboundEmail/QueueLease statements attributable to the after() tick; confirm the take-lease updateMany matched 1 (i.e. the lease is re-taken every view).

findings.title: Dev drain with EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 but no RESEND_API_KEY marks rows 'sent' off a console.log, violating the queue's own core invariant
findings.expected: 'Nothing may record a send on the strength of a console.log' (sendMail's own comment, from the 2026-08-12 incident) — a process that cannot genuinely send must not move queued rows.
findings.actual: queueIsSendable (email-queue.ts:118-147) checks RESEND_API_KEY only in the production branch; in dev it requires just EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1 and ADMIN_EMAIL. With that combo and the key absent, the drain runs, claims rows addressed to ADMIN_EMAIL, and sendMail falls into the no-key branch (email.ts:189-198) which prints to the terminal and returns `{ ok: true }` — no providerId, nothing sent. claimAndSend then writes status='sent' with sentAt, terminally retiring the row and spending a slot of the SHARED production database's 95/day budget count. Blast radius is limited to rows addressed to the owner (localDrainRecipient scope), but the row is falsely terminal and the invariant the 2026-08-12 fix established is breachable by unsetting one env var.
findings.argument: Order of guards in sendMail: the EMAIL_DEV_SEND suppression branch (170-180, correctly ok:false) is skipped when the flag is 1; the no-key branch (189-198) returns ok:true outside production. queueIsSendable's dev branch never consults RESEND_API_KEY. claimAndSend line 319-333 records 'sent' on result.ok alone.
findings.proofPlan: Locally: EMAIL_DEV_SEND=1, ADMIN_EMAIL set, RESEND_API_KEY unset; enqueue a verify addressed to ADMIN_EMAIL (throwaway flow), load a page, observe the row flip to sent with sentAt set and only a terminal print. (Or accept the static trace — every branch condition is visible in the two files.)

findings.title: Dismissing a same-day-bounced row deletes its sentAt and hands back a phantom budget slot (B-071 regression vector)
findings.expected: The daily budget counts what Resend accepted today, immune to later status changes — the whole point of counting off sentAt (B-071).
findings.actual: A bounce webhook flips a sent row to status='failed' while keeping sentAt (webhook route lines 106-128); dismissMail then hard-deletes any failed row (`prisma.outboundEmail.delete`). If the admin dismisses bounced rows the same UTC day they were sent, each delete removes a row dailyBudget's `sentAt >= startOfUtcDay()` count (email-queue.ts:397-399) was counting, so the app re-spends slots Resend already counted. More than 5 same-day dismissed bounces eats the deliberate DAILY_CAP margin (95 vs 100) and pushes sends into hard provider rejections — the exact B-071 failure resurrected through the admin's own button.
findings.argument: dailyBudget counts rows, not a ledger; delete removes the row; the bounce path is the one way a failed row carries a same-day sentAt; nothing in dismissMail checks sentAt's day.
findings.proofPlan: Rolled-back transaction: BEGIN; SELECT the budget count; DELETE one OutboundEmail row with sentAt >= today's UTC midnight and status='failed'; re-SELECT and observe the count drop; ROLLBACK. Code trace covers the webhook half.

findings.title: A provider-quota-deferred verify row shows 'A link has been sent to your email' for up to 24 hours, with no resend button
findings.expected: The banner never claims a mail was sent when nothing was accepted; 'queued' (the only state naming a delay) covers any row deferred to the next budget window.
findings.actual: When Resend answers daily_quota_exceeded (real quota out of step with the local count — drift the 5-message margin can lose to timeouts-that-landed, dev fake-sends, or dismissed bounces), bookFailure leaves the row 'queued' with nextAttemptAt = next UTC midnight (email-queue.ts:268-270). verificationMailState's 'queued' answer is gated only on OUR arithmetic (`budget.verifyRemaining <= 0`, line 873); with local budget apparently available, the row is merely not `due` (line 883), the send is skipped, the fresh re-read still says 'queued', and the function returns 'imminent' (line 913) — whose comment 'it is minutes, not tomorrow' is false for this branch. The banner renders imminent as 'A link has been sent to your email. Tap on it to verify your account.' (verify-email-banner.tsx:198-201) and hides the resend button, for up to a day. The same overstatement shows during ordinary transient backoff windows (1-60 min) after a first-attempt provider hiccup, when nothing has ever been accepted.
findings.argument: The state machine has no branch for 'row individually deferred to the budget window while global arithmetic shows budget'; row-level nextAttemptAt only suppresses the send, never selects the 'queued' answer; the imminent copy asserts a completed send.
findings.proofPlan: Deterministic code trace of verificationMailState lines 843-913 against a row with status='queued', nextAttemptAt=tomorrow, plus a browser step: set such a row for a test account (rolled back after) and read the banner text on any authenticated page.

findings.title: DRAIN_LEASE_MS (45s) is shorter than a worst-case pass (8 sends x 10s timeout ≈ 80s+), so the one-pass-at-a-time guarantee lapses exactly during provider brownouts
findings.expected: One drain pass fleet-wide (the B-072 fix): the lease outlives any pass it guards, or is renewed mid-pass.
findings.actual: A pass sends up to BATCH=8 rows; each sendMail is bounded only by SEND_TIMEOUT_MS=10s (email.ts:77), plus per-row mint/DB work. During a Resend brownout where sends time out, one pass runs ~80s while the lease expires at 45s and is never renewed between iterations — so the next page view's drain takes the lease and runs concurrently, re-creating the parallel-pass 429 pressure the lease exists to prevent, at the exact moment the provider is struggling (each 429/timeout burning a deferral on some row). Per-row claims still prevent double-sends and budget counts in-flight rows, so the damage is bounded to overlapping passes and faster deferral burn. mail-policy.test.mjs:76 pins ONE_PASS_MS=30_000 as 'the time one pass takes', which the 45s lease and the 80s worst case both contradict.
findings.argument: Arithmetic on committed constants: 8 x 10_000ms > 45_000ms; drainWithLease's loop (704-744) neither re-checks nor extends the lease; takeDrainLease's expiry predicate (`expiresAt: { lte: now }`) hands the lease over the moment it lapses.
findings.proofPlan: Constant arithmetic plus a code read; optionally simulate with a stubbed sendMail sleeping 10s per row and two concurrent drainMailQueue calls in a script against a scratch schema (orchestrator's call — no live DB needed to validate the arithmetic).

findings.title: sendTimeLabel's docblock claims browser-timezone formatting while the code formats in IST, and the banner shows the IST time with no timezone marker
findings.expected: The comment and the code agree, and a member abroad can read 'your link goes out tomorrow at 5:30 am' as a time on their own clock or see which zone it belongs to.
findings.actual: The JSDoc (lines 38-43) says 'Formatted in the BROWSER's timezone: the server cannot know where the reader is', but the implementation passes `timeZone: VALLEY_TIME_ZONE` (IST) to toLocaleTimeString and compares valley day-keys. A member in London reading 'tomorrow at 5:30 am' is off by 4.5-5.5 hours; the admin page's identical clock at least appends 'IST' (admin/mail/page.tsx:100-107), the banner does not. The inner comment shows the IST choice was deliberate, which makes the outer docblock the defect (the brief's rule: a comment that mis-describes its code is bug evidence) plus a missing 'IST' in the member-facing copy.
findings.argument: Direct contradiction between lines 38-43 and lines 47-57 of the same function; banner renders `Your link goes out {timeLabel}` with no zone suffix (line 189).
findings.proofPlan: Read the function; render the banner with a queued state in a browser whose locale/timezone is non-Indian and confirm the label is IST-anchored and unmarked.

findings.title: Demo visitors cannot save the profile contact block or admission number: EDITABLE_PROFILE_FIELDS drifted behind the schema (showEmail, phone, phones, admissionNumber missing)
findings.expected: docs/spec/demo.md ('They can ... edit their own profile') and the demo.ts comment ('the visitor DOES get to edit their own profile ... this is generous') promise profile editing works in the demo; a contact-block or admission-number save should either succeed or refuse with a written demo sentence.
findings.actual: Every save of the profile contact block, and any admission-number edit, throws DemoWriteError and surfaces as the misleading generic 'That did not go through. Check your connection and try again.' (callAction's ACTION_FAILED). Confirmed by executing the policy function: demoWriteAllowed('User','update', <exact updateContactMethods payload>) === false and <admissionNumber payload> === false.
findings.argument: EDITABLE_PROFILE_FIELDS (src/lib/demo.ts:120-147) was written 2026-08-07 and never updated for columns added since: showEmail (audit B-050), phones (repeater), admissionNumber (commit 7ae062a). updateContactMethods (src/components/profile/profile-actions.ts:307-330) UNCONDITIONALLY includes showEmail, phone and phones in its data object, so isOwnProfileEdit (demo.ts:227-246) hits a non-allowlisted key and returns false on every call — even when the visitor only edited instagram. updateProfileField's admissionNumber case (profile-actions.ts:~105-115) writes data.admissionNumber, also absent from the set. Both are live UI paths: letterhead-profile.tsx:456 calls updateContactMethods and :413 calls updateProfileField, and the demo persona's own profile renders the editable letterhead. The Prisma extension (prisma.ts:81-84) throws DemoWriteError; profile-actions has no runAction wrapper, so the rejection reaches callAction (src/lib/call-action.ts) which returns the 'check your connection' sentence. Latent sibling: updateUserProfile (src/components/settings/actions.ts:110-132, writes phone/phones/admissionNumber) is equally refused, though it appears to have no UI caller since the settings page was removed.
findings.proofPlan: Already proven at policy level by executing demoWriteAllowed with the exact action payloads (returns false). Live confirmation: on the demo deployment, open your own profile, edit any contact row (or just toggle nothing and press save), observe the generic connection error while name/bio/city edits save fine. Fix-validation: add the four columns to EDITABLE_PROFILE_FIELDS and re-run node --test src/lib/demo.test.mjs.

findings.title: Production's daily /api/demo/reset cron GET is redirected to /login by the proxy — the carefully-built 200 no-op branch is unreachable, defeating its own stated purpose
findings.expected: route.ts:86-91 and docs/spec/demo.md:299-301 both state that on the production deployment the nightly 20:00 UTC cron GET returns { ok: true, skipped: 'not the demo deployment' } with a 200, 'so the nightly run reports success instead of raising a failed-cron alert every morning'.
findings.actual: On production the cron GET never reaches the route handler: publicPaths in proxy.ts (lines 203-247) lists /api/catchups/tick and /api/retention/sweep but NOT /api/demo/reset, so the sessionless server-to-server GET falls through to the !sessionCookie branch (proxy.ts:256-265) and is answered with a 307 redirect to /login?next=/api/demo/reset — daily. The comment and spec describe behavior the middleware makes impossible.
findings.argument: vercel.json ships the 0 20 * * * cron to both projects (both deploy from this repo; the spec confirms 'The same cron entry exists on the production project'). The proxy matcher covers /api/demo/reset (only _next/static, images etc. are excluded). Vercel's cron invoker sends no session cookie. The two sibling cron routes were each explicitly added to publicPaths with comments saying they are listed 'only to get past the redirect-to-login' — the identical treatment was forgotten for this route when the GET no-op was added. On the demo deployment it works only because the IS_DEMO branch (proxy.ts:110-125) passes everything through before the auth check. Consequence depends on how Vercel's dashboard records a 307 (failed-cron noise that trains the owner to ignore cron alerts, or a spurious 'success' against /login if redirects are followed) — either way the designed contract does not hold.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: curl -sI 'https://rishivalley.space/api/demo/reset' (GET, no cookies, no auth header) — expect HTTP 307 Location /login?next=%2Fapi%2Fdemo%2Freset instead of the JSON no-op. Then check the production project's Vercel dashboard cron history for the recorded daily status. Fix-validation: add '/api/demo/reset' to publicPaths and re-curl for the 200 JSON.

findings.title: Demo has zero rate limiting plus unbounded allowlisted creates; a disk-fill makes the nightly reset itself fail (30s transaction cannot clear a bloated table), so the demo cannot self-heal
findings.expected: The demo's stated safety story is 'the worst a visitor can do is scribble on a sandbox that restores itself every night' (demo.ts header) and rate-limit.ts's header claims 'its own default-deny Prisma allowlist is its real wall'. Abuse should at worst vandalize content until 20:00 UTC.
findings.actual: rateLimit()/hasBudget()/consume() all return open unconditionally when IS_DEMO (rate-limit.ts:156, 175, 190; the demo project deliberately has no Upstash keys either, :116). ALLOWED_WRITE_MODELS permits unbounded anonymous create on Post/Comment/Like/Notification/CatchupEntry etc., with postSchema allowing 20,000 chars per row (validators.ts postSchema + POST_CONTENT_MAX.letter). A trivial loop against createPost (no login, no token, no throttle) grows the free-tier demo Postgres without bound. The recovery mechanism then breaks on its own guard: seedDemo's clear phase runs post.deleteMany({}) inside one transaction capped at SEED_TRANSACTION_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000 (src/lib/demo-seed/seed.ts:74, 519-530); a table pushed into the millions of rows exceeds 30s on a free-tier instance, Prisma aborts, the transaction rolls back, and every reset — cron and button — 500s forever, leaving the demo permanently vandalized/full until manual SQL intervention.
findings.argument: The allowlist governs WHICH models can be written, not HOW MUCH; the 'real wall' claim is false for volume. The unfiltered-bulk-write check (demo.ts:204) blocks a one-call wipe but not a many-call fill. The reset's atomic-rewrite design (correct for consistency, audit M61) is exactly what makes it unable to clear a huge table incrementally: partial progress always rolls back. Compounding: each anonymous request also gets a full server-action execution and Postgres write with no per-IP ceiling anywhere on the demo deployment.
findings.proofPlan: No live attack needed. (a) Code trace above is complete; (b) read-only scale check against any Postgres of the demo's tier: EXPLAIN/timing of DELETE on a synthetic multi-million-row table inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK shows >30s; (c) optionally, on the demo deployment, script ~50 createPost calls in a minute and observe none are throttled (then press Reset to clean up). Mitigation shape for the fixer: a modest per-IP limiter for demo writes (Upstash keys on the demo project, or an edge-level cap), and/or batched pre-transaction deletes in seedDemo when row counts are large.

findings.title: 'Start a Catch-up' is reachable in the demo but structurally can never succeed: Group/GroupMember are not allowlisted, so creation dies as a generic retryable error
findings.expected: demo.ts's allowlist rationale says the Catch-up loop 'is worth letting people drive end to end'; every deliberately-closed catchup action carries a written demo sentence (endCatchup:801, leave/archive/delete:1811/1856/1894, nudge:1993). Creation should either work or refuse with such a sentence, or /catchups/new should be in DEMO_CLOSED_PATHS.
findings.actual: /catchups/new is not in DEMO_CLOSED_PATHS (demo.ts:263-282 / proxy.ts:30-49), createCatchupWithPeople has no IS_DEMO front door, its gates all pass in demo (member-gate.ts:57 ok, rate-limit open), and the transaction's first statement tx.group.create (actions.ts:508, with nested members create) is model Group — absent from ALLOWED_WRITE_MODELS — so the extension throws DemoWriteError. runAction (actions.ts:170-179) converts it to 'Something went wrong. Please try again.', an invitation to retry something that can never work. Executed proof: demoWriteAllowed('Group','create',{data:{...members:{create:[]}}}) === false.
findings.argument: The three-layer posture worked as designed (layer 3 caught it), but the product outcome is a flagship flow in the showcase that renders, accepts input (people picker via the open /api/users/search), and then fails generically. Either Group+GroupMember belong on the allowlist (creation writes are then wiped by reset — group/groupMember/groupInvite ARE in seedDemo's clear list, so reset already handles visitor-created ones), or the flow needs a front-door sentence / closed path. createCatchup (actions.ts:332, the groupId variant) has the same hole one layer later.
findings.proofPlan: On the demo deployment: /catchups -> Start a Catch-up -> name it, pick two people, submit; observe 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' and no catchup created. Policy half already proven by executing demoWriteAllowed.

findings.title: demoWriteAllowed passes nested writes into disallowed models wholesale when the top-level model is allowlisted, contradicting the guard's 'born blocked, not born exposed' contract
findings.expected: The backstop's stated contract is that a write on a model the policy does not list is refused wherever it appears, and demo.test.mjs claims 'a visitor cannot smuggle a write through a nested relation'.
findings.actual: The nested-relation defense exists only for the User-model special case (isOwnProfileEdit rejects object-valued data). For any model in ALLOWED_WRITE_MODELS the verdict is `return true` (demo.ts:206) with args never inspected, and the Prisma extension fires once per top-level operation — so nested writes ride through. Executed proof: demoWriteAllowed('Post','update',{where:{id},data:{author:{update:{role:'admin'}}}}) === true, and demoWriteAllowed('PhotoLove','create',{data:{photo:{create:{url:'https://evil/x.png',...}}}}) === true — the latter is a nested create of Photo, the model the policy most emphatically closes.
findings.argument: Not currently exploitable: no reachable server action passes visitor-controlled data into a nested-write position (actions build their own data literals; images go through ownedUploadUrls; the only nested creates are group.members, blocked at the Group level anyway, and poll options, which are allowlisted). But the guard's entire justification is defending against 'a server action added six months from now', and for the nested-write shape that future action is born exposed, not born blocked. The unit test's name overstates the coverage, which is itself the kind of comment-vs-code drift this audit flags.
findings.proofPlan: Policy half already proven by executing demoWriteAllowed with the two payloads above (both true). Wiring half, if desired: scripts/demo/verify-guard.mts extended with a nested-write probe against the demo DB (orchestrator-run, demo DB only). Fix shape: recursively scan data for relation-operation keys (create/update/delete/connectOrCreate/upsert/deleteMany/updateMany/set on object values) and refuse them on allowlisted models too, or refuse any object-valued data field the same way the User branch already does.
findings.taxonomy: defense-in-depth gap / nested-write bypass of model allowlist

findings.title: First-open race on /notice/[id] still mints duplicate admin threads (the exact M46 failure, incompletely fixed)
findings.expected: Resolving an old admin_note notification into a thread is idempotent under concurrency: two simultaneous first opens produce exactly one AdminThread.
findings.actual: The page does findFirst (memberId, kind:'notice', createdAt) then openAdminNoticeThread -> prisma.adminThread.create with no backing unique constraint. Two concurrent first opens both read null and both create, leaving the member two identical conversations and the admin inbox two rows — the precise scenario the comment block (lines 41-53, 'bug audit M46') claims is fixed. The fix only made SEQUENTIAL revisits idempotent (the link-rewrite check at line 37).
findings.argument: AdminThread (prisma/schema.prisma:637-665) has no @@unique on (memberId, kind, createdAt) — only reportId is unique — so nothing at the database level collapses the two creates. The check-then-insert window spans lines 54-69; both racers then run notification.update (line 71) last-write-wins, so one of the two threads is linked and the other is orphaned but visible in /messages and the admin inbox forever. openAdminNoticeThread (src/lib/admin-threads-server.ts:94-118) is a plain create, not an upsert.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only confirmation is already complete (no unique in schema, plain create in code). Live proof: against a test account holding an unresolved admin_note notification, fire two concurrent authenticated GETs at /notice/<id> and count AdminThread rows where memberId=<test> and kind='notice' — 2 rows reproduces it; the comment promised 1.

findings.title: getWordleAnswer has no fetch deadline: a hanging NYT endpoint blocks the /dark-mode render instead of reaching the fallback
findings.expected: Per the file's own header ('if the endpoint is unreachable ... a small deterministic fallback keeps the gate functional rather than unpassable'), any NYT failure mode degrades to the FALLBACK_WORDS pick.
findings.actual: The fetch carries no AbortSignal/timeout, so the try/catch only covers FAST failures (DNS refusal, TCP reset, bad JSON). A SLOW failure — the connection accepted but the response never arriving, throttling, a blackholed route — hangs the await until the platform kills the function, so /dark-mode answers 500/504 for the first visitor of each IST day (later visitors ride the 1-hour data-cache entry once one good fetch lands) and the fallback is never reached.
findings.argument: src/app/(main)/dark-mode/page.tsx:29 does `await getWordleAnswer()` in the server render path; wordle.ts:36-40 is `fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 3600 } })` with no `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(...)`. The catch at line 47 only fires on rejection, and a hang does not reject inside the function's budget. The data cache is keyed on the IST-dated URL, so the first request of every valley day re-takes the risk.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is sufficient (no signal in the options object). Safe local repro: run the same fetch shape in node against a non-routable address (e.g. 10.255.255.1) and observe it exceed any page budget before rejecting, versus the same call with AbortSignal.timeout(3000). Bonus check while there: curl https://www.nytimes.com/svc/wordle/v2/<tomorrow-IST>.json at ~19:00 UTC to confirm the endpoint serves IST-ahead dates at all.
findings.taxonomy: unbounded external call in render path / resource leak

findings.title: A stale or revoked session cookie drops the deep link: (main) layout redirects to /login without the ?next= the proxy preserves
findings.expected: A member following a shared deep link (a letter, a profile, a Catch-up) lands back on that link after signing in — the behaviour bug audit B-022 established for the no-cookie case via proxy.ts line 263.
findings.actual: The B-022 fix only covers visitors with NO session cookie. A visitor with an EXPIRED or REVOKED cookie (JWT past maxAge, or credentialVersion bumped by a password reset/block) passes the proxy's cookie-presence check, reaches the (main) layout, fails auth(), and hits the bare `redirect("/login")` at line 25 — no next param — so after signing in they land on /feed and the link they followed is lost.
findings.argument: proxy.ts:256-264 appends `next=pathname+search` only when the cookie is ABSENT; when a cookie exists but auth() rejects it (src/app/(main)/layout.tsx:22-26), the layout redirects without one. The layout has the path available (x-pathname is read three lines later for touchLastSeen via currentPath(), line 147-150), so `redirect("/login?next=" + encodeURIComponent(path))` is possible with data already in hand. Revocation-by-credentialVersion makes stale-cookie-in-browser a designed, recurring state, not just a 30-day-expiry corner.
findings.proofPlan: In a browser, set authjs.session-token to any garbage value (or use a session ended by a password reset on a test account), open /letters/<some-id>, observe the Location chain: layout redirect to /login with no next param; sign in; land on /feed instead of the letter.
findings.taxonomy: boundary value / inconsistent handling of the same case across two gates

findings.title: drainPendingImagePurges can throw P2025 from its failure branch when a concurrent drain deleted the row
findings.expected: The drain is race-safe against its own concurrency, as the delete branch's catch (line 331, 'row already taken by a concurrent drain') shows the authors intended.
findings.actual: Only the DELETE branch is guarded. The failure branch's `prisma.pendingImagePurge.update({ where: { id: row.id } })` (lines 338-341) throws P2025 if a concurrent drain removed the row between this drain's findMany and its update. The throw propagates out of drainPendingImagePurges: in the nightly sweep it is absorbed by step()'s catch (retention.ts:97-99, step aborts early), but in deletePost (src/app/(main)/feed/actions.ts:82) and the collection delete (collection/actions.ts:630) it rejects the server action AFTER the post is already deleted, so the member sees the generic failure toast for a delete that succeeded.
findings.argument: Two drains can hold the same row: the sweep's unfiltered findMany (take 500) and a purge/post-delete's url-scoped drain. Sequence: A reads row X, B reads row X; A's delImage succeeds and deletes X; B's delImage returns false (an R2 refusal — the exact bad-minute case this table exists for); B enters the else branch and updates a row that no longer exists; Prisma update on zero matches throws P2025. No catch on that await.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace plus a unit-style simulation: stub delImage to return false and prisma.pendingImagePurge.update to throw a {code:'P2025'} object, call drainPendingImagePurges, observe the rejection. Fix-shape check for the validator: the update needs the same .catch(() => {}) or an updateMany that the delete branch already models.
findings.taxonomy: unguarded concurrent-delete race in an error path

findings.title: viewport themeColor is hard-coded to the light background, so dark-theme members get warm-paper browser chrome around a charcoal app
findings.expected: The browser chrome matches the rendered page in both themes — the stated purpose of the constant (its own comment: iOS chrome slabs 'ruin the immersive nature vibe', owner 2026-07-30).
findings.actual: viewport.themeColor is the static light token #E4E1D5. Dark mode shipped 2026-08-02 (.dark --background is #1C2420, globals.css:291) and the theme cookie is already read in this same file (line 68), but the viewport export predates dark and was never made conditional — so a dark-theme member on iOS gets light-paper Safari chrome around a dark page, the exact mismatch the constant exists to prevent, inverted. manifest.ts:26-27 has the same fixed values (defensible for an install-time splash, but the same drift).
findings.argument: Next.js supports `export async function generateViewport()` which can await the same getThemeCookie() the layout already calls and return themeColor '#1C2420' for dark. Nothing does; grep confirms the only themeColor in src is this static one.
findings.proofPlan: As a dark-theme test account, view the document head: <meta name="theme-color" content="#E4E1D5"> while <html class="dark">. Visual: open the site dark on an iPhone and look at the Safari toolbar colour.
findings.taxonomy: stale constant after a feature shipped / theme divergence

findings.title: PostHog config comment promises input-content masking that the two lines under it do not implement
findings.expected: Per the comment ('Belt and braces on top of replay being off: never transmit the contents of an input'), the config adds an explicit masking layer over autocapture.
findings.actual: The two options set are `mask_all_element_attributes: false` (which EXPLICITLY leaves attribute capture ON — the opposite register of the comment) and `mask_personal_data_properties: true` (which masks personal data in event/campaign properties, not element content). Neither governs input contents. Input values not being captured currently rests entirely on posthog-js autocapture's own defaults (it treats input/select/textarea as sensitive), not on anything this config asserts; the option that would implement the stated belt-and-braces is `mask_all_text` (plus flipping mask_all_element_attributes to true).
findings.argument: This is the brief's 'comment that mis-describes its code' class: if a future posthog-js default change or an autocapture config tweak ever loosened input handling, this file believes it has a second layer and has none. The privacy stakes are the stated ones — a private alumni network with names, addresses and phone numbers on screen.
findings.proofPlan: Read posthog-js config docs/source for mask_all_element_attributes, mask_personal_data_properties and mask_all_text; confirm mask_all_text is absent here. Optional live check: with NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_DEV=1 on a dev server, click near a filled input and inspect the outgoing /ingest autocapture payload for element attributes.
findings.taxonomy: comment/config mismatch — guard that does not guard

findings.title: Notification pagination silently ends when the cursor row was pruned by another device's bell-open
findings.expected: Scrolling the bell keeps paging until the real end of the member's notifications.
findings.actual: getNotifications pages with `cursor: { id }` + skip 1. The KEEP=100 prune (lines 44-62) is skipped for cursor pages so THIS scroll cannot delete its own cursor — but a first-page open on another device or tab prunes read rows for the same member, and if the pruned set includes the row this device is holding as nextCursor, Prisma's cursor-on-a-missing-row returns an empty result, so hasMore flips false and the list quietly ends mid-scroll.
findings.argument: The comment at line 43 ('scrolling can never delete rows out from under its own cursor') is true per-request but the guard is per-request only; the cursor lives across requests in client state (notification-bell.tsx nextCursor) while any concurrent first-page open (deviceB, a second tab, even the same tab reopening the panel — handleOpen refetches page one and prunes) can delete it. Prisma documents that a nonexistent cursor record yields no results rather than resuming after it.
findings.proofPlan: Two-tab repro on a test account with >120 notifications, most read: tab A opens the bell and scrolls one page (cursor now held); tab B opens the bell (fires the prune); tab A scrolls again and the list ends early despite hasMore having been true. Read-only alternative: confirm Prisma's missing-cursor semantics against a scratch query.
findings.taxonomy: pagination edge — cursor at deleted row

findings.title: createPost skips the verified-member gate for any submission carrying saveAsDraft=true, so an unverified account can publish a plain post to the whole feed
findings.expected: Only kind=letter submissions with saveAsDraft may skip requireVerifiedMember (drafts are private); anything that will be stored status=published must pass the Stage 2 gate, as the comment and audit M32 intend.
findings.actual: The gate-skip condition and the draft condition disagree. Line 113 computes savingDraft from the raw form flag alone (`formData.get("saveAsDraft") === "true"`) and skips requireVerifiedMember; line 203 computes isDraft as `kind === "letter" && saveAsDraft === true`. A crafted call with saveAsDraft="true" and kind omitted (defaults to "post") skips the gate but is NOT a draft, so line 261 stores status:"published". requireVerifiedMember (src/lib/member-gate.ts:59-60) is what enforces BOTH emailConfirmed and verifyState==="verified", so a Stage 0 account (email never confirmed) can publish text posts visible to every member. AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING (src/lib/posts.ts:60) only filters isBlocked, so the post renders normally in every feed.
findings.argument: Gate: lines 113-117 `const savingDraft = formData.get("saveAsDraft") === "true"; if (!savingDraft) { const gate = await requireVerifiedMember(); ... }`. Draft decision: line 203 `const isDraft = parsed.data.kind === "letter" && parsed.data.saveAsDraft === true;`. postSchema (src/lib/validators.ts:245) allows saveAsDraft on any kind (`saveAsDraft: z.boolean().optional()` with only a comment saying it is 'only meaningful when kind === letter'). Nothing between line 117 and the create at 247 re-checks verification for the non-draft path. publishDraft has its own gate but this path never goes through it.
findings.proofPlan: Create a throwaway account via signup and do not confirm the email. From its session, invoke the createPost server action with FormData {content:"probe", saveAsDraft:"true"} (no kind field). Expect {success:true, isDraft:false} and the post visible on /feed from a second account. Delete the row and the throwaway afterwards. Pure code trace also suffices: the two conditions quoted above are the whole mechanism.
findings.taxonomy: auth-gate bypass / boolean condition mismatch between gate and effect

findings.title: confirmContribution (and the webhook's captured branch) can flip a refunded/disputed contribution back to paid, re-inflating the recovery total and regranting a bird pick
findings.expected: "paid" transitions should only be reachable from created/failed. A row Razorpay has moved to refunded or disputed must stay there; replaying the browser success callback must be a no-op.
findings.actual: confirmContribution guards with `if (contribution.status !== "paid")` then updates to paid unconditionally (lines 181-186), stamping a fresh paidAt. A member whose payment was refunded or charged back (webhook moves paid→refunded/disputed at razorpay/webhook/route.ts:229-233) can re-invoke confirmContribution with the signature triple their browser legitimately received at payment time — the signature stays valid forever and identifies the order, not its current state — and the row returns to "paid". Consequences: the /support recovered total and "Given, all time" count money that came back, and chooseBird's regrant rule (`paidAt: { gt: me.birdPickedAt }`, support/actions.ts:249) sees the refreshed paidAt as a NEW paid contribution, opening another bird pick for money the member no longer gave. The webhook's own captured branch has the sibling hole: its CAS is `status: { not: "paid" }` (route.ts:163-175), so a redelivered payment.captured event after refund.processed also resurrects the row.
findings.argument: confirmContribution: check-then-write with the wrong predicate — it excludes only the state it wants to reach, not the terminal reversal states. The webhook comment says '"paid" is terminal' but neither writer treats refunded/disputed as terminal. chooseBird's ledger explicitly trusts paidAt because it 'is written by the same signature-verified paths that set status' — true, and exactly why the replay works.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only trace is sufficient (predicates quoted above). Live check without money: in a rolled-back transaction via run-sql.mjs, set a test-mode contribution row to status='refunded', then reason through confirmContribution's two statements; or in test-mode keys make a payment, mark the row refunded by hand, replay the stored callback params from the browser console, and read the row back: status='paid', paidAt=now.
findings.taxonomy: check-then-write with incomplete terminal-state predicate / replayable idempotency token

findings.title: Feed infinite scroll dies silently when the keyset cursor post is deleted (or leaves the visible set); loadComments has the same hole — the M39 fallback was added to the directory only
findings.expected: A post deleted (or hidden/blocked) between two pages of scrolling should not end the feed: the next page should recover, as loadDirectoryPage does with its audit-M39 offset fallback.
findings.actual: loadPosts (recent sort) passes `cursor: { id: keysetCursor }` with no recovery: per the project's own verified M39 record (src/app/(main)/directory/actions.ts:77-91, 'Prisma's cursor needs the row it names to be INSIDE the filtered set... this query answers nothing for a list with hundreds of rows left'), a cursor row that was hard-deleted (deletePost), admin-hidden, or whose author was blocked between pages makes the next page return [], so hasMore=false and "Load more"/infinite scroll ends with older posts unreachable until a full reload. loadComments (line 1414) has the same shape: a cursor root comment that stops matching VISIBLE_COMMENT (author blocked with no visible replies) ends the thread pagination early. getNotifications (notifications/actions.ts:34) is a third instance: the KEEP=100 prune on another device can delete this device's read cursor row mid-scroll.
findings.argument: Same Prisma cursor semantics the first audit proved and fixed for the directory (M39) and admin people list (Low 12); the fix was never propagated to loadPosts, loadComments, or getNotifications. Posts are the surface where hard deletes actually happen (deletePost is member-facing), so the feed is the likeliest place a member hits it.
findings.proofPlan: In dev: load /feed, note the nextCursor post id after page 1, delete that post from a second session, request page 2 with the old cursor (call loadPosts from the console) — expect posts:[], hasMore:false while older posts exist. The directory file's comment already documents the identical measured behavior on this exact stack.
findings.taxonomy: pagination edge: cursor at deleted row, missing recovery fallback

findings.title: submitEntry (catch-up answer autosave) has no lost-update guard: a stale device silently overwrites a newer answer, and the clear-to-withdraw path can delete or resurrect content under out-of-order saves
findings.expected: The same protection editPost got in audit M66: an autosaving surface open on two devices must not let the stale copy silently replace the newer one, and out-of-order completion of rapid saves must not clobber newer state.
findings.actual: submitEntry is an unconditional upsert keyed on (promptId, authorId) with no version token: a member with the answer sheet open on laptop and phone who writes three paragraphs on one, then touches the other, has the stale copy overwrite the paragraphs — both say saved (the exact scenario M66 fixed for letter drafts). Additionally lines 1432-1436 delete the row whenever the post-upsert read shows all fields empty; with two saves in flight out of order (save A carrying text, save B clearing it), B committing first deletes the row and A then re-creates it, resurrecting text the member deleted — or A committing first is wiped by B, per-field conditionality notwithstanding, because both writes touch the same field.
findings.argument: Compare editPost's baseUpdatedAt CAS (feed/actions.ts:582-609, audit M66) — same autosave shape, same multi-device exposure, guard present there and absent here. CatchupEntry has updatedAt available for the same token approach.
findings.proofPlan: Open the same catch-up answer in two browser profiles. Type a paragraph in A and let it save; in B (still showing the old text) change one character and blur. Reload: A's paragraph is gone with no warning. Contrast the letters desk, which answers 'This letter has changed somewhere else.'
findings.taxonomy: lost update: read-modify-write autosave without version precondition; out-of-order completion

findings.title: submitPrompt's cap-and-position transaction claims a concurrency guarantee READ COMMITTED does not give: two simultaneous submits can both pass the cap and take the same position
findings.expected: The comment: 'inside the same transaction as the cap check so two questions arriving together cannot both see room for the last slot' — i.e. the ceiling holds and positions stay unique under concurrency.
findings.actual: The $transaction at 894-921 wraps an aggregate (max position + count) and a create, but no isolationLevel is passed and src/lib/prisma.ts sets none, so both concurrent transactions run READ COMMITTED: each aggregate reads the pre-insert state, both see count < MAX and the same _max, both insert. Result: the per-Round ceiling overshoots by the number of concurrent submitters, and two prompts land on the same position (no unique on [editionId, position] — deliberately, per TRAPS — so render order for the pair is undefined until a Keeper reorders). The brief's rule applies: a comment that mis-describes its code is itself bug evidence.
findings.argument: Postgres READ COMMITTED does not lock rows an aggregate merely read; a transaction gives atomicity, not mutual exclusion between two aggregates. The intended guarantee needs SERIALIZABLE (with a P2034 retry), a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE anchor, or an advisory-free CAS shape like the ones the same file uses elsewhere.
findings.proofPlan: Fire two submitPrompt calls concurrently at an edition holding MAX-1 accepted prompts (script with Promise.all against a dev catch-up); read back count = MAX+1 and duplicated position values. Or accept the isolation-level argument as the proof and just fix the comment/shape.
findings.taxonomy: TOCTOU inside a non-serializable transaction; comment mis-describes code

findings.title: setReminderPref and submitEntry use bare upserts on @@unique keys without the P2002 retry the codebase's own rule requires, so a double-tap first-write yields a false 'Something went wrong'
findings.expected: Per upsertCatchupPref's own docblock ('The P2002 retry is not decoration: upsert is a read-then-write inside Postgres') and the charter's sweep rule, every writer behind a @@unique handles P2002.
findings.actual: setReminderPref (line 1977) writes CatchupPref [catchupId,userId] with a plain prisma.catchupPref.upsert instead of the upsertCatchupPref helper eight lines above it: two concurrent first-writes both miss the row, the loser throws P2002, runAction converts it to the generic 'Something went wrong. Please try again.' even though the setting saved. submitEntry's upsert on CatchupEntry [promptId,authorId] (line 1398) has the same exposure for two concurrent first autosaves of an answer.
findings.argument: Prisma upsert on Postgres is findUnique-then-create/update unless it can use the atomic INSERT..ON CONFLICT fast path; the codebase treats the race as real everywhere else (upsertCatchupPref, votePoll, joinBatchGroup all carry the retry) and these two writers were missed.
findings.proofPlan: Promise.all two setReminderPref calls for a catch-up with no pref row from a dev account; observe one {error: 'Something went wrong...'} while the row exists. Code-shape check alone is convincing given the helper's own comment.
findings.taxonomy: missing P2002 handler on @@unique writer (charter sweep class 1)

findings.title: startThread and replyToThread have no double-submit guard: a double-tap or two-tab send files the same message twice and pages the admins twice
findings.expected: Free-text creators carry the DOUBLE_SUBMIT_MS twin check (createPost, createComment, createCatchupWithPeople all do, per audit M35/Low 29): the second identical write within 10s returns the first row.
findings.actual: startThread creates an AdminThread + first message with no twin lookup (line 88), and replyToThread creates a message with none (line 138); the only guards are hourly rate limits, which two concurrent taps both pass. A mobile double-tap on Send creates two identical threads (or two identical replies), each with its own notifyAdmins fan-out — one row of admin-bell noise per admin per duplicate, and the member sees two conversations for one message.
findings.argument: double-submit.ts names its consumers as 'the feed and Catch-ups'; the messages surface was left out despite being the same shape (free text, no possible unique index, client in-flight ref can't see a second tab). Class 1 of the charter's three race classes, at a writer that pages a human.
findings.proofPlan: Throttle the network in dev, double-click Send on /messages' composer; observe two AdminThread rows with identical body and createdAt within a second, and two admin notifications.
findings.taxonomy: duplicate rows from double invocation; no unique constraint, no twin-window guard

findings.title: Collection contributions have no duplicate guard: concurrent double-submission mints two Photo rows (and two stored objects), and the per-account quota is check-then-insert
findings.expected: One tap, one photo; the MAX_PHOTOS_PER_ACCOUNT quota holds.
findings.actual: contributePhotoDirect (create at line 418) and contributePhoto (line 218) have no twin check: two overlapping invocations with the same staged key both HEAD/fetch the original before either deletes it, both re-encode, and both create Photo rows with distinct createId() object names — a duplicate photo in the approval queue and duplicate bytes billed in R2 (the sequential case fails safe because the first call deletes the staged original). photoQuotaError (lines 114-120) is a count-then-refuse with no constraint behind it, so N concurrent contributions can overshoot the quota by N-1.
findings.argument: Class 1 (double invocation → duplicate rows, nothing unique to dedupe on) plus classic check-then-insert on the quota. Bounded blast radius (per-account, admin-moderated), hence Low.
findings.proofPlan: In dev, call contributePhotoDirect twice in one Promise.all with a single staged key; read back two Photo rows sharing uploaderId and createdAt. Quota half: set a test account to quota-1 and fire two concurrent contributions; count exceeds MAX by one.
findings.taxonomy: double-invocation duplicates; check-then-insert TOCTOU on quota

findings.title: A family of admin/maintenance writes uses unconditional update/delete on possibly-stale rows and throws raw P2025 instead of answering — two admins moderating together get an unhandled error
findings.expected: The B-040/Lows 52-65 standard the member-facing writers were all converted to: updateMany/deleteMany or a caught P2025, so a row that moved on yields a sentence, not a throw.
findings.actual: approvePhoto (collection/actions.ts:591) is a bare update on a caller-supplied id: if a second admin declined (deleted) the photo first, it throws P2025 out of the action. Same shape at: declinePhoto's photo.delete inside its transaction (line 626, second concurrent decline throws), adminHidePost (src/components/profile/admin-actions.ts:229 on a post the author just hard-deleted), blockWrite's user.update (admin-actions.ts:52 against a just-purged user), adminUpdatePerson (admin/people/actions.ts:127), dismissMail's delete (admin/mail/actions.ts:78 after the findUnique), and drainPendingImagePurges' failure-path update (src/lib/account-purge.ts:338, which unlike its success path has no .catch and can abort a whole drain when a concurrent drain already removed the row). All are admin- or maintenance-facing, so impact is a confusing error surface, not corruption.
findings.argument: Each is find-then-write (or bare write) with no precondition and no isRecordNotFound handling, in a codebase whose own prisma-errors.ts exists precisely to answer these three codes. Client callAction converts the rejection to the generic ACTION_FAILED toast, so the admin is told their action failed when it in fact already happened.
findings.proofPlan: Two admin sessions on /admin's photo queue; approve and decline the same pending photo simultaneously (or approve twice with the row deleted between). Expect one generic failure toast and a P2025 stack in the server log. Code trace of each listed call site is equally conclusive.
findings.taxonomy: missing P2025 handling on stale-row admin writes (grouped)

findings.title: Concurrent avatar replacement orphans an R2 object forever and can leave the older photo live (out-of-order completion)
findings.expected: Replacing an avatar deletes exactly the object being replaced; the newest choice wins; no object survives unreferenced (the TRAPS invariant: 'a URL the code cannot claim is a photograph whose bytes survive its own deletion, silently and for ever').
findings.actual: updateAvatar does read-prev → update → delete-prev with no precondition: two overlapping uploads (two tabs, or a retry racing a slow first call) both read the same prev; whichever update commits second becomes the live photoUrl — which under out-of-order completion is the OLDER choice — and the other call's freshly-uploaded object is referenced by nothing and deleted by nothing, permanently. Both delete prev (idempotent, harmless). removeAvatar racing updateAvatar has the same shape.
findings.argument: Class 3 (out-of-order completion clobbering newer state) plus a resource leak: nothing sweeps `avatars/<id>/` objects that no User.photoUrl names; PendingImagePurge is only populated by delete paths, not by lost races.
findings.proofPlan: In dev (filesystem storage), fire two updateAvatar calls in one Promise.all with different files; list public/uploads/avatars/<id>/ afterwards: two objects, one referenced. Bytes-leak half is provable by the listing alone.

findings.title: skipTrailingSlashRedirect is global but the proxy reinstates no trailing-slash handling, so every trailing-slash URL 404s
findings.expected: A member opening /feed/, /letters/ or /directory/ (hand-typed, autocompleted, or an old link with a slash appended) is redirected to the canonical /feed etc., as Next does by default.
findings.actual: skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true disables that redirect app-wide (added only so PostHog's slash-sensitive /ingest capture endpoint survives), and src/proxy.ts implements no replacement: the App Router receives the pathname with the slash, matches no route, and serves the 404 page (signed-out visitors get the /login bounce of bugs.md 5b).
findings.argument: next.config.ts:199 sets the flag for the /ingest rewrite (comment at :197-198). The installed Next docs (node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/03-file-conventions/proxy.md:229) state the flag 'disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes' and show the expected pattern: the proxy itself re-adds the redirect for all non-exempt paths. src/proxy.ts (read in full, 324 lines) contains no pathname.endsWith('/') handling anywhere — the public-path matcher and DEMO_CLOSED matchers tolerate the slash (startsWith(path + '/')), but the route resolution downstream does not.
findings.proofPlan: With the dev server running: curl -sI http://localhost:3000/letters/ (with a session cookie, or compare /login/ vs /login signed out). A 404 where the slashless URL serves 200/307 confirms it. Fix shape is the doc's own example: in proxy(), redirect any non-/ingest path ending in '/' to its slashless form before the auth check.

findings.title: Back/forward navigation restores stale like/love state on letters/[id] and collection/[id], and one tap then silently inverts the member's real state
findings.expected: Returning to a letter or Collection photo via the browser Back/Forward buttons shows the heart the way the member left it; tapping an unfilled heart likes the item.
findings.actual: The page is restored from the client Router Cache payload rendered BEFORE the like, so the heart shows unliked with the old count. Because toggleLike/toggleBookmark/togglePhotoLove are blind toggles (delete-first), tapping the stale unfilled heart DELETES the existing like: the UI now shows liked/count+1 while the database says unliked, and the two disagree until some later fresh render.
findings.argument: Three facts compose: (1) toggleLike (feed/actions.ts:697-700), toggleBookmark, and togglePhotoLove (collection/actions.ts:559-586) deliberately call no revalidatePath (heart scroll-jump fix), so the Client Cache entry for the detail page is never purged — revalidatePath is exactly what would purge it (revalidatePath.md:175). (2) Next 16's router cache 'Pages are not cached by default but are reused during browser back/forward navigation' (glossary.md:47) and staleTimes.md: 'This doesn't change back/forward caching behavior'. (3) LetterEngagement (src/components/letters/letter-engagement.tsx:34-49) and PhotoLoveButton (collection/[id]/page.tsx:168-172) seed useState from server props and, on tap, set the OPTIMISTIC next value, ignoring the returned {liked:false} — so the inversion is never corrected. Feed/profile/saved surfaces are immune (posts client-fetched on mount); catchup round entries are immune (toggleEntryLove revalidates the round path, catchups/actions.ts:1484/1508 — the in-repo counterexample proving the letters/collection omission is the gap).
findings.proofPlan: Browser against a test account: open a letter, like it, click 'All letters', press browser Back twice / Forward to return to the letter — heart is empty. Tap it, then hard-reload: heart is empty and the Like row is gone (server unliked). Minimal fix: have the handlers adopt result.liked/result.loved from the action response instead of trusting the optimistic value, or revalidate the detail path only (detail pages have no scroll-jump exposure comparable to the feed).

findings.title: Unauthenticated /_next/image plus the *.r2.dev wildcard remotePattern is an open image-optimization amplifier billed to the owner
findings.expected: The image optimizer only transforms photographs from this project's own buckets.
findings.actual: remotePatterns allows ANY https host ending in .r2.dev with no pathname restriction, and the proxy matcher (src/proxy.ts:318-322) exempts _next/image from the session check — so an anonymous stranger can drive /_next/image?url=https://pub-<their-own-free-bucket>.r2.dev/<unique>.png&w=3840 in a loop. Every unique source URL is a fresh transformation of attacker-chosen bytes (arbitrarily large images) on the owner's Vercel account: a quota/cost and CPU amplifier reachable without an account, which is exactly the stability/DoS class this audit was told is in scope.
findings.argument: The wildcard exists to keep pre-2026-08-21 URLs rendering (comment at next.config.ts:210-214), but the legacy bucket host is ONE known pub-<hash>.r2.dev address, not the whole r2.dev namespace; anyone can create a free R2 bucket on that suffix. next/image consumers are real (BirdAvatar routes member photos through the optimizer, bird-avatar.tsx:666). Next 16 clamps w to configured sizes and q to qualities, which caps per-request size but not the per-unique-source-image billing dimension.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: confirm the exact legacy host with grep for pub- in src/lib/upload-shared.ts / env, then check that no stored URL uses any OTHER r2.dev host (read-only SELECT on the six URL columns). Fix is pinning hostname to the one historical pub-<hash>.r2.dev host. Live check: request /_next/image?url=https://pub-unrelated.r2.dev/x.png&w=640 signed out — a 4xx would refute, a fetch attempt confirms.

findings.title: Permissions-Policy payment=() may block PaymentRequest-based methods (Google Pay / UPI intent) inside Razorpay checkout
findings.expected: Every payment method Razorpay offers works in the checkout modal on the /support contribution flow, the most money-sensitive path on the site.
findings.actual: The header 'payment=()' (comment: 'Powerful features nothing here uses') denies the Payment Request API to ALL origins — including the checkout.razorpay.com iframe the site embeds (support-contribute.tsx:157) and the top frame, and a header policy is a ceiling no iframe allow attribute can lift. Razorpay's card/netbanking/UPI-QR flows don't need the API (and 'Confirmed working in production 2026-08-05' at support-contribute.tsx covers those), but its Google Pay and some UPI-intent flows on Chrome/Android use PaymentRequest; those would fail or vanish from the method list for mobile contributors.
findings.argument: securityHeaders (next.config.ts:112-118) applies to '/:path*', so the document embedding the Razorpay iframe carries payment=(). Permissions-Policy inheritance: a feature disabled by the top-level header is disabled for all nested browsing contexts regardless of allow= on the iframe. The comment's claim 'nothing here uses' is contradicted by the site actively integrating a payment provider, which is the comment-mis-describes-code pattern this audit was told to treat as evidence.
findings.proofPlan: Chrome DevTools device emulation is insufficient (Payment Handler needs real Chrome Android); nearest safe checks: (1) open /support, start a contribution, and read the console for Permissions-Policy violation reports; (2) document.featurePolicy.allowsFeature('payment') in the console — false confirms the block is live; (3) a real Android phone attempting the GPay option settles it. Fix if confirmed: payment=(self "https://api.razorpay.com" "https://checkout.razorpay.com").

findings.title: One vercel.json ships both crons to both Vercel projects: /api/demo/reset bounces off the login redirect on production nightly, and /api/catchups/tick fires against the demo
findings.expected: Each deployment runs only its own cron, and every configured cron either succeeds or its failure means something.
findings.actual: Both projects autodeploy from this repo, so both get both crons. On production, /api/demo/reset is not in src/proxy.ts's publicPaths (verified against the full list at proxy.ts:205-247), so the sessionless cron GET is answered 307 → /login every night at 20:00 UTC — the route never runs (correct) but the cron log shows a permanent non-2xx/redirect, training the owner to ignore cron failures, which is how a REAL /api/catchups/tick failure gets missed. On the demo project, /api/catchups/tick passes the demo proxy branch (not in DEMO_CLOSED_APIS, proxy.ts:80-85) and runs nightly against the demo database; it needs CRON_SECRET set on that project or it 401s nightly — and MEMORY records CRON_SECRET as still owed by the owner.
findings.argument: vercel.json:5-14 declares both crons unconditionally; nothing branches on DEMO_MODE at config level (vercel.json cannot). The proxy's demo/real branching determines what each request actually meets, as traced above.
findings.proofPlan: Owner checks both Vercel projects' cron logs: production's demo-reset entries should show 307s; demo's tick entries show whatever CRON_SECRET state produces. Code-side fix options: add /api/demo/reset to publicPaths gated by IS_DEMO only (it already is reachable only in demo), and have each route no-op with 200 on the wrong deployment so the logs stay green and meaningful.

findings.title: /catchups/[catchupId] generateMetadata reveals the Catch-up's custom title to non-members that the page body withholds
findings.expected: The tab title discloses no more than the page: the not-member wall (line 544-557) deliberately shows only the GROUP name ('Join {groupName}...'), and the sibling round page's generateMetadata (round/[editionId]/page.tsx:130-158) checks membership before titling.
findings.actual: This generateMetadata performs no auth() and no membership check: it returns homeTitle(catchup.title, group.name), so a signed-in NON-member opening a shared/guessed catchupId gets the Catch-up's custom title in the browser tab, history, and any link-preview context — the exact tab-title-leak class the first audit fixed on letters (M31) and this feature's own round page guards against.
findings.argument: Lines 60-76: params → prisma.catchup.findUnique({select: {title, group.name}}) → return title, inside a bare try/catch. The page body's loader (line 227-231) returns kind 'not-member' for the same viewer and renders only the group name. The incremental leak over the wall is the custom title alone (the group name is already shown), which is why this is Low rather than Medium — but the inconsistency with the two in-repo precedents makes it look forgotten rather than chosen.
findings.proofPlan: Test account not in some group: visit /catchups/<id> of a Catch-up with a custom title; the tab reads the title while the page shows the members-only wall. Fix: mirror the round page's metadata shape (auth + loadMembership, fall back to 'Catch-ups').

findings.title: User.theme is write-only: the promised 'drift back to the DB truth on next sign-in' does not exist, so a dark-mode member gets light on every new device
findings.expected: Per the comments — theme-actions.ts:55-57 ('a forgotten device should eventually drift back to the DB truth on next sign-in') and lib/theme.ts:6 ('The source of truth for a signed-in member is User.theme') — signing in on a new device, or after the 1-year cookie expires, restores the member's stored dark preference.
findings.actual: grep confirms THEME_COOKIE has exactly one writer (theme-actions.ts:47) and User.theme has no reader that feeds rendering (only the profile edit draft at profile/[id]/page.tsx:419 round-trips it): nothing at sign-in or session establishment copies User.theme into the cookie. Root layout falls back to light (layout.tsx:68), next-themes localStorage is also empty on a new device, so the member who completed the dark gauntlet sees light everywhere and must redo the gauntlet per device. The DB column is dead weight the comments describe as the source of truth.
findings.argument: The audit Low 95 fix deliberately keyed the profile dark-mode TILE on the device cookie, but that decision is about which fact a tile reads, not about abandoning restore-on-sign-in — which two comments still promise. Comment-mis-describes-code, per the brief, is itself the evidence.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace is complete (single grep for THEME_COOKIE and User.theme readers). Live: set dark, sign in from a private window — app renders light with no prompt. Fix options: set the rv-theme cookie from User.theme in the sign-in flow, or delete the column and the two comments so the per-device model is stated honestly.

findings.title: /catchups/join/[token] is the one async DB route with no loading.tsx
findings.expected: Every async route ships a loading.tsx with the warm shimmer (project rule in CLAUDE.md, honored by all 33 other async routes — full find of loading.tsx vs page.tsx compared).
findings.actual: The join page awaits auth() plus two Prisma queries before anything paints, with no loading boundary — and it lives OUTSIDE the (main) group, so a stranger opening an invite link from WhatsApp on a cold Vercel function stares at a blank tab for the whole TTFB of the invite lookup, on the single page whose job is a first impression on a non-member.
findings.argument: find src/app -name loading.tsx lists boundaries for every other async route; src/app/catchups/join has only page.tsx. Because every route renders dynamically (theme cookie), there is no static shell to serve either; a loading.tsx is the only way this route streams anything early.
findings.proofPlan: ls src/app/catchups/join/[token]/ confirms the gap; a throttled-network open of an invite link shows the blank wait. One-file fix following any sibling loading.tsx.

findings.title: Profile page serializes four independent data fetches into a waterfall
findings.expected: After the user row is fetched, the independent reads — viewer cities, the three tab counts, the Photos-grid posts, the contacts-visibility check — run in one parallel batch, as the directory page already does (directory/page.tsx:289 gathers everything in one Promise.all).
findings.actual: Line 143 awaits getViewerCities, then line 158 awaits the counts Promise.all, then line 165 awaits photoPosts, then line 220 awaits viewerMaySeeContacts — three extra sequential round trips to Supabase per profile view. Only viewerCities is a true prerequisite (it feeds visiblePostsWhere); the counts, photoPosts and the contacts check are mutually independent and could join one Promise.all after it.
findings.argument: Read of the page body lines 110-230: visiblePostsWhere depends on viewerCities; postCount/letterCount/savedCount, photoPosts and viewerMaySeeContacts each depend only on visiblePostsWhere or nothing, never on each other. At bom1→ap-south-1 latency this is milliseconds today, but it is the heaviest member-facing page pattern the charter names, and it compounds under pool contention (max 5 connections/instance) at the 2k-member target.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices; if numbers are wanted, next-devtools get_logs timing on a profile view before/after batching. Fix: const [counts, photoPosts, maySeeContacts] = await Promise.all([...]).

findings.title: Catch-up 'days left' disagrees across surfaces: index/status/reminders count 24h blocks, answer page counts valley calendar days
findings.expected: After audit Low 28 established that a calendar word must count valley calendar days, every member-visible countdown for the same deadline should agree.
findings.actual: Only the answer page was converted. `daysUntilLabel` (catchups.ts:700-708, feeding `editionCountdownLabel` and `describeEditionStatus`, rendered on /catchups index cards at src/app/(main)/catchups/page.tsx:164 and the Catch-up home at src/app/(main)/catchups/[catchupId]/page.tsx:371) still computes `Math.ceil(diff/DAY_MS)`, and the daily reminder copy (src/lib/catchups-notify.ts:194-196, daysLeft from `daysLeftUntil`, also duration-ceil) does too. The answer page's `closesLabel` (src/app/(main)/catchups/[catchupId]/answer/page.tsx:56-69) uses `valleyDaysBetween` calendar days.
findings.argument: For a cron-anchored deadline (tick 02:00 UTC = ~07:30 IST, so answersCloseAt = 07:30 IST on day D): from ~07:30 IST on D-1 until midnight (~16.5 hours), the index card and home masthead say 'Answering now, last day' and the bell notification says 'Last day to answer', while clicking through to the answer page says 'Answers close tomorrow.' Separately, every morning between 00:00 IST and the anchor hour, the card reads one day higher than the page ('3 days left' vs 'Answers close in 2 days'), because duration-ceil crosses its boundary at the anchor hour, not at valley midnight. Two member-visible surfaces one click apart contradict each other during the exact hours the label matters most.
