findings.proofPlan: Pure unit check, no DB: evaluate daysUntilLabel({answersCloseAt: '2026-03-11T02:00:00Z'}, now='2026-03-10T04:00:00Z' [09:30 IST D-1]) => 'last day', versus valleyDaysBetween(same at, same now) => 1 ('tomorrow'). Or in the app: set a test edition's answersCloseAt ~22h ahead and view /catchups next to /catchups/<id>/answer.

findings.title: Cron-anchored catch-up deadlines land inside the next tick's jitter window; a quiet group's phase slips a full day roughly half the time
findings.expected: A 7-day answer window closes at the tick 7 days later; the 24h 'Preparing the Round' hold publishes at the next day's tick; nextOpensAt opens the next Round at the tick after the cadence gap.
findings.actual: Every phase deadline for a group nobody visits is minted as `now + N*24h` where `now` is the tick's own invocation instant (advanceDueCatchups sets now = new Date(); answeringPatch:470, preparingPatch:505-510, addCadenceGap via nextOpensAt:957). computeStatus passes only when `t >= m` (catchups.ts:381-385). Vercel Hobby crons fire with up to ~an hour of delay that varies run to run, so the tick N days later has ~50% odds of firing earlier-in-the-hour than the anchoring tick did — missing the deadline by seconds-to-minutes and deferring the transition 24h to the following tick. The layout's lazy tick cannot compensate for a quiet group: it is scoped to `group.members.some.userId` of whoever loads a page (catchups.ts:1156).
findings.argument: Anchor tick T0 fires 02:00 UTC + d0 (d0 in 0..~60min, Hobby). Deadline m = T0 + N*24h exactly. Tick T_N fires 02:00 UTC + dN. If dN < d0, then t < m at T_N, nextEditionStatus returns null, and the transition (answers close, publish, or next-Round open) waits for T_{N+1}. Member-visible: a quiet group's Round sits in 'Preparing the Round' for ~2 days instead of the promised 24h hold, the answer window silently runs ~a day long, and the cadence drifts later at each phase. Self-heals only if any member of that group loads any authenticated page after the deadline passes.
findings.proofPlan: Read two consecutive /api/catchups/tick invocation timestamps in the Vercel logs to measure real jitter; then unit-check computeStatus({status:'preparing', publishAt: X}, now = X - 30s) => 'preparing'. A read-only query for editions whose publishAt is 24h+ past while status='preparing' would show any live occurrences.

findings.title: Admin growth chart and joinedMonth bucket months by naive UTC timestamp, unlike every other bucket in the same file
findings.expected: Month buckets in the valley's calendar, i.e. date_trunc over ("createdAt" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' — the exact shape lines 444, 599-600, 645 and 980 of this file use, with the audit Low 46 / B-101 comments explaining why.
findings.actual: loadGrowth (line 834-838: `date_trunc('month', "createdAt")`) and loadMemberMetrics' joinedMonth (line 1002: `to_char(u."createdAt", 'Mon YYYY')`) truncate the naive UTC wall-time directly. One line above 1002, line 980 does the conversion correctly with a comment 'The valley's day, not UTC's (audit Low 46)'.
findings.argument: Post.createdAt-style columns are timestamp WITHOUT time zone holding UTC wall time. A member who joins between 00:00 and 05:30 IST on the 1st of a month (18:30-24:00 UTC on the last day of the prior month) is counted in the previous month on the /admin/analytics growth curve and shown the wrong 'joined' month in the member metrics table. Admin-only surface, month granularity, 5.5-hour window per month boundary — small but the identical defect class the audit already fixed elsewhere in this file.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only SQL: SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE ("createdAt" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata' >= date_trunc('month', ...) mismatch vs date_trunc('month', "createdAt") for any row created 18:30-24:00 UTC on a month's last day; or insert nothing and just compare the two expressions over existing rows.
findings.taxonomy: UTC-vs-IST day boundary in raw SQL bucketing

findings.title: addMonths uses setUTCMonth, so a monthly/quarterly cadence anchored on the 29th-31st overflows into the following month
findings.expected: publishedAt Jan 31 + 'monthly' lands in February (clamped to Feb 28/29), keeping a monthly rhythm monthly.
findings.actual: addMonths (catchups.ts:308-312) does `d.setUTCMonth(d.getUTCMonth() + n)` with no day clamp: Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 31 = Mar 3; Oct 31 + 1 = Dec 1; Nov 30 + 3 (quarterly) = Feb 30 = Mar 2. addCadenceGap (319-329) feeds nextOpensAt, which is shown to members in footer-tease.tsx ('Next Round opens ...') and drives openNextRoundIfDue; the cadence-change reschedule (catchups/actions.ts:658-669) recomputes from origin through the same function.
findings.argument: JS Date month arithmetic overflows day-of-month silently. A Round published on the 31st schedules the next open 1-3 days past the intended month (and for 'monthly' from Jan 31, no round opens in February at all). Occurrence requires publishedAt on day 29-31, ~10% of monthly publishes; the displayed date is self-consistent so the symptom is only a rhythm that slides.
findings.proofPlan: node -e "const d=new Date('2027-01-31T10:00:00Z'); d.setUTCMonth(d.getUTCMonth()+1); console.log(d.toISOString())" => 2027-03-03. Confirms without touching the app.

findings.title: sendTimeLabel's docstring claims browser-timezone formatting while the code pins IST, and the printed clock time carries no zone marker for diaspora readers
findings.expected: The docstring describes what the code does, and a promised clock time is checkable by the person reading it.
findings.actual: Lines 38-42 say 'Formatted in the BROWSER's timezone: the server cannot know where the reader is', but the code (44-58) formats with `timeZone: VALLEY_TIME_ZONE` and compares valley day-keys — a deliberate later fix (inner comment, lines 54-56) that left the outer docstring describing the pre-fix behaviour. Consequence with teeth: a member abroad whose verification mail is budget-deferred reads 'tomorrow at 5:30 am' — an IST wall time with no 'IST' on it — and checks their inbox at 5:30 am local; the refill is UTC midnight (email-queue.ts nextBudgetResetAt), i.e. midnight in London, 7pm in New York.
findings.argument: The mechanism is exactly the class the audit brief flags: a comment that mis-describes its code. The code itself is internally consistent (IST clock + IST day), but the label omits the zone, so the 'real clock time is a promise somebody can check' rationale fails for any non-IST reader, and the stale docstring invites a future session to 'fix' it back to browser-local, recreating the disagreement the inner comment says was already fixed once.
findings.proofPlan: Code read is sufficient for the docstring contradiction (lines 38-42 vs 47-49). For the copy: render the queued banner state with a machine timezone other than IST and confirm the string shows 5:30 am with no zone qualifier.
findings.taxonomy: comment-code mismatch / missing timezone qualifier in member copy

findings.title: Audit-log purge dates are UTC day-strings while the member's email names the valley day; the two disagree by one day for requests made 00:00-05:30 IST
findings.expected: The date the admin reads in /admin/audit for a deletion request matches the date the member was promised in the confirmation email.
findings.actual: The audit detail uses `purgeAt.toISOString().slice(0, 10)` (UTC day, settings/actions.ts:339) and the retention sweep's purge entry uses `deletionRequestedAt?.toISOString().slice(0, 10)` (retention.ts:252), while the member email formats purgeAt in VALLEY_TIME_ZONE (settings/actions.ts:353-358, with a comment citing audit Lows 19/47/91/94 as the reason the email must be a valley date).
findings.argument: purgeAt = request instant + 60*24h. For any request made between 00:00 and 05:30 IST (18:30-24:00 UTC), the UTC date of purgeAt is one day earlier than its IST date. An admin cross-checking a deletion dispute against /admin/audit reads 'purge due 2026-10-19' while the member's email said 20 October 2026. Same-file precedent says these strings are meant to be valley dates.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace only: new Date('2026-08-22T19:00:00Z' + 60d) — toISOString().slice(0,10) vs toLocaleDateString en-GB Asia/Kolkata differ by one day. No live check needed.
findings.taxonomy: UTC-vs-IST day boundary in operator-facing strings

findings.title: backup.yml's schedule comment claims it matches the catch-ups cron in one quiet-hours window; the two actually run 5.5 hours apart
findings.expected: The comment justifying 20:30 UTC ('matching the existing catchups cron in vercel.json so all the quiet-hours work happens in one window') is true of vercel.json.
findings.actual: vercel.json schedules /api/catchups/tick at '0 2 * * *' = 02:00 UTC = 07:30 IST (morning in India), not 02:00 IST. The backup at 20:30 UTC = 02:00 IST therefore shares no window with the tick; either the backup comment's premise is wrong, or whoever wrote the tick schedule believed Vercel crons run in IST and the tick was intended for 02:00 IST quiet hours but actually fires at 07:30 IST.
findings.argument: Comment-mis-describes-config, and it encodes a live misunderstanding about which zone Vercel cron schedules use. No member harm today (07:30 IST transitions/reminders are arguably better than 02:00), but the false 'matching' claim will steer the next schedule change wrong, and it is the second place (after finding 5) where the recorded reasoning and the shipped timing disagree.
findings.proofPlan: Read .github/workflows/backup.yml:32-34 against vercel.json crons (both quoted in this audit); confirm the tick's actual fire time in Vercel's cron dashboard/logs.

findings.title: writeAudit failures are completely invisible in production - no console line, no Sentry
findings.expected: The audit log is the accountability record (sign-ins, admin.block/delete/merge, account.purge, retention.sweep, razorpay reversals). A failed audit write in production should leave at least a log line, and per the M09 pattern (reportSwallowed in src/lib/report-error.ts) a Sentry event, so holes in the trail are discoverable.
findings.actual: The catch at audit.ts:74 logs only when NODE_ENV !== 'production'. In production a failed AuditLog insert vanishes entirely: no console.error, no Sentry, and the caller's real work (block, delete, purge) proceeds. The function's own doc comment invokes 'a guard that hides its own breakage is worse than none' while the production branch is fully silent - the exact contradiction the brief flags. reportSwallowed exists for this and is wired only into catchups.ts and retention.ts (verified by grep: those are the only two call sites).
findings.argument: writeAudit wraps prisma.auditLog.create in try/catch; the catch body is `if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production') console.error(...)`. Unlike delImageByKey (which logs 'whatever the environment' - storage.ts:244) and unlike retention.ts's step() (which calls reportSwallowed), audit.ts has no production-visible path. If AuditLog writes start failing systematically (schema drift, constraint, retention-sweep contention, pool exhaustion under load), every admin action and sign-in event goes unrecorded with zero evidence anywhere, and the retention sweep's own 'retention.sweep' summary row (retention.ts:295) silently never lands - defeating the 'is retention actually running' answerability the code claims.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace only: confirm grep shows reportSwallowed is absent from audit.ts, and that no caller of writeAudit inspects a return value (it returns void). Optionally, in a dev session, point writeAudit at a nonexistent table name and observe that with NODE_ENV=production semantics simulated, nothing is emitted while the calling action succeeds.

findings.title: advanceEdition swallows engine failures with console.error only, bypassing the M09 Sentry reporter
findings.expected: Audit M09 established that Catch-up engine failures must be reported to Sentry via reportSwallowed, because 'nobody notices it stop - the symptom is Rounds that never open'. advanceDueCatchups (line 1200) and openNextRoundIfDue's wrapper (line 1190) both do this.
findings.actual: advanceEdition - the function that performs every transition, extension, reminder and its notification fan-out via applyEditionAction - catches all errors at line 1087-1090 and emits only `console.error("[catchups] advanceEdition failed", err)`. Because advanceEdition never throws, the reportSwallowed calls in advanceDueCatchups can never see a per-edition failure. The M09 fix covers only round-OPENING; round-ADVANCING failures are still invisible in production.
findings.argument: advanceDueCatchups loops `await advanceEdition(ed, now)` (line 1172); any repeatable error inside applyEditionAction - e.g. the notification create inside the shared transaction throwing (notify.notifyAnswersOpen at line 961 rolls the CAS back with it), a constraint violation, a query timeout - is caught inside advanceEdition and reduced to a Vercel log line. Rounds then sit stuck in collecting/answering on every page view and every nightly tick, while /api/catchups/tick answers 200 unconditionally (route returns {ok:true} regardless) and Sentry hears nothing. The only mitigation is the admin worklist's stuckCatchups count (src/lib/admin.ts:234), which requires the owner to open /admin and notice.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: confirm advanceEdition's catch is console-only and that advanceDueCatchups' report() is unreachable for errors thrown inside advanceEdition. To confirm live, temporarily make notifyReminder throw in a dev session and observe: no Sentry event (with SENTRY_DEV=1), edition stops advancing, tick still returns 200.

findings.title: sendMail's timeout race leaves the losing Resend promise unhandled - a late transport failure becomes an unhandled rejection
findings.expected: When the 10s timeout wins the Promise.race, the still-pending api.emails.send() promise should carry a rejection handler (e.g. send.catch(() => {})), since the code's own catch block documents that the SDK can reject on DNS/reset-socket/TLS failures.
findings.actual: Line 208 creates `const send = api.emails.send({...})`; line 215 races it against a 10s timer that RESOLVES null. When the timer wins, sendMail returns at line 221 with {transient:true} and nothing is ever attached to `send`. If the SDK call later rejects (the exact scenario of a provider that has stopped answering: hang, then socket reset at 30-60s), that rejection is unhandled.
findings.argument: Promise.race does not cancel or absorb the loser. The catch at line 238 only handles rejections that occur BEFORE race settles. After a timeout return, a late rejection of `send` hits Node's unhandledRejection path. In production the Sentry Node SDK (instrumentation.ts, enabled on VERCEL) registers a global handler, so the consequence there is a spurious captured error with no context; in any process where Sentry is not enabled and no handler is registered (scripts, tests, local dev exercising scheduleDrain's void-fallback branch), Node's default --unhandled-rejections=throw terminates the process mid-drain, which can strand a claimed OutboundEmail row in 'sending' until the 2-minute stale sweep. The failure mode fires precisely when Resend is having the bad minute the timeout exists for.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of email.ts:200-247 confirms no handler is attached to the losing promise. Reproduce safely offline: `node -e "const p=new Promise((_,rej)=>setTimeout(rej,50)); Promise.race([p,new Promise(r=>setTimeout(()=>r(null),10))]).then(()=>{});"` exits 1 with an unhandled rejection, demonstrating the shape.

findings.title: Razorpay refund/dispute arriving before the capture event is acknowledged with 200 and permanently lost
findings.expected: Webhook events can arrive out of order (the file's own comment at line 226: 'the webhook can arrive in any order'). A refund.processed or payment.dispute.created event that finds the row not-yet-paid should either be retried later (non-2xx) or remembered, so the reversal is applied once the capture lands.
findings.actual: The reversal branch runs `updateMany({ where: { id, status: "paid" }, data: { status: to } })` (line 230-233); when the row is still 'created' (capture webhook delayed/retrying, browser callback lost - the exact tab-death scenario this route exists for), moved.count is 0, and the handler falls through to `return NextResponse.json({ received: true })` at line 248. Razorpay treats the 200 as delivered and never resends. When payment.captured later arrives, the row flips to 'paid' and stays there: the refunded/disputed money counts forever in the /support recovery bar, 'Given, all time', and the member's contribution history - the precise lie audit M58 was fixed to prevent.
findings.argument: The in-code justification ('a refund for an order we never recorded as paid is not something to invent a state for') covers the never-paid case but not the not-YET-paid case, which the same file's capture branch proves is real (it exists because the callback can die). Sequence: capture delivery fails once (5xx/timeout on our side) -> Razorpay schedules a retry minutes later -> owner refunds quickly (test payments, an accidental double gift) -> refund.processed arrives first, no-ops, 200 -> retried capture arrives, row becomes 'paid'. No audit entry is written for the skipped reversal (the writeAudit at line 238 is inside `if (moved.count === 1)`), so nothing anywhere records that a reversal was seen and dropped.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of the three branches plus Razorpay docs (webhooks retried only on non-2xx, no ordering guarantee). Safe DB-free check: unit-style reasoning over the branch conditions; or against a test-mode Razorpay account, deliver refund.processed before payment.captured to the local route and read the row status afterwards.

findings.title: delImage's failure boolean is ignored on the moderation and avatar paths - 'removed' bytes can silently survive with no worklist
findings.expected: storage.ts's delImageByKey doc (lines 217-230) says the boolean exists because a silent miss 'mattered most where it was quietest... this is a moderation and GDPR path'. Callers that delete bytes with no surviving row pointer should either check the boolean or write a PendingImagePurge row, as purgeUserAccount and deletePostWithImages both do.
findings.actual: adminRemovePhoto (collection/actions.ts:669-673) fires Promise.all([delImage(thumb), delImage(url), delImage(original)]) and discards all three booleans; the action then returns { success: true }. Same pattern at settings/actions.ts:258 and :276 (replace/remove avatar - the old avatar URL is overwritten/nulled first, then delImage's result is dropped) and admin/people/actions.ts:389 (merge deletes the duplicate's avatar). None of these write PendingImagePurge, so a transient R2 failure leaves the bytes publicly fetchable forever at a URL no row remembers - with only a console line naming the key.
findings.argument: Audit M11's whole point was that a hidden photo's file 'stayed at a public, permanent R2 URL that anyone who had noted it could still fetch forever'. In the delImage-failure case that exact outcome recurs, now reported to the admin as success. For removeAvatar the member's motive is often privacy; 'success' while the photograph survives is a member-visible lie with GDPR teeth. The nightly sweep's PendingImagePurge retry (retention.ts:271) cannot help because these paths never enqueue there. Mechanism is one line per site: the awaited boolean is not read.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of the four call sites against storage.ts's contract. Safe live check: none needed - the contract violation is syntactic (return value unused). To see the consequence, run a dev session with R2 creds made invalid and click Remove on a collection photo: toast says removed, object remains, nothing queued.

findings.title: Mail drain failure paths log to console only - a systematically failing drain never reaches Sentry
findings.expected: The queue is the only way any email leaves the app and has no cron; per the repo's own M09 rule, a swallowed failure in it should reach Sentry (reportSwallowed), since report-error.ts exists exactly because 'console.error on Vercel is a line in a log nobody reads'.
findings.actual: scheduleDrain (email-queue.ts:527-540), scheduleSend (:512-525) and the (main) layout's after() backstop (layout.tsx:81-87) all catch drain errors with bare console.error. Additionally takeDrainLease's create-catch (:623-628) treats ANY error - including connection refused or a missing/drifted QueueLease table - as 'somebody else holds the lease' and returns null, so a structural failure reads as 'the queue is busy'.
findings.argument: Per-row send failures are well-booked on the row (lastError, attempts, deferrals) and surface in mailHealth/admin - that half is sound. What has no production telemetry is a failure BEFORE row bookkeeping: takeDrainLease throwing or mis-catching, dailyBudget failing, the reclaim updateMany failing. In that state every enqueue and page view schedules a drain that dies quietly; queued mail (including password resets, the one thing RESET_RESERVE protects) sits unsent until someone reads the admin panel's waiting count. The archetype is the file's own 2026-08-13 incident (a drain that never ran), now recurrence-proofed against scheduling but not against invisible failure.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: grep confirms no reportSwallowed/Sentry import in email-queue.ts or the layout's drain callback. Dev check with SENTRY_DEV=1: make drainMailQueue throw and confirm no event is captured while pages render normally.

findings.title: Rate limiters fail open with console-only evidence - a Redis outage silently disables every limit in the app
findings.expected: Failing open on a limiter backend error is a defensible availability choice, but a persistent backend failure (bad Upstash creds after an env-var edit, quota exhaustion) should be observable somewhere a human looks - Sentry or the admin panel - because its blast radius is every guard at once: login failure budget, reauth password-guess budget, uploads, contributions, reports, signups.
findings.actual: rateLimit (:162-165), hasBudget (:181-184) and consume (:195-197) each catch all errors, console.error, and return ok/true. Nothing distinguishes a one-off timeout from hours of misconfiguration; nothing reaches Sentry; no admin surface shows limiter health. The razorpay webhook's own comment (route.ts:37) acknowledges 'failing open is the one behaviour this must not have' for its context - the same posture is global here with no alarm.
findings.argument: The mechanism is deliberate (documented 'failed open'), so the finding is the observability gap, not the policy: during a sustained limiter outage, brute-force protection on login and on the reauth door (deletion, password change) is off, and the only evidence is per-call console lines in Vercel's log stream. Stability/DoS is explicitly in scope for this audit and this is the single switch that turns off every metering guard at once, silently.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace plus one dev run: set an invalid UPSTASH_REDIS_REST_URL, exercise login failures past the budget, observe unlimited attempts and no Sentry event with SENTRY_DEV=1.

findings.title: pick-bird treats a failed contribution query as 'not a supporter' and bounces a paid member to /support
findings.expected: A database error while summing a member's paid contributions is 'broken', not 'zero'. The page should error (or retry) rather than confidently mis-classify a paying supporter.
findings.actual: `.catch(() => 0)` on the aggregate (line 36) and `.catch(() => null)` on the user read (line 42) convert any query failure into myPaidPaise=0 / me=null, after which the non-admin branch redirects to /support - the page whose call to action is to pay. A supporter who just paid and got the 'pick the bird' notification hits a pool-timeout under load (precisely the busy moment payments cluster) and lands on the ask-for-money page with no error shown anywhere.
findings.argument: The catch does not distinguish expected-and-fine (no rows -> _sum null, already handled by `?? 0` in the .then) from broken (connection refused, query_timeout). The comment frames the gate as 'only decides what a visitor SEES', but what a paid member sees on a transient DB error is a silent denial plus an implicit second-payment invitation. The fresh-pick findFirst at line 65 has the same `.catch(() => null)` -> redirect shape.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of the two catches and the redirect conditions. Dev check: throw from the aggregate (e.g. temporarily rename the model call) while signed in as a paid test account and observe the redirect to /support with no error surfaced.

findings.title: Batch-group auto-join failure at signup is swallowed with no retry - the member is silently missing from their batch group forever
findings.expected: Best-effort is right (a failed join must not sink the signup), but a failure should leave a repair path: a later self-heal, an admin worklist entry, or at least a production-visible report.
findings.actual: The catch at :178-180 console.errors and moves on. Nothing ever retries the join: no later code path re-checks 'alumnus with batchYear but no batch-group membership'. The member's batch group simply never appears for them, batch-targeted posts and batch Catch-up fan-outs exclude them, and nothing anywhere says why. Unlike the verification email one line below (explicitly recoverable via the banner's resend button, as its comment says), this swallow has no recovery story.
findings.argument: The upsert/find-or-create inside joinBatchGroup can fail transiently (pool checkout timeout at a launch-day signup burst is the realistic case - exactly when many signups race the same 'Batch of X' create). The cost lands on a brand-new member whose first experience of the community is quietly wrong, and diagnosis requires correlating a Vercel log line with a complaint weeks later.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace: grep for other joinBatchGroup callers (none) and for any membership self-heal (none). Read-only DB check the orchestrator can run: count alumni with batchYear set who lack a GroupMember row in their 'Batch of {year}' group.

findings.title: Photo viewer download fetch never checks res.ok - an error response is saved as the photo
findings.expected: A non-2xx response (deleted object -> R2 404/XML error body, CDN error page) should take the catch's fallback path (open in new tab) or show an error, not be handed to the member as a downloaded file.
findings.actual: download() does `const res = await fetch(current.src); const blob = await res.blob();` with no res.ok check. fetch only rejects on network/CORS failure, so a 404 or 5xx resolves, and the member 'successfully' downloads a file named like a photo whose contents are an error document. Silent, and the member discovers it later when the file will not open.
findings.argument: Straight-line mechanism: lines 184-191. The catch at 192 covers only rejections. Reachable for any photo whose object was since deleted (adminRemovePhoto deletes bytes while rows elsewhere may still reference the URL - e.g. a coverPhoto written before the Low-106 clearing, or a stale cached page).
findings.proofPlan: Browser step against dev: open the viewer on an image URL pointing at a deleted object and press Download; inspect the saved file. Or code trace alone - the missing res.ok is syntactic.

findings.title: Direct-upload presign fallback is still fully silent - the failure mode that hid for weeks has no witness even now
findings.expected: TRAPS.md records that this exact silent fallback concealed 'direct uploads had never actually worked in production' until 2026-08-21. After that incident, a CORS/CSP-blocked PUT should at minimum leave a console.warn (client-side) so the next regression - a new domain, an edited CSP, a Vercel preview origin missing from the bucket allowlist - is diagnosable.
findings.actual: Both catches (:38-40 network failure on presign, :55-60 blocked PUT) return null with no logging of any kind. The caller (create-post-form's uploadViaPresign:529) then silently downscales in-browser and proxies through the server, so uploads keep 'working' at degraded quality/resolution and the regression is invisible again - the identical concealment mechanism the incident write-up describes, unchanged.
findings.argument: The fix on 2026-08-21 was to the CSP, not to the observability of this path; storage.ts's presign doc itself warns that a new origin 'quietly take[s] the slower proxied path instead of failing loudly'. Cost when it recurs: every photograph stored from the browser-downscaled copy instead of the full original (the stated single purpose of presigning), discovered only by someone noticing image quality months later.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of the two catches plus TRAPS.md's account. Browser step: remove the S3 endpooint from connect-src in a dev build, upload a photo, confirm the upload succeeds with zero console output.

findings.title: copyPostImagesToCollection can reject despite its 'resolves rather than throwing' contract, and a partial failure orphans fresh R2 objects
findings.expected: The doc comment (lines 36-41) promises 'the whole thing resolves rather than throwing' because it runs post-response in after() with nobody to tell. All awaited work should therefore sit inside the per-image try/catch or an outer one, and bytes PUT before a failed row-create should be cleaned or queued.
findings.actual: The two top-level reads (user.findUnique:57, photo.count:69) run before any try/catch; if either throws, the after() callback rejects and the member's ticked 'Also add to the Collection' silently does nothing (only Next's generic after-error log). Inside the loop, both putImage calls (:101-108) can succeed and then prisma.photo.create (:111) fail, landing in the catch at :133 - two freshly written R2 objects with no row and no PendingImagePurge entry, orphaned forever.
findings.argument: The comment mis-describes the code (the brief's 'a comment that lies' class): the total-resolution guarantee holds only for the mapped section. The orphan path mirrors the finalize route's shape (finalize/route.ts:116-120, where urls already PUT are abandoned when a later file 422s) - a small but permanent R2 byte leak class with console-only evidence, in a codebase that built PendingImagePurge precisely so unreferenced bytes are never unreachable.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of lines 45-141 against the doc comment. Dev check: make photo.create fail (e.g. exceed a caption constraint artificially) and confirm the two objects exist in the local public/ store with no Photo row and no PendingImagePurge row.

findings.title: Verify-banner refill time is printed in IST under a comment claiming the browser's timezone - members abroad read a wrong, unlabeled clock time
findings.expected: sendTimeLabel's own doc (lines 38-42) and email-queue.ts's nextBudgetResetAt doc (:779-780) both promise the moment is 'formatted in the BROWSER's timezone... a real clock time is a promise somebody can check'. Either the copy should honour that, or the rendered time should carry a zone label.
findings.actual: The implementation pins `timeZone: VALLEY_TIME_ZONE` (IST) and locale 'en-GB' (:47-53), so a member in New York whose verification is budget-deferred reads 'tomorrow at 5:30 am' - a bare clock time that is wrong by 9.5 hours for them, with no IST marker. The comment directly above still describes the previous behaviour; the hydration comment at :124-131 likewise still claims 'the reader's own locale'.
findings.argument: The valleyDayKey comparison (:57) shows the IST pinning was a deliberate same-day-boundary fix, but the two surrounding comments were not updated and the copy consequence (an unlabeled IST time shown worldwide to exactly the diaspora audience an alumni site serves) was not addressed. Cosmetic with teeth: the one state whose entire design goal is 'a promise somebody can check' renders a time most overseas members cannot check.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace of :44-58; then a browser step with the machine timezone set to America/New_York rendering the queued state and reading the label.

findings.title: Launch-day verify-mail backlog: last confirmation sends ~3 days after signup at 300 signups, while the banner promises tomorrow's UTC midnight to everyone
findings.expected: The mail queue absorbs a launch-day signup surge, and the verify banner's promised send time reflects the member's actual position in the queue.
findings.actual: Effective verify budget is 75/day (DAILY_CAP 95 minus RESET_RESERVE 20, email-queue.ts:76,87). At the owner's stated expectation of >100 day-one signups: 300 signups queue 300 verify mails; sends go out 75/day, so signups #76-150 wait ~1 day, #151-225 ~2 days, #226-300 ~3 days. Until the mail arrives each member is Stage 0 (member-gate.ts:20: no directory names, no profiles, no writes, contacts hidden). Meanwhile verificationMailState returns { state: 'queued', sendingAt: nextBudgetResetAt() } — always the NEXT UTC midnight regardless of how many rows sit ahead — and VerifyEmailBanner renders it as a concrete clock time ('tomorrow at 5:30 am', verify-email-banner.tsx:34-42). For everyone past ~position 75 that promised time passes with no mail, up to three midnights in a row.
findings.argument: email-queue.ts:872-875: `const budget = await dailyBudget(); if (budget.verifyRemaining <= 0) return { state: 'queued', sendingAt: nextBudgetResetAt() }`. nextBudgetResetAt() (line 781-786) is `Date.UTC(y, m, d+1)` — pure calendar arithmetic, no queue-depth term. Queue depth ahead of this row is `count(status queued, kind verify, createdAt < row.createdAt)`; days-to-send = ceil(position / 75), which the state machine never computes. The capacity ceiling itself is structural: DAILY_CAP=95, RESET_RESERVE=20, drain sends oldest-first within priority (drainWithLease:713-736).
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices for the banner half: grep email-queue.ts for any queue-position input to sendingAt (there is none). Capacity half is arithmetic from the two constants plus the owner's own launch estimate recorded in the file header (email-queue.ts:31-34). Optional live check: read-only count of OutboundEmail rows per day after launch. Fix directions for the next session: raise the Resend plan before launch, and/or compute sendingAt from queue position (count of eligible rows ahead / 75 days forward).
findings.taxonomy: third-party-quota / capacity arithmetic / wrong user-facing promise

findings.title: Feed load-more dies silently when the cursor post is deleted, hidden, or its author blocked (no M39-style recovery, unlike directory and admin people)
findings.expected: Scrolling the feed keeps paging even if the post at a page boundary is deleted or leaves the visible set between pages, the way the directory (directory/actions.ts:77-105, audit M39) and admin people list (admin-people-query.ts:70-98, audit Low 12) already recover.
findings.actual: loadPosts' keyset branch passes `cursor: { id: keysetCursor }, skip: 1` with no fallback. If the cursor post has been deleted, or has left the filtered set (moderator hides it, its author is blocked — the where includes isHidden:false and AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING), the query returns [], hasMore computes false, nextCursor null, and infinite scroll silently ends mid-archive with no error. The first audit proved this exact Prisma mechanism live for the directory ('this query answers nothing for a list with hundreds') and fixed it in two places; the feed, saved-posts is fine (single page), but the feed keyset, comment-thread paging (feed/actions.ts:1405-1414, a root whose visibility flips), and bell paging (notifications/actions.ts:30-35, a row the 100-cap prune or nightly sweep deletes mid-scroll) all still carry the unrecovered shape.
findings.argument: feed/actions.ts:1109-1118: `rows = await prisma.post.findMany({ where, include, orderBy: [{createdAt: 'desc'},{id:'desc'}], take: PAGE_SIZE+1, ...(keysetCursor ? { cursor: { id: keysetCursor }, skip: 1 } : {}) })` — Prisma's cursor requires the named row to exist inside the filtered set (mechanism already proven and documented at directory/actions.ts:77-81); a vanished row yields zero rows, which the code reads as end-of-feed. Deleting one's own post is a routine member action, and blocking an author removes ~20 candidate boundary rows at once.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step against a test account: load feed, note the 20th post (the page-boundary row), delete it from a second account (or hide it as admin), press load more — expect an empty response and the feed to end though older posts exist. Alternatively code-compare against directory/actions.ts:97-103 which retries with skip when `rows.length===0 && cursor`.

findings.title: Visit rows are minted from a client-controlled cookie with no throttle: an authed member can create one row per request forever, or write into another member's Visit row
findings.expected: Presence telemetry is attributed server-side; a member cannot choose the Visit primary key, cannot mint unbounded rows, and cannot touch another member's row.
findings.actual: proxy.ts:297-301 takes the visit id from the member's own `rv-visit` cookie, validated only as /^[0-9a-z-]{8,64}$/, and stamps it into the x-visit-id header; touchLastSeen then runs `prisma.visit.upsert({ where: { id: visitId }, create: {...}, update: {...} })` on every authed page render. Two consequences: (1) rotating the cookie value per request mints one new Visit row per page GET with no rate limit anywhere on the path — at a scripted 20 req/s that is ~1.7M rows/day (~0.5-1 GB/day at the measured ~750B/row), against a Supabase free plan whose disk cap makes the whole database read-only when exceeded, and the only cleanup is the 180-day retention sweep; (2) the upsert's update branch is not scoped to userId, so a member who replays another member's visit id (seen or guessed) increments that member's view count and overwrites its endedAt/device/geo columns — corrupting the owner's presence analytics.
findings.argument: proxy.ts:297: `const existing = request.cookies.get(VISIT_COOKIE)?.value` then `visitId = existing && /^[0-9a-z-]{8,64}$/.test(existing) ? existing : derivedVisitId(...)` — any conforming client-supplied string passes. last-seen.ts:118-161: `visit.upsert({ where: { id: visitId } })` with create writing a fresh row for any unseen id and update having no `userId` condition. No limiter covers page GETs (rate-limit.ts limits writes and lookup APIs only). The DoS class is explicitly in this audit's scope (the security audit excluded it deliberately).
findings.proofPlan: Read-only code trace is sufficient for the mechanism. Live confirmation with a throwaway account: send 5 GETs to /feed with 5 distinct rv-visit cookie values, then a read-only `SELECT count(*) FROM "Visit" WHERE "userId" = <throwaway>` — expect 5 rows. Fix direction: derive the id server-side from (userId, bucket) or scope the upsert to (id, userId) and cap rows per user per day.

findings.title: Visit table alone approaches the 500MB Supabase free-tier cap at the 2,000-user target (Place already spends 97MB of it)
findings.expected: The presence tables stay comfortably inside the database plan at the owner's stated 2,000-user headroom target.
findings.actual: Legitimate-traffic arithmetic: 2,000 members x 20 views/day at the standard 30-min session gap is ~2-3 visits/member/day, i.e. ~5,000 rows/day; the 180-day retention window (retention.ts:58) holds ~900k live rows at steady state. Measured live cost is 184kB for 243 rows (docs/planning/audits/db-sizes-live.json) ≈ 750B/row including its three indexes; even allowing better packing at scale (~400-500B/row), 900k rows is ~360-680MB. The Place gazetteer is already 97MB, and the plan is 500MB (the ContentView design comment at schema.prisma:1152-1156 records the '500MB plan' constraint and did exactly this arithmetic for views — but Visit, one row per session with 180-day retention, was never run through the same numbers). At full target utilization the database exceeds its plan within ~3-6 months of launch; Supabase free projects over disk go read-only, which is hard-down for every write on the site.
findings.argument: Visit model (schema.prisma:1060-1109): ~19 columns including 8 free-text (paths, referrer, device/os/browser/language, country/city/region/timezone) plus 2 composite indexes and the PK. One row per session, written by touchLastSeen on every authed render, deleted only when endedAt < now-180d (retention.ts:147-151). The 180-day window is justified in retention.ts:47-58 as 'double what any surface reads' (deepest lookback is 90 days) — it was sized for privacy, not for the 2k-user storage budget.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: `SELECT pg_total_relation_size('"Visit"')/count(*) FROM "Visit"` for the true per-row cost, then multiply by 5k/day x 180. If the number lands over ~250MB, halve the presence window to the 90 days the analytics room actually reads, or upgrade the Supabase plan before launch.

findings.title: PostHog free tier (1M events/month) is ~5-8x exceeded at the 2,000-user target; OPERATIONS.md's '600k a year' sizing is two orders of magnitude off at that scale
findings.expected: Analytics volume stays inside the free tier at the owner's headroom target, or the overage behavior is a decision someone has made.
findings.actual: Config sends autocapture (every click), capture_pageview on history_change, and capture_pageleave (posthog-provider.tsx:74-80). Arithmetic at target: 2,000 users x 20 views/day = 40k pageviews + 40k pageleaves + ~2-4 autocaptured clicks per view (~100-160k) ≈ 180-240k events/day ≈ 5-7M/month against the 1M free tier. docs/OPERATIONS.md:194-195 asserts 'Free tier is 1M events a month against usage of maybe 600k a year, so there is no bill to reach' — true at today's 52 members, off by ~100x at the stated ceiling. With no card on file PostHog stops ingesting at the cap, so funnels/paths silently truncate mid-month; with a card it bills. No member-facing impact either way.
findings.argument: Event multipliers are all switched on in the init options at module scope; nothing samples or caps client events. The failure is quota exhaustion at the vendor, not in this codebase — the finding is the arithmetic plus the stale sizing claim in OPERATIONS.md that would stop anyone re-checking it.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: confirm the three capture options in posthog-provider.tsx and the claim at docs/OPERATIONS.md:194. Validation of the multiplier: PostHog's own usage dashboard after any active day, extrapolated linearly by member count. Owner decision item: sample autocapture, drop pageleave, or accept the paid tier before the community grows.

findings.title: Sentry sampling sized for today's traffic, not the target: 10% tracing is ~120k traces/month against a 10k-span free plan, and one hot-path bug exhausts the 5k error budget in ~3 hours
findings.expected: Sampling rates hold at the 2,000-user target so the smoke alarm still works in the month's fourth week.
findings.actual: tracesSampleRate 0.1 with the in-code justification 'this site's traffic is tiny, so this stays comfortably inside' the 10,000-span/month free plan (instrumentation.ts:55-58, plan confirmed docs/OPERATIONS.md:118). At target traffic (2,000 x 20 = 40k requests/day), 10% is 4,000 traces/day ≈ 120k/month — 12x the span budget even counting one span per trace, so performance data stops days into each month. Separately, the 5,000-errors/month budget: a single feed-breaking regression (the exact incident class Sentry was installed for, per the file header) at 40k views/day errors ~1,700/hour and exhausts the month's quota in ~3 hours; every later error that month — including a different, new bug — is dropped silently. Both degrade gracefully (no member impact) but the alarm goes deaf exactly when the site is busiest.
findings.argument: The rate is a hard-coded constant whose stated justification ('traffic is tiny') inverts at the audit's mandated scale; no dynamic sampling, no beforeSend dedup budget. Arithmetic: 40,000 req/day x 0.1 x 30 days = 120,000; 5,000 errors / (40,000 views/day / 24h) ≈ 3 hours of a 100%-reproduction hot-path error.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: the two constants and the plan numbers are all in-repo (instrumentation.ts:55-58, OPERATIONS.md:118). Fix direction for the next session: tracesSampleRate ~0.005-0.01 at launch, and rely on Sentry's server-side spike protection knowingly rather than accidentally.

findings.title: Type-ahead search limiter spends Upstash commands per keystroke; at target scale it can exhaust the free command quota, silently turning every rate limit off
findings.expected: Rate-limit plumbing itself stays inside the Upstash free tier at 2,000 users, or its exhaustion mode is a recorded decision.
findings.actual: The search limit (120/min) is checked once per request on three type-ahead endpoints (people search, place gazetteer, batch roster), and each sliding-window limit() costs ~2-3 Redis commands. A member typing one 10-character name is ~10 requests ≈ 30 commands. At 2,000 members x 3-5 searches/day that is ~200-450k commands/month from search alone, before login/posts/comments/uploads checks — at or past Upstash's free command cap (500k/month as of 2025; verify the current number). Exhaustion is graceful by design: every limiter fails OPEN (rate-limit.ts:159-166), so the site keeps working but signup/login/reset/trivia throttles are all silently off for the rest of the month — the exact window (a busy launch month) when they matter, with only console noise to say so.
findings.argument: rate-limit.ts:152-166: `limiter.limit(key)` per call, sliding window (multi-command); the search endpoints call it per keystroke request with no client-side coalescing of the quota cost. Fail-open posture is deliberate and documented (header comment), which converts quota exhaustion from an outage into a silent security/DoS-protection gap.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only: confirm per-request limit() in src/app/api/users/search/route.ts, src/app/api/places/search/route.ts, src/app/api/users-by-batch/route.ts; check the Upstash console's command count after one active day and extrapolate. Fix direction: only rate-limit search server-side per N requests, or move the search limiter to a fixed-window (1 command) profile.

findings.title: Feed rail's pulse module reads every post row of the trailing week on every feed render, and its count includes blocked authors' posts the feed itself hides
findings.expected: The two rail integers (posts this week, distinct authors) cost two aggregate queries, and agree with what the feed shows.
findings.actual: PulseModule runs `prisma.post.findMany({ where: { isHidden: false, ...PUBLISHED_ONLY, createdAt: { gte: week } }, select: { authorId: true } })` with no take, on every render of the feed — the most-loaded page in the app. At an active 2,000-member community (~500-1,500 posts/week) that is ~1k rows fetched and a Set built per feed view, i.e. ~40M row-reads/day at target traffic, to produce two numbers a `count()` plus `groupBy(['authorId'])` (or one groupBy) would return in ~2 rows. Secondarily, the where omits AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING (compare feed/actions.ts baseWhere), so 'N posts shared this week' counts posts by blocked members that the feed beside it refuses to show.
findings.argument: pulse-module.tsx:24-34: full findMany then `new Set(weekPosts.map(p => p.authorId)).size` in JS; no cache, no take, server component re-run per request (feed-rail.tsx:52 renders it inside the dynamic feed page). The row count is bounded only by community posting rate, which is exactly what grows with the 2k target.
findings.proofPlan: Read-only code trace (the query and its render site). Fix is mechanical for the next session: `prisma.post.count(...)` + `prisma.post.groupBy({ by: ['authorId'], where })` (or a single groupBy with _count), adding AUTHOR_IN_GOOD_STANDING to match the feed.
findings.taxonomy: unbounded-findMany / over-read on hot path / filter drift

findings.title: Image URL strings pass ownership checks with no length cap; a verified member can store multi-megabyte 'images' JSON that every feed reader then downloads
findings.expected: Every image URL stored into Post.images / CatchupEntry.images is bounded in length, the way adminMessageSchema.imageUrl is capped at .max(500) for the identical column class.
findings.actual: postSchema declares `images: z.string().optional()` with no .max on the JSON string, and ownedUploadUrls (src/lib/upload-ownership.ts:31-40) validates only array-length<=3, app-minted prefix, traversal and root — never URL length. createPost then stores JSON.stringify(ownership.urls), i.e. the client's raw strings (feed/actions.ts:160-162). Same gap in editPost's draft images path (feed/actions.ts:501-534) and submitEntrySchema `images: z.array(z.url())` (catchups/actions.ts:157) — z.url() carries no length cap either. Server actions accept 25MB bodies (next.config.ts:148 bodySizeLimit '25mb').
findings.argument: A URL of the form `https://images.rishivalley.space/uploads/<own-userId>/` + N megabytes of junk + `.webp` satisfies isUploadedImageUrl (prefix startsWith, upload-shared.ts:113-117), keyForUrl (no '..' segment, root 'uploads' in KNOWN_ROOTS, storage.ts:263-291) and decideOwnedUploads (key.startsWith(`uploads/<userId>/`)). Three such URLs ≈ 24MB land in Post.images (unbounded text column). loadPosts returns `images: p.images` verbatim to every member's feed page, so one hostile post makes every feed page containing it a ~24MB response; PostCard also JSON.parses it per render. Only the rate limit (10 posts/10min) meters volume, not size.
findings.proofPlan: With a throwaway verified account, invoke createPost with images = JSON.stringify([base + 'uploads/<uid>/' + 'a'.repeat(100000) + '.webp']) — it returns success; then fetch the feed as a second account and measure the payload. Delete the post afterwards. Pure code trace also suffices: no .max exists anywhere on the URL path from postSchema through decideOwnedUploads to prisma.post.create.

findings.title: /api/places/search q has no length cap into a raw ILIKE over 234k rows — the exact gap audit M44 closed in /api/users/search but not here; feed and collection search share the class
findings.expected: Free-text search inputs are length-capped before reaching a LIKE/ILIKE scan, as users/search does (`q.trim().slice(0, FULL_NAME_MAX)` per audit M44, users/search/route.ts:38).
findings.actual: places/search reads `q` with only a minimum check (`raw.length < 1`), builds prefix and %contains% patterns from it, and interpolates them into $queryRaw over the 234,934-row Place table (three LIKE clauses in WHERE plus two more in ORDER BY, plus altNames ILIKE when >=4 chars). Feed's loadPosts opts.search (feed/actions.ts:1022-1037) and collection's loadPhotos search/area (collection/actions.ts:455-474) are equally uncapped Prisma `contains` filters — and loadPosts has NO rate limit at all while accepting a 25MB server-action body.
findings.argument: The 'search' bucket allows 120 calls/min per account (rate-limit.ts:99). Each call with a ~16KB pattern (URL-length bound) forces a sequential comparison across 234k rows; LIKE cost is O(rows × pattern). Prisma's pool is max 5 connections/instance with a 20s query_timeout, so a single hostile verified account can keep pool slots saturated with slow scans — pool-checkout timeouts then surface as errors for other members on the same instance. loadPosts is worse in body size (25MB pattern possible) though the Post table is smaller. Stability/DoS is explicitly in this audit's scope.
findings.proofPlan: Code diff against users/search/route.ts:38 shows the missing slice. Live check (orchestrator): signed-in fetch /api/places/search?q=<8KB of 'a%a%a%...'> and time the response vs a normal query; EXPLAIN of the equivalent LIKE via a read-only session confirms the sequential scan.

findings.title: Keyset pagination dead-ends at a deleted cursor row in feed, comments and notifications — the recovery audit M39 added to the directory was not applied to the other three paginators
findings.expected: When the row a cursor names has been deleted (author hard-deletes a post mid-scroll), the next page still loads, as directory/actions.ts:91-105 does with its explicit fallback ('a page of the directory rather than the silent end of it', audit M39).
findings.actual: loadPosts (recent sort, line 1114), loadComments (line 1414) and getNotifications (notifications/actions.ts:34) all pass `cursor: { id: <client cursor> }` with no recovery. Prisma returns an empty result set when the cursor row is absent from the filtered set, so rows.length===0, hasMore=false, nextCursor=null — infinite scroll silently ends mid-list.
findings.argument: nextCursor is always the id of the LAST row of the current page. For the feed that is a Post any author can hard-delete (deletePost) at any moment; for comments, a root comment that becomes invisible (blocked author, VISIBLE_COMMENT filter) leaves the cursor outside the roots WHERE; for notifications, another device's first-page open runs the KEEP=100 prune (the code comment at notifications/actions.ts:43 only defends against the SAME device's scroll). In each case the next page request answers empty and the client is told there is nothing more, though older rows exist. Refresh recovers, but nothing tells the member to.
findings.proofPlan: Two test accounts: A loads the feed and captures nextCursor (the 20th post's id, authored by B); B deletes that post; A requests the next page — expect posts: [], hasMore: false while older posts exist. Confirms without any DB write outside the normal app flows.

findings.title: The live inline profile editor enforces looser caps than every other writer of the same columns (120 vs 100, 100000 vs 10000, year<=2100 vs valleyYear+7), and its name field's UI maxLength=80 re-creates the audit-Low-84 lockout
findings.expected: One cap per column across all writers — the exact invariant audits Low 84 / M45 established ('the two cannot drift apart a second time', validators.ts:93) — and a batch-year ceiling of valleyYear()+ahead, which audits Lows 40/50/108/112 built deliberately.
findings.actual: updateProfileField (the ONLY live editor of these columns; updateUserProfile in settings/actions.ts has no remaining callers) caps jobTitle/workplace at 120 (line 101) where profileSchema and onboarding's registerStepSchema cap the same columns at 100; admissionNumber at 100000 (line 111) vs 10000 in both schemas; and every year field at a static YEAR_MAX=2100 (lines 28-29, 135) vs the valleyYear()+ahead refine (batchYear ceiling ~currentYear+7) everywhere else. Separately, the editor's name input carries maxLength={80} (letterhead-profile.tsx:911) while FULL_NAME_MAX=100: a member whose legal 81-100-char name signup accepted cannot re-type or extend it in the one place names are edited — the exact failure Low 84 fixed server-side.
findings.argument: A member can save batchYear 2099 through the inline editor (Number.isInteger, 1926<=n<=2100 passes); it then renders in bylines, directory batch tiles and filters (parseBatchYear's LAST_BATCH_YEAR is also 2100, so the filter accepts it) — the typo-rejection the yearField refine exists for is absent on the live path. A 115-char workplace saves here but would be refused by every schema-based writer. The 80-char UI clamp blocks legal long names from being edited at all.
findings.proofPlan: In the browser as a test account: set batch year to 2099 in the inline editor (saves; every other form refuses it), set a 115-char workplace (saves), and paste a 90-char name (input clamps at 80). Code diff of the three cap pairs settles it without a browser.

findings.title: submitPrompt's comment claims the transaction stops two concurrent submissions both seeing room / the same position; READ COMMITTED provides no such guarantee
findings.expected: The code does what its comment says: 'inside the same transaction as the cap check so two questions arriving together cannot both see room for the last slot' — i.e. the aggregate+create pair is race-safe.
findings.actual: The $transaction wraps a plain aggregate (max position, count) followed by a create with no row lock, no serializable isolation and no unique on (editionId, position) — the last being deliberately absent per docs/TRAPS.md (the reorder needs it absent). Two concurrent submissions both read count=39/max=N and both insert: the 40-cap can be exceeded by one, and both prompts land on position N+1.
findings.argument: Under Postgres READ COMMITTED (Prisma's default through pgbouncer), two transactions' reads do not block each other and neither sees the other's uncommitted insert, so the CAS the comment describes does not exist. Consequence is small (a 41st prompt, or two prompts sharing a rendered slot until the Keeper reorders), but the comment mis-describes the mechanism, which the audit brief flags as bug evidence in itself, and the same aggregate feeds the wasFirst/dormant-revival decision.
findings.proofPlan: Code reading settles the mechanism (no FOR UPDATE, no isolationLevel argument, no unique). A live proof needs two parallel submitPrompt calls against one edition and a read of the resulting positions — duplicate position values confirm.

findings.title: Several actions throw raw exceptions (500 digests) instead of returning {error} when a crafted call sends the wrong runtime type — the class audit Low 83 fixed in updateContactMethods survives at five other sites
findings.expected: A server action is a public POST endpoint; anything not the expected shape is refused with the loose {error} contract, as updateContactMethods was rewritten to do (audit Low 83) and as postSchema/commentSchema do via Zod.
findings.actual: updateProfileField calls raw.trim() on an unvalidated second argument (line 80: TypeError if a number/object/null arrives). reportPost/reportUser call reason?.trim() (report-action.ts:86,184: optional chaining does not save a non-nullish non-string — (5).trim() throws). requestAccountDeletion passes a File-typed 'password' into bcrypt.compare (settings/actions.ts:300,316). editPost's manual checks pass a File-typed 'content' clean through (`!content` false, `content.length>cap` → undefined>cap false, feed/actions.ts:488) into prisma.post.update, which throws PrismaClientValidationError; a File 'title' throws at title?.trim() (line 591). loadDirectoryPage's `Math.max(0, Math.trunc(loaded))` passes NaN through to Prisma skip on the fallback path (directory/actions.ts:102).
findings.argument: Each site reaches a method call or Prisma argument with a value whose runtime type was never checked; the throw escapes the action (none are inside runAction), producing an opaque digest error instead of a refusal. Only crafted calls reach these — no data corruption — but it is the same noise-vs-refusal class the audit already ruled on for one of the six sites.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace per site (each is a one-line type check away from Low 83's pattern). Optionally: invoke updateProfileField('about', 123 as never) from a dev console against a test session and observe the 500 digest rather than {error}.

findings.title: Letter autosave timer races an explicit Publish/Save: its in-flight guard reads stale closure state
findings.expected: Clicking Publish or Save-as-draft cancels or excludes the pending 2.5s autosave, so exactly one editPost carries the version token at a time (the code comment says the submittingRef 'covers Save-as-draft too' and handleSubmit awaits autosaveRunRef for this reason).
findings.actual: A timer that is armed but not yet fired when Publish is clicked still fires mid-publish: its guard `if (submitting || savingDraft) return;` (line 314) reads those flags from the closure of the last effect run (deps are [content, title, images, postId], line 367), which happened before setSubmitting(true), so the guard always passes. handleSubmit (line 643) only awaits an autosave that has already STARTED (autosaveRunRef), and never clears autosaveTimer. Two concurrent editPost calls then carry the same baseUpdatedAt; editPost's updateMany precondition (feed/actions.ts ~line 597) makes the loser return 'This letter has changed somewhere else. Reload the page before you carry on...' — either shown as a spurious 'Not saving. Kept on this device.' failure during a successful publish, or aborting the publish itself with an error blaming a phantom other device.
findings.argument: The autosave effect re-runs only on content/title/images/postId change, so setSubmitting(true) from handleSubmit re-renders but does not re-create the pending timer's closure; the timer callback therefore observes submitting=false. The correct check would be submittingRef.current (already set synchronously at line 639) — the ref exists precisely for this and the timer does not read it. Both writes send the same baseUpdatedAtRef token (autosave reads the ref at fire time; handleSubmit advances it only after its own editPost resolves), so the server's lost-update guard (updateMany where updatedAt = base, count 0 ⇒ conflict error) is guaranteed to refuse exactly one of the two identical writes.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace suffices (all three pieces are in the two files cited). Live confirmation: on a resumed draft at /letters/[id]/edit with network throttled, type a character and click 'Publish letter' within ~1.5s; watch two editPost POSTs race and one return the 'changed somewhere else' error — as a failure toast during a successful publish, or as a refused publish.

findings.title: Autosave never persists an audience-only change and can save a stale cityScope: audienceCity is missing from the autosave effect's deps
findings.expected: Changing the letter draft's audience ('Show to' city) is autosaved like content/title/images, since editPost was specifically extended (bug audit B-048) so a draft's saved audience always matches what the desk shows.
findings.actual: The autosave effect's deps are [content, title, images, postId] (line 367, eslint-disabled); audienceCity is read inside runAutosave (line 328, `fd.set("cityScope", audienceCity ?? "")`) from the closure of the last content-triggered run. So (a) picking or clearing an audience with no subsequent typing never schedules any autosave — the chrome keeps saying 'Saved' while the choice is unsaved, and abandoning the tab loses it (the B-048 scenario returns: a draft that looks scoped publishes to everyone on resume, or vice versa); (b) a timer armed by a keystroke before the audience change fires with the OLD audienceCity and writes the stale scope to the row.
findings.argument: Deps array at line 367 omits audienceCity while the payload at line 328 sends it unconditionally; the effect closure freezes its value between content changes. Only an explicit Publish/Save (line 662, reads current state) persists the fresh value.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace, plus a browser step: open a resumed draft, wait for 'Saved', change the audience chip only, wait 5s (no autosave request fires — check the network panel), close the tab, reopen the draft: the audience is back to its previous value.

findings.title: Letters desk loses everything typed since the last 2.5s idle pause on navigate/close: no flush on unmount, no beforeunload/pagehide, and resumed drafts have no local belt except on save failure
findings.expected: A letter mid-write survives the writer leaving: the B-043 'crash net' promises 'the browser keeps a copy... so a close or a crash during an outage does not take them', and the desk chrome says 'Saved'.
findings.actual: Both the autosave (resumed drafts, line 313) and the localStorage belt (fresh letters, line 265) fire only after 2.5 seconds of idle, and each timer restarts on every keystroke and is cleared by the effect cleanup on unmount (line 364) without flushing. There is no beforeunload/pagehide/visibilitychange handler anywhere in src (grep-confirmed: only motion.tsx listens to visibilitychange). For a resumed draft, writeLocalDraft runs ONLY in runAutosave's failure branch (line 354) — during normal typing nothing but React state holds the delta. So: write fluently (each keystroke <2.5s apart), then click 'All letters', the browser Back button, or close the tab — every word since the last ≥2.5s pause is gone silently, while the chrome still shows 'Saved' from the previous flush.
findings.argument: The only writers of the draft row / localStorage are the idle-debounced timers; unmount cleanup (line 363-365, and 266-267 for the belt) cancels the pending write instead of executing it, and no page-lifecycle event is wired to flush. The catch-up answer surface has the same shape one tier down (answer-card.tsx flushes only on blur/advance; a tab close with focus still in the field saves nothing).
findings.proofPlan: Browser step on a throwaway draft: type a sentence continuously, immediately click 'All letters' (or close the tab), reopen the draft — the sentence is absent and localStorage has no rv:letter-draft entry for it. Fix-shape check: flush in the effect cleanup and add a pagehide handler that calls writeLocalDraft synchronously.
findings.taxonomy: missing debounce flush on unmount / data loss window

findings.title: Comment hearts, letter heart/bookmark, and catch-up entry hearts have no in-flight guard: a double-tap desyncs the heart from the database
findings.expected: One like toggle in flight at a time. post-card.tsx:148-156 documents exactly why and carries likeBusy/bookmarkBusy refs ('two calls still race to decide the final state, and the heart would settle wherever the slower one landed'); photo-love-button.tsx:22 copies that guard.
findings.actual: Three sibling implementations lack the guard: CommentItem.handleLike (comments-section.tsx:581-591), LetterEngagement.handleLike and handleBookmark (letter-engagement.tsx:40-60), and EntryLoveButton.handleToggle (entry-love-button.tsx:31-41, whose header comment cites LetterEngagement as its model, propagating the unguarded shape). A double-tap — the Instagram reflex on a heart — fires two concurrent toggle actions. Server-side (toggleCommentLike/toggleLike, feed/actions.ts:626/1308) each call is individually idempotent (delete-first, unique-violation-tolerant), but two interleaved calls are order-nondeterministic: both deleteManys can run before either create, so both 'create', one absorbs the P2002, and both return liked:true while the UI's second optimistic flip shows unliked. The heart then reads wrong until reload (and the wrong state may have minted a like notification).
findings.argument: No busy ref, no disabled state, and the optimistic flip re-renders fast enough that the second tap computes the opposite toggle from the first — client intends net-zero, server may settle at net-one (or vice versa when unliking). The codebase's own B-040/M35 notes record this class as empirically real, which is why the two guarded siblings exist.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step with a test account: throttle to Slow 3G, double-tap a comment heart, reload — compare the heart/count against what was shown before reload. Code-diff check: add the same likeBusy ref the post card carries to the three files.

findings.title: Collection 'Load more' lacks the stale-response generation guard its two siblings have: a filter change mid-flight stitches two result sets together
findings.expected: A page fetched under old filters is dropped when it lands after the filters changed — the exact M36/Low-75 fix that post-feed.tsx (listGeneration, line 60) and directory-client.tsx (line 134) both carry, each with a comment naming this bug.
findings.actual: collection-client.tsx has no generation counter. handleLoadMore (lines 174-192) captures `page` and appends unconditionally: change When/Part-of-school/search/sort while page 2 is loading, the first-page effect (line 148) replaces photos with the new set, then the in-flight response appends the OLD query's page onto it (`setPhotos(prev => [...prev, ...data.photos])`, line 183) and adopts its hasMore/total/page — so the grid shows two different result sets interleaved, the count is wrong, and every later 'Load more' continues from the wrong page number against the new filters (offset pagination, so pages skip or repeat). There is also no id-dedupe (unlike the feed's comments/directory), so an overlapping page renders duplicate `key={p.id}` tiles.
findings.argument: The two guarded implementations exist in the same codebase with comments citing audits M36 and Low 75; this third copy of the pattern predates or missed that fix. Offset (`page`) pagination amplifies it: `setPage(next)` after a stale append commits the old sequence position to the new query.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: on /collection with enough photos for 2+ pages, throttle the network, click 'Load more', immediately change the When filter; watch the grid grow with photos that do not match the new filter and the result count disagree with what is shown. Code fix mirrors post-feed's listGeneration ref.

findings.title: Feed and profile 'Load more' have no synchronous re-entry guard and no id-dedupe: a double-tap appends the same page twice
findings.expected: A second activation while a page is in flight is a no-op. The codebase treats the state-only `disabled` as insufficient — audit M35 (create-post-form.tsx:159, comments-section.tsx:101) records that 'disabled only takes effect on the next render' and that a click-plus-Enter or key repeat empirically reached an action twice; comments-section guards its pager with loadingMoreRef and dedupes by id, directory-client dedupes by id.
findings.actual: PostFeed.handleLoadMore (lines 170-195) and ProfileAuthorFeed.handleLoadMore (profile-author-feed.tsx:78-94) rely solely on `disabled={loadingMore}` set via setState, and append with no dedupe (`setPosts(prev => [...prev, ...data.posts])`, line 187). Two activations before the re-render (double-tap on a janky phone, held Enter on the focused button) fetch the same cursor twice and append the page twice: every post on it renders twice with duplicate React keys (`key={post.id}`), which also feeds auto-animate duplicate keys.
findings.argument: Both calls read the same `cursor` state (not yet advanced) so they fetch identical pages; the generation check only rejects cross-query staleness, not same-query duplicates. The two sibling paginators that dedupe prove the risk was recognized and this copy missed it.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: throttle network on /feed with 10+ posts, rapidly double-activate 'Load more' (Enter key twice on the focused button); observe duplicated posts and the duplicate-key console error. Fix is the loadingMoreRef + seen-set shape comments-section already carries.

findings.title: Message composer and Collection contribute dialog keep state-only double-submit guards the M35 audit already ruled insufficient
findings.expected: Actions that create a row per invocation are guarded with a synchronous ref, per the M35 fix applied to the post composer (submittingRef, create-post-form.tsx:162), comments (comments-section.tsx:106), and the catch-up create form (create-catchup-form.tsx:63) — the comment there records a double comment 'with two notifications' happening through the state-only guard.
findings.actual: MessageComposer.handleSend (message-composer.tsx:90-92) checks only `canSend` (closure over `sending` state); Cmd/Ctrl+Enter key-repeat plus the Send click can reach startThread twice, filing two identical admin threads. ContributeDialog.handleSubmit (contribute-dialog.tsx:118-120) checks only `submitting` state; a double-click submits two presign+contribute rounds, creating two identical pending Collection photos for the moderators.
findings.argument: Same mechanism M35 documents: setState guards only bind on the next render, and the project's own empirical record says the gap is reachable. Consequences here are duplicates that humans must clean up (an admin sees the same message twice; a moderator reviews the same photo twice), not data corruption — hence Low.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace against the three ref-guarded siblings; live: hold Cmd+Enter for a beat in the message box on a test account and count the created threads at /messages.

findings.title: Removing a catch-up photo while another photo is uploading resurrects the removed one (stale images closure)
findings.expected: The photo list after an upload completes reflects any removals made while the upload was in flight.
findings.actual: handleFiles closes over the `images` prop at click time and, on completion, calls `onChange([...images, ...(data.urls as string[])])` (line 81). The per-photo Remove button stays enabled during an upload (only the Add tile is disabled, line 127), so: attach photo B while photo A is uploading? — concretely: with A already attached, start uploading B, remove A during the flight; when B's upload lands, onChange spreads the stale closure that still contains A, putting A back. The parent then autosaves the resurrected list (answer-experience.tsx persist), so the server row re-includes the photo the member deleted.
findings.argument: Stale closure over a controlled prop across an await; the parent's per-prompt save queue serializes the writes but cannot repair the wrong payload. Window is the upload duration — meaningful on a slow phone with a large photo.
findings.proofPlan: Browser step: on an answer with one photo, throttle uploads, add a second photo, remove the first while 'Adding...' shows; when the upload finishes both photos are present again. Fix shape: pass an updater or recompute from the freshest prop via a ref.

findings.title: Composer preview object URLs are never revoked on successful post or unmount
findings.expected: Every URL.createObjectURL is paired with a revoke when the preview is discarded (removeImage does this at line 631).
findings.actual: On successful post, setPreviews([]) (line 725) drops the array without revoking the object URLs created at line 606, and nothing revokes on unmount; each posted photo's original File stays pinned by a live blob URL for the SPA session. Since previews are deliberately created from the full-resolution originals (up to 20MB each) and the app is a long-lived single-page session, the registry grows with every photo post. File-backed blob URLs mostly pin disk-backed handles rather than heap, so the cost is bookkeeping and handle lifetime, not an OOM — which is why this is Low and not Medium.
findings.argument: Asymmetric lifecycle: creation at line 606 (URL.createObjectURL(original)), revocation only in removeImage; the success path and the component teardown both skip it.
findings.proofPlan: Code trace; optional live check via chrome://blob-internals after posting three photos and navigating away — the entries persist.

findings.title: skipTrailingSlashRedirect is on with no manual trailing-slash handling, so every URL with a trailing slash 404s
findings.expected: A request to /feed/, /about/, /directory/ or any other app path with a trailing slash is normalized (Next's default installs an internal permanent redirect '/:path+/' -> '/:path+') and renders the page.
findings.actual: skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true (set for the PostHog /ingest capture endpoint in commit 86d5475) removes that internal redirect for the WHOLE site, and src/proxy.ts adds no replacement: a signed-in member visiting /feed/ passes the proxy (NextResponse.next()) and the router finds no matching route, rendering the 404 page; a signed-out visitor to /privacy/ or /login/ passes the publicPaths prefix check (pathname.startsWith(path + "/") matches the bare trailing slash) and also lands on a 404, while /feed/ signed-out bounces to /login?next=/feed/ and then 404s after sign-in.
findings.argument: node_modules/next/dist/lib/load-custom-routes.js:529 shows the automatic '/:path+/' -> '/:path+' redirect is only unshifted when !config.skipTrailingSlashRedirect; the installed proxy.md docs (line ~229 and the example that follows) state the app must then apply trailing-slash handling inside the proxy itself, and src/proxy.ts (full read, lines 107-312) contains no endsWith('/') handling of any kind. Nothing else in the repo normalizes paths. bugs.md item 5b covers signed-out unknown paths generally but not this distinct mechanism, and the Settled list has no trailing-slash entry.
findings.proofPlan: With the dev server up: curl -sI http://localhost:3000/about/ (public page) and, with a session cookie, GET http://localhost:3000/feed/ — expect 404 rather than a 308 to the slashless path. Or one live check: curl -sI https://rishivalley.space/privacy/. The fix direction (for the fixing session, not this one) is the docs' own pattern: redirect slash-suffixed paths to their slashless form in proxy.ts for everything except /ingest.

findings.title: Mail-drain lease (45s) is shorter than a worst-case drain pass (~80s+), so concurrent passes resume exactly when Resend degrades
findings.expected: One drain pass fleet-wide at a time — the QueueLease exists specifically because parallel passes produced a self-inflicted 429 storm against Resend's ~2 req/s limit (bug audit B-072), and its expiry should outlive any pass that is still legitimately working.
findings.actual: DRAIN_LEASE_MS = 45_000 but a pass is bounded only by BATCH (8, email-queue.ts:92) x SEND_TIMEOUT_MS (10_000, src/lib/email.ts:77) plus ~5 DB round trips per iteration — worst case well over 80s. The lease is taken once in drainMailQueue (line 660) and never renewed mid-pass, and drainWithLease never re-checks that it still holds it; when Resend is slow or timing out (precisely the B-072 condition), the lease expires at 45s while the first pass is on send #5, another page view's after() takes the lease, and two (then three) passes run concurrently — each 10s-timeout on the first pass burning a slot while new passes pile on, spending deferrals (MAX_DEFERRALS) faster across rows and pushing reset/verify rows toward terminal 'failed' during a provider incident. The per-row claim in claimAndSend prevents same-row double-sends, so the damage is rate-storm plus accelerated deferral burn, not duplicates. Relatedly, the whole pass runs inside after() with no maxDuration export anywhere, so at the platform duration cap a mid-send kill leaves rows in 'sending' — self-healed by the 2-minute stale sweep, with the double-send edge the code already documents at writeIfStillClaimed.
findings.argument: The comment on DRAIN_LEASE_MS ('Comfortably longer than BATCH sends at Resend's pace') sizes the lease for the happy path (~0.5s/send) and mis-describes the bounded worst case: sendMail races a 10s timeout per send (email.ts:217), render() adds a mint (2 writes), and the loop runs dailyBudget (2 counts) + findFirst + claim + attempts-read per iteration. 8 x 10.5s ≈ 84s > 45s. takeDrainLease (line 612) only fences on expiresAt <= now, so expiry alone hands the lease over while the holder is alive and unfrozen.
findings.proofPlan: Pure arithmetic on constants already in the file — a validator can confirm by reading email-queue.ts:92/602 and email.ts:77. A live proof without touching real mail: unit-style trace or a stubbed sendMail that sleeps 10s with 3+ queued rows and two concurrent drainMailQueue calls 46s apart, observing both hold 'the' lease.
